Introduction

It is year 39 of the Era Imperium, a new age for the continent of Edhela following the Great War that ravaged its lands. To the west, the Republic of Oriande is steadily rebuilding, its forces crippled in the war, and its Senate now embroiled in heated discussions about the future of republican rule under an Empire. Southward, Thalore, the home of Wizardry, kept its grand cities mostly unscathed by conflict, but wounded pride festers among Edhela’s most powerful mages. In the frigid Northern Sea, the Meian Isles have bowed to the Empire, seeking its protection and aid against marauding Giants, yet the fate of their ancient polytheistic culture grows unsteady beneath religious Arysian imperial rule. And the Holy Kingdom of Paerdland, once a pawn for Edhela's scheming powers and the very stage of its bloodiest war, now sits proudly at the Empire's heart—a new arena for its feudal lords to vie for relevance and power.

This Era Imperium has ushered in an unprecedented age of connectivity for Edhela. For the first time, knowledge and goods flow freely across mountains, reaching even commoners, while culture and ideas spread at an unmatched pace. For almost four decades, peace has reigned under the first Emperor. While many hope this heralds a long, stabilizing dynasty, others yearn for freedom from an overlord they never consented to serve.

As the Era Imperium approaches its fourth decade since the Great War's end, the powers of Edhela, once crippled by war, have had time to regain their strength. New ideas have taken root and spread, while stubborn grudges, wounded pride, and long-simmering conspiracies have had ample time to brew beneath the surface. Though many believe Edhela has never been more peaceful, the signs of a turning tide are unmistakable to those who understand history's currents. The next conflict to scar the lands of Edhela is not a matter of if, but when…

In Ascension, you and your fellow players embody a party of individuals, united by a common cause, striving to direct—or at least influence—the rapidly flowing river of Edhelan history through politics and warfare. You will forge alliances, uncover conspiracies, and battle those who oppose your cause. Though you may begin with little renown, in time, you could lead an army whose name echoes throughout Edhela…

Playing Ascension

In this book are the rules and tools you will need in order to play a game of Ascension.

Part One of this book, Characters in Ascension, has an explanation of each element that makes up a character as well as the lifepath: Ascension’s system of character creation.

Part Two, Playing the Game, is about narrative play and social conflict in Ascension.

Part Three, Going to Battle, has all the rules for small-scale combat.

Part Four, Items and Enhancements, contains all of the special abilities and gear your characters will take with them to battle.

Part Five, Armies and Mass Combat, has all the rules for mass combat and using armies in Ascension.

Part Six, Gamemastering, has all the tools and advice needed for GMs running the game, like setting encounter objectives and making non-player characters.

And Part Seven, Lore, contains a primer on Edhela, Ascension’s primary setting.

What You Need

In order to play a game of Ascension, you’ll need some dice, character sheets, and a group of friends to play with. Ascension functions best with a group of 4-6 players, including one Game Master (or GM), whose role is to facilitate the game, guide the story, and adjudicate the rules.

Ascension uses two kinds of dice: twenty-sided dice (d20s) and six-sided dice (Challenge Dice or [CD]). The rules will often refer to a “dice pool” which is the group of dice, made up of either d20s or [CD], that you roll at once for accomplishing a Task or determining a Task’s effectiveness respectively. It will be helpful for every player, as well as the GM, to have at least two d20s and several [CD], though the more the better, as players may roll up to 5d20 or 10+ [CD] at a time.

Challenge Dice are a special type of six sided dice used in Ascension primarily for determining the amount of damage dealt in combat, but also when determining the progress of negotiations or longer Extended Tasks. Each CD has four unique faces for determining results—a face with a 1, a face with a 2, two blank faces, and two faces with a unique symbol to denote an Effect, shown in this book as a [!]. If you do not have any challenge dice, you may instead use a regular 6-sided die with 1 and 2 treated as normal, 3 and 4 treated as blanks, and 5 and 6 treated as Effects.

For running combat scenarios, you will also want a hex or square-tiled battlemap and tokens to represent units on the battlefield.

Narrative Play and Combat

When playing Ascension, it’s important to know and be able to identify the two spheres of gameplay: free-form narrative play and combat.

During narrative play, characters can act naturally, pursuing the story without a rigid structure to how they can take actions. Interpersonal conflicts, forging alliances, investigating mysteries, and strategizing for upcoming battles are just a few examples of the kind of scenes encapsulated by narrative play. The majority of your campaign’s story and character interactions will likely occur in narrative play.

Combat, however, is a more structured kind of gameplay, where characters take turns taking actions, often with the goal of defeating enemy combatants. Ascension has two kinds of combat: small-scale combat, where characters fight other characters without the support of their army; and mass combat, where in addition to facing enemy combatants, they are also fighting against an enemy army, and must strategically command their own forces on the battlefield in order to lead their side to victory.

While the rules of Ascension assume that each campaign will utilize both combat and narrative play, there is no “right” way to play the game. Both sets of rules exist for your group to use (or not use) as you see fit!

Tasks

Characters in Ascension are presumed to be competent and skilled individuals, who can overcome certain obstacles and challenges with ease. However, when the success of a character’s endeavor is in question, or in a situation where failure might have interesting consequences, your character will attempt a Task in order to determine what happens next.

Attempting a Task involves rolling two or more d20s and comparing the results to your target number, which is determined by adding together the values of the Attribute and Skill needed to accomplish the Task (for example, a Task to pickpocket someone would use Coordination + Intrigue; if your Coordination was 10 and your Intrigue was 3, the target number would be 13). Dice with results that are lower than or equal to your target number are successes, and dice with results higher than your target number are failures. Each die that rolls a 1 is a critical success, and counts as two successes instead of just one, and each die that rolls a 20 is a critical failure, creating a Complication in addition to the normal failed result. If the number of successes rolled is equal to or more than the Difficulty of the Task (set by the GM), then you have succeeded on the Task and will achieve your desired result. If the number of successes is less than the Difficulty of the Task, then you have failed the Task and will suffer the relevant consequences.

A character’s chances of success or failure can also be modified by the character’s unique abilities; players spending Momentum, a shared resource between the players; or by the GM spending Threat, a GM-only resource.

All Tasks are resolved in this way: by comparing the results of your dice roll to your target number, and this rule is the basis for resolving the outcomes of most actions in Ascension. For more detailed rules about Tasks, see Part Two: Playing the Game.

Rolling Challenge Dice

Challenge Dice or [CD], described above, are used in many circumstances after a successful task such as determining damage in combat, progress in an Extended Task, or earning favor in a negotiation. While regular six-sided dice may be used as challenge dice, the rolled faces give different values from usual.

[CD] Face

When a 1 or a 2 is rolled, their value is added to the total result directly. Blanks do not contribute any value to the result, and are considered a value of 0. When Effects ([!]) are rolled, they add 1 to the result and trigger any effects, if relevant. Usually these effects are damage effects, defined by the weapon or talent used during the attack. However, in non-combat scenarios, some [CD] uses may still have certain effects trigger upon an effect rolled. If there are no effects applicable to the roll, then rolling an effect only counts as a 1 for the total value.

Golden Rule: Specific before General

The golden rule of Ascension that always applies is that specific rules will always overrule a general rule. Many special abilities granted by things like Talents will have specific rules that change or break the way a general rule works, and in the event that a specific rule contradicts a general rule, the specific rule wins. For example, all characters can only use the Opportunity Attack reaction once per round, but with the Hold the Line 2 Talent, a character may use the Opportunity Attack reaction more than once per round.

Part One: Characters in Ascension

Chapter One: Player Characters

When playing Ascension, the primary force driving the story are the characters you create and the actions they take during the course of the narrative. These characters are protagonists, whose decisions are central to the campaign and shape its events, and each element that makes up a player character is a representative of the unique traits and abilities that make up a person and allow them to influence the world around them. This chapter contains the basics of the mechanics that make up each player character and how to use them as you play this game (for guidance on making characters as a GM, see Chapter Twelve: Running the Game).

Anatomy of a Character

Characters in Ascension are made up of the following elements: Traits, Values, Attributes, Skills, Focuses, and Talents.

Traits

Traits are a description of a persistent or permanent part of a character’s identity or existence, summed up in a single word or short phrase. The role of a Trait is to define what a character is and, when invoked in play, affect what they do and how well they can do them. When faced with a Task in which a character’s Trait might be relevant (either advantageously or otherwise), the player or GM can invoke that Trait in order to gain a 1 Momentum or Threat discount on Creating an Advantage/Complication.

Traits are neutral, objective facts about a character, and they are obtained during the character creation process. Each choice you make on each step of your character’s lifepath creates a Trait; your character’s social class, upbringing, education, career, and their life events are traits that you and your GM can invoke during play. For example, a character with the Trait “Commoner” may invoke their trait to create an Advantage, spending only 1 Momentum to lower the Difficulty on a Task to try to ingratiate themself to a character who hates nobles. On the flipside, a GM could invoke that character’s Commoner trait in order to create a Complication, spending only 1 Threat to raise the Difficulty on a Task to convince a guard that they should be let into the palace.

In addition to the Traits gained from each stage of the lifepath, each character has a Defining Feature, which is a unique Trait that you choose at the end of character creation. A Defining Feature is exactly what it says on the tin: it’s a short phrase or descriptor that sums up a defining characteristic about your character. Because this is a Defining Feature, it is unlikely to change during play, but if something happens that would alter your Defining Feature, you should consult your GM in order to change it.

Occasionally, further Traits may be acquired during play, from physical or psychological changes a character might incur after a traumatic experience, or as the result of a change in status. For example, a character might gain the Trait “One-eyed” after suffering an injury in battle, or they might gain the Trait “Married” if their character gets married. Though Traits are objective facts, they may also change as your character changes. A married character whose spouse dies during the campaign might lose the Trait “Married” and gain the Trait “Widowed.” Additional Traits beyond your starting ones must be approved by your GM before being used.

Values

Values, as opposed to Traits, are statements that describe what a character believes. These are always subjective, as they reflect what your character thinks and feels about the world they exist in, and can be changed in play as your character’s beliefs are challenged by their experiences.

Values are created during the process of character creation, as certain stages in Lifepath Creation prompt you to come up with an attitude, belief, or conviction of your character as they’ve been shaped by an element or stage in their life. Values are not simple opinions about a character’s preferences, but are the bedrock of a character’s belief system, the values that define who they are as a person and why they behave the way they do. A character who has lost an important person in their life and been jaded by it might have the Value: “Love is weakness by another name. I’m best on my own.” But if experiencing loss instead made them more determined to persevere, they might have the Value: “I will fight to keep the love that I have.”

While all Values are reflections in some way of the relationship between a character and the world around them, sometimes a Value might reflect a relationship between your character and someone else. These Values do not need to be positive—grudges and old resentments towards someone make for great Values—but they do need to be significant. The Value “I like my little brother” could be a statement about a character’s relationship with their brother, but doesn’t say much about who they are as a person or what they believe. “I will do whatever it takes to keep my little brother safe” as a Value conveys something significant about that character and how their relationship with their brother has shaped them and their behavior.

Just like our beliefs and convictions in real life, a character’s Values are not meant to be static. Values drive a character and reflect their deeply held beliefs or motivations, but as a character grows and gains new experiences, they may begin to feel differently about the world and shift their perspective. When characters would significantly change or challenge their Values, they may gain mechanical benefits (see Chapter Three: Basic Rules for rules about Determination).

Sample Values

A good ruler prioritizes the well-being of their people above everything, even themselves.

The pen is greater than the sword.

A good ruler upholds the law.

The only family you can ever truly trust are those with whom you share blood.

Sometimes battles must be lost in order to win wars.

Obedience to the chain of command is the cornerstone of a functioning army and society.

I have a responsibility to uphold my father's legacy.

Not every rule needs to be followed.

Love can transcend the divide of status or wealth.

It is the duty of the strong to protect the weak.

The ends often justify the means.

I owe my first allegiance to the Church.

Everyone can be bought if you're willing to pay.

I will protect my family at all costs.

Being behind the throne is often better than being on it.

My life is not worth more than anyone else’s.

If the law is unjust, it can only be just to break it.

A true noble is honest and benevolent.

The only virtue that matters is strength.

Never show weakness in front of an enemy.

Attributes

Every character in Ascension has seven Attributes which represent their physical and mental capabilities. These attributes are Agility, Awareness, Brawn, Coordination, Faith, Presence, and Reason. Each Attribute has a number (called a rating) that reflects your character’s aptitude in activities using that Attribute, with higher numbers meaning greater ability, where lower numbers mean lesser ability. For player characters, these attributes will range from 6 to 12, with 7-8 representing average capabilities.

Sometimes you may encounter situations where more than one Attribute may be applicable to the Task being attempted, or where you may wish to use an Attribute instead of the one that the GM has prompted. When faced with such situations, the context of the situation and the Task you’re attempting as well as the specific way your character is going about attempting the Task will determine which Attribute is most applicable. For example, when attempting to persuade a priest, you might reasonably use Presence to charm him with your demeanor and personality; Faith to impress him with your conviction and strength of belief; or Reason to make an argument based in logic and knowledge of theology. Ultimately, the choice of Attribute will be determined by your GM, who has the final say.

Agility:

Agility is a mixture of speed, balance, and muscle memory, and is responsible for much of a character’s movement and similar activities.

Brawn:

Brawn is your character’s fortitude and ability to endure physical hardship, as well as their ability to employ force. It also encompasses your character’s endurance, and their general health and physical conditioning.

Coordination:

Coordination is your character’s control of their body: their fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and accuracy.

Awareness:

Awareness is your character’s ability to notice things that are not readily apparent, such as spatial awareness, seeing through deceit, and discovering the enemy’s weaknesses.

Reason:

Reason is your character’s ability to apply logic, intellect, and the known facts to a situation.

Faith:

Faith is your character’s sense of self and their place in the world, as well as their mental fortitude and strength of conviction.

Presence:

Presence is your character’s ability to command a room, and to use their words and personality to draw attention and sway the opinions of others.

Skills

In addition to their Attributes, every character in Ascension has six skills, which represent the broad areas of expertise that they are the most learned and trained in. These Skills are Skirmish, Authority, Diplomacy, Study, Medicine, and Intrigue. Each Skill has a rating from 0-5 (though player characters will have at least 1 in each Skill).

Skills are combined with Attributes in order to perform Tasks, and as such can be used to attempt a variety of activities.

Skill

Meaning

0

Untrained, unskilled, lacking in innate aptitude.

1

Basic training, rudimentary skill, or a raw but undeveloped aptitude.

2

Professional competence, from a combination of training and talent.

3

Experienced and well-trained, or an aptitude developed through study and training.

4

Excellence, achievable through dedication and experience.

5

Exceptional, often a combination of intense training, hard-won experience, and natural aptitude.

Skirmish:

Skirmish is your character’s martial prowess and general combat training for how well prepared you are for a fight, or for general feats of physical activity. It might use:

  • Agility to wield a sword deftly in battle or to climb up a wall.
  • Brawn to grapple an enemy, to attack with an axe, or to carry a heavy payload.
  • Coordination to attack with a spear or to stay astride a mount while in battle.
  • Awareness to defend against attacks from range or to attack with a bow.
  • Reason to identify the participants of a battle by studying the aftermath, to devise a plan for a dangerous situation, or to make an attack with Arcane Magic.
  • Faith to steel yourself against the clamor of battle, or to make an attack using Light Magick.
  • Presence to intimidate an enemy to lay down arms, or to make a demoralizing attack.

Authority:

Authority is your character’s ability to lead, to manage an organization or estate, and to convince others of their ability to do so. It might use:

  • Agility to lead a charge into battle on foot, or to have a crowd get out of your way when you are rushing through it.
  • Brawn to impress subordinates with feats of strength, to intimidate someone into obeying your commands with physical force, or to display undeterred resolve to followers while injured.
  • Coordination to guide followers through difficult terrain or dense foliage.
  • Awareness to assess the fighting capacity of your troops, to gauge the loyalty of a vassal, or to determine how to convince someone to listen to you.
  • Reason to create a cunning battle plan, to efficiently delegate the servants of a household, or to build a compelling legal argument.
  • Faith to give allies hope when all seems lost, or to appeal to the ideals, religion, or philosophy of your subordinates.
  • Presence to rally or inspire others during a difficult situation, to command the attention or respect of someone else, or to command troops in battle.

Diplomacy

Diplomacy is your character’s ability to navigate a social situation or impress others, as well as your general ability to be persuasive and charming. It might use:

  • Agility to perform feats of physical performance to wow a crowd, like juggling or sword-dancing.
  • Brawn to win over a foreign commander’s friendship with a friendly spar, to intimidate using your strength and stature, and to convince others that you are a capable warrior.
  • Coordination to carefully navigate a tense political discussion without inadvertently causing offense, to calm the room during a tense situation, or to dance with a partner in a social setting.
  • Awareness to see through deceit, or to identify personality traits of other characters.
  • Reason to appeal to logic in a diplomatic situation, and to convince others of your own intellectual prowess.
  • Faith to appeal to the beliefs of others in a diplomatic situation, and to convince others of your own conviction.
  • Presence to persuade someone to help you, to make a convincing argument, or to woo a target of affection.

Study:

Study is your character’s academic knowledge, training in professional or artistic pursuits, and your ability to recall and learn information. It might use:

  • Agility to perform a well rehearsed acrobatics routine or to hurriedly take the fastest route possible through a city.
  • Brawn to perform accurate research while fatigued or injured or to build a heavy and complicated construct.
  • Coordination to perform a delicate magick ritual, to solve a complicated puzzle that requires precise manipulation, or to paint a painting.
  • Awareness to identify magick from watching someone cast it, or to identify subtle details of a person’s character by visual observation.
  • Reason to make inferences about events using your scholarly understanding, to understand a magick spell in an old tome, or to recall information you may have previously studied.
  • Faith to recall religious knowledge, to quote religious texts, to cite ideological works or arguments, and to identify holy and unholy magick and creatures.
  • Presence to win over an audience during a philosophical debate, or to explain in an engaging manner complex magickal theory to someone without magickal knowledge.

Medicine:

Medicine is your character’s training in administering medical care and administer treatments to the sick and the wounded, as well as your knowledge of poisons and of culinary skills. It might use:

  • Agility to swiftly relocate a patient or evacuate them from a battle.
  • Brawn to resist poisons or to restrain a patient in distress.
  • Coordination to perform medical procedures like surgery.
  • Awareness to diagnose a patient at a glance, to identify the cause of death of a cadaver, or to find a rare ingredient.
  • Reason to diagnose and treat a patient through research and examination, to cook a delicious meal, to craft a healing tonic, or to brew a deadly poison.
  • Faith to provide treatment via therapeutic or magickal means, or to convince others a treatment is the best course of action.
  • Presence for bedside manner and to soothe a patient in distress, or to communicate a patient’s situation to them or others to convince them of a course of action.

Intrigue:

Intrigue is your character’s training in gathering and concealing information, as well as performing actions while undetected. It might use:

  • Agility to hide from enemies, move silently, and slip into an area unnoticed.
  • Brawn to hold out while under interrogation, or withstand torture.
  • Coordination to build traps or snares, to pickpocket, or to subtly swipe something from a table.
  • Awareness to search for hidden figures or traps, to determine whether someone is in disguise, or to investigate an area for evidence after a crime.
  • Reason to come up with and write in codes, or to break the codes of others.
  • Faith to interrogate criminals and others you find reprehensible (e.g. inquisiting heretics).
  • Presence to tell a convincing lie, or withhold information without looking suspicious.

Focuses

Where a character’s Skills are broad, Focuses allow you to give your character unique specializations and expertise in specific activities or areas of study. Focuses are not bound to any specific Skill or Attribute, and characters may always use one of their Focuses when attempting a Task so long as the Focus is relevant to what you are trying to accomplish. For example, a character with a Focus in “Archery” could apply their Focus to a Skirmish Task to shoot a bow, or to an Authority Task to give a division of bowmen an order. Much like with Attributes, you may sometimes be faced with a Task where multiple of your Focuses could be relevant, or where you’d like to use a Focus that may not seem obviously applicable. In these situations, consider the context and your approach to the Task, but ultimately your GM has final say over whether your Focus applies or not.

Each player character starts with six Focuses, which should each be a specific area of interest narrower than their Skills, but not so specific that they don’t come up in play. For example, “Talking” is a focus that is way too broad, whereas “Fixing door hinges” is a focus that is probably too specific to be used frequently. If you’re not sure whether a Focus would be too broad or too specific for use, consult your GM.

Talents

While every character—player or NPC—will have Attributes, Skills, and Focuses, Talents are what set player characters apart. Mechanically, Talents are specific advantages or abilities that players can use under specific circumstances, and may often have requirements that must be fulfilled before they can be selected, such as a certain number in an Attribute or Skill. Talents are split into two categories: Narrative Talents, which are Talents that can only be used during non-combat scenarios; and Combat Talents, which are Talents that can only be used in combat scenarios. For more, see Chapter Six: Talents.

Chapter Two: Lifepath Creation

Lifepath creation is the method of constructing a character who has been shaped by their environment and life events, which is represented in each step in the lifepath process. The lifepath consists of six steps, with each step allowing for choices to be made that give characters different abilities and add to their Attributes and Skills.

Starting Point: Each character starts with a score of 6 in each Attribute and a 1 in each Skill, which will increase as they go along the lifepath. Though Attributes and Skills can go up to 12 and 5 respectively, characters begin with lower ratings to allow room for them to grow. When you begin, your character can have no more than 11 in any Attribute, and can only have one Attribute at 11, and can have no more than 4 in each Skill, and can only have one Skill at 4. If your character has scores above these limits during lifepath creation, you will correct it in the Finishing Touches step.

Lifepath Overview

  1. Social Class
  1. +1 to two attributes
  2. A Value
  1. Upbringing
  1. A Focus
  2. +1 to two Attributes
  3. +1 to one Skill
  4. A Value
  1. Education
  1. A Focus
  2. +1 to two Attributes or +2 to one Attribute
  3. +1 to one Skill
  1. Career
  1. Three points to spend on 2 or 3 Attributes
  2. +2 to one skill, +1 to two others
  3. Two Focuses
  1. Life Events
  1. Everyone gets two life events. Each life event taken gives you the following:
  1. +1 to an Attribute
  2. A Value
  3. A Focus
  1. Finishing Touches
  1. Two Narrative Talents and Four Combat Talents
  2. +1 to three Attributes
  3. +1 to two Skills
  4. Personal Details

Step One: Social Class

Though not all nations and societies have the same kind of social ordering, many nations and cultures have social hierarchies consisting primarily of commoners and nobility. These social classes are determined by a character’s parents and the social class that they’ve been born into, and dictate much of a character’s life and perspective. Because social class is a construct that is imposed upon each character by the society they live in, there are no features or abilities inherent to a person of any particular class. However, social class can often limit a character’s choices when it comes to what kind of life they want to pursue, as well as limiting the ways they can interact with others and the society they live in. These class limitations are represented by a single Trait, either “noble” or “commoner”, and the effects of their social class can weigh heavily on a character with the skills and ambition for a path that their status would make difficult for them.

Each social class provides characters with a Value and two points to put into the two Attributes that are listed with that class. When choosing your character’s social class, you should pick the one that they were born into. Of course, within this simplified breakdown of class there are many complications, exceptions, and deviations from the rule (e.g. a nobleman’s son who’s run away from home and settled as a farmer). If you wish to create a character that moves or has moved between these categories or perhaps exists outside them, choose the class that best reflects how others would perceive your character at first glance.

While your character’s social class will automatically become a Trait, the legitimacy or, perhaps more importantly, the illegitimacy of one’s birth also functions as a Trait. Illegitimate children are often a source of shame for their parents (though this can also depend on the social status of the parents, as some nobles are so powerful they may feel above such judgements), and they are sometimes ignored, treated poorly, or even abandoned because of it. If your character was born out of wedlock, they gain the Trait “Illegitimate,” and though this may not be easily perceivable to others, it can impact your character’s experience in society and serves as a prompt for the Gamemaster to affect a character differently when they interact with others.

  • Commoner (Peasant) - The lowest on the hierarchy of social class, peasants are commoners who labor for a living. They typically don’t own any land, instead paying rent to landlords (usually minor nobility) in exchange for getting to live on the land and cultivate it. This social class also encompasses skilled laborers like bakers, blacksmiths, and leatherworkers, who learned trades from their parents or have been taken on as apprentices by other craftsmen. Most peasants live in small, rural villages or in the rural countryside where their farms are located, though there are also large populations of commoners in urban areas, where they work primarily as craftsmen and servants.
  • Attributes: +1 Faith, +1 Brawn
  • Value: The character gains a single Value, which should reflect how they perceive their place in the social hierarchy and the lessons they’ve learned as a result, or perhaps even a reflection on the social hierarchy itself and what morals the character does (or doesn’t) glean from it. Does the character accept their place in the hierarchy? Do they accept the system itself and its way of ordering society?
  • Example Values: Commoners must protect each other when the highborn won’t.
  • Commoner (Merchant) - Though still commoners, the merchant class exists higher on the social ladder than peasants due mainly to one thing: wealth. While laborers and craftsmen tend to be poor, those of the merchant class (bankers, artists, scholars, lawyers, priests, etc) are wealthy enough to own property and wield influence over politics and trade, and sometimes live in enough luxury as to resemble members of the nobility. Members of the merchant class live almost exclusively in cities where the industries and guilds that make their wealth are located.
  • Attributes: +1 Presence, +1 Reason
  • Value: The character gains a single Value, which should reflect how they perceive their place in the social hierarchy and the lessons they’ve learned as a result, or perhaps even a reflection on the social hierarchy itself and what morals the character does (or doesn’t) glean from it. Does the character accept their place in the hierarchy? Do they accept the system itself and its way of ordering society?
  • Example Values: I can prove I’m as good as any nobleman.
  • Petty Nobility - Above the common classes, but at the bottom of the nobility, the petty nobility is made up of minor nobles, often those who have been ennobled by a duke or monarch but without their own lands to control (e.g. knights, baronets, etc). These minor nobles are typically in the direct service of another, more noble family or lord, and as such their status as a noble is not guaranteed across generations, but rather is an earned title that can be easily lost.
  • Attributes: +1 Agility, +1 Brawn
  • Value: The character gains a single Value, which should reflect how they perceive their place in the social hierarchy and the lessons they’ve learned as a result, or perhaps even a reflection on the social hierarchy itself and what morals the character does (or doesn’t) glean from it. Does the character accept their place in the hierarchy? Do they accept the system itself and its way of ordering society?
  • Example Values: I owe a debt to Lord Fife, and I will repay it.
  • Landed Nobility - Landed nobility are powerful aristocrats who control their own territories and hold their own courts, though still owe their fealty to an overlord, typically a monarch. The titles and territories of the landed nobility—and responsibilities that come along with each—are typically passed down to their descendants, and so heirs and inheritance is a major pressure for these noble families. Because of how important descendants are when it comes to securing your dynasty and making political alliances via marriage, it’s not uncommon for the families of landed nobility to be rather large, with their wealth and greater access to magick and medicine allowing for the survival of more children than commoners.
  • Attributes: +1 Awareness, +1 Coordination
  • Value: The character gains a single Value, which should reflect how they perceive their place in the social hierarchy and the lessons they’ve learned as a result, or perhaps even a reflection on the social hierarchy itself and what morals the character does (or doesn’t) glean from it. Does the character accept their place in the hierarchy? Do they accept the system itself and its way of ordering society?
  • Example Values: The hierarchy of nobility is the natural order of things, and upholding it preserves peace.
  • Royalty - Obviously at the top of the social hierarchy, members of the royalty are the sovereigns of territories or nations, whose families have been invested with power by the divine right of kings, or merely by virtue of dynasty. Though members of the royalty are quite obviously above commoners and lesser nobles, they are in many ways beholden to those beneath them, as the security of a monarch’s reign is often dependent on the relative satisfaction of their subjects and the stability of their nation. Not all who belong to this class are necessarily kings or queens, as powerful and independent major nobles who don’t have an overlord can be considered royalty (For example, the Prince of Fnjoska is a royal, despite their title being technically equal to a duke).
  • Attributes: +1 Presence, +1 Faith
  • Value: The character gains a single Value, which should reflect how they perceive their place in the social hierarchy and the lessons they’ve learned as a result, or perhaps even a reflection on the social hierarchy itself and what morals the character does (or doesn’t) glean from it. Does the character accept their place in the hierarchy? Do they accept the system itself and its way of ordering society?
  • Example Values: It is better to be feared than loved.

Step Two: Upbringing

The nature of a person’s upbringing—their family, their surroundings, and the expectations of both—have a massive impact on a person, and a character’s early circumstances will shape the trajectory of the life that follows. Each upbringing gives characters two points to add to two Attributes. Which Attributes can be increased is determined by their specific upbringing and by whether or not your character accepted or rebelled against it. Characters also gain a single point to add to a single Skill, and a single Focus, which should relate in some way to the upbringing chosen.

After choosing your character’s upbringing, you will also get to decide whether they accepted or rebelled against that upbringing. Accepting an upbringing doesn’t have to mean that your character has to follow in the footsteps of their parents, but it will signify that whatever expectations or values that your character was brought up with are something that they are genuinely trying to live up to. For example, a character who accepts their religious upbringing might go on to be a devout priest, or they might choose a different career path but still remain a devout follower of the religion they were brought up in. On the flipside, a character who rebels against their upbringing is someone who rejects the expectations or values they were brought up with, and is trying to forge a path in opposition to their upbringing. This can mean choosing a career opposite to the career your character might have been expected to choose, or it can mean following in the path set up by your character’s upbringing but with a subversive or unique approach. For example, a character who rebels against their religious upbringing could still choose being a priest as their career path but might instead be a priest of a different religion or might secretly be an atheist. When you choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, you also give them a Value that reflects how they feel about their upbringing and how their worldview has been shaped by accepting or rebelling against it.

  • Agrarian: Your character was brought up in the countryside, working the land and tending livestock alongside their family. Kept mostly away from the bustling life of urbanity, your character grew up surrounded by more nature than people, and is no stranger to doing hard labor.
  • Attributes: Increase Brawn by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Skirmish or Medicine.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples include: Animal Handling, Athletics, Axes, Cooking, Farming, Home Medicine, Manual Labor, Tracking
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Courtly: Your character was brought up in a noble court, not as a true member of its gathered nobles, but as their servant. Whether a true servant—like a scullery maid or footman—or in a position of some privilege—like a lady-in-waiting or a court painter—your character’s place in court has been dependent on the patronage of someone of higher rank. As such, you’re familiar with the political games and intricacies of the nobility, and all too aware of the very real consequences that they have on the lives of the people below them.
  • Attributes: Increase Presence by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Diplomacy or Intrigue.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Astrology, Counseling, Eavesdropping, Etiquette, Estate Management, Oratory, Poetry, Philosophy
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Craftsman: Your character was brought up by artisans, taught the ins and outs of their craft as well as the details and politics of business and trade. Most artisans in well-populated areas are members of their local guild, a political entity organized by and for all the craftsmen of a specific trade, and as such, you know that there is more to a craftsman than just their trade—whether that be leatherworking, carpentry, or baking. After all, every artisan must also know how to sell their goods, gain patrons and clients, and navigate the complicated politics of the guild.
  • Attributes: Increase Coordination by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Diplomacy or Study.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Brewing, Construction, Glass-blowing, Map-making, Sculpture, Smithing, Tailoring, Woodworking
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Mercantile: Your character was brought up surrounded by wealth, though more than likely it was mostly not their own. Whether as a merchant or a banker (though the latter are often also the former), your character is familiar with the intricacies of finance and has experience interacting with people of all social classes.
  • Attributes: Increase Reason by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Intrigue or Study.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Bribery, Contracts, Estate Management, Finances, Haggling, Persuasion, Travel Logistics
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Military: Your character was brought up for the battlefield. Whether as a member of an esteemed mercenary family or as the young squire to a knight-commander, your character has grown up with the expectation that they would take up arms someday, following in the footsteps of the soldiers that helped raise them.
  • Attributes: Increase Brawn by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Authority or Skirmish.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Field Medicine, Hand-to-Hand Combat, Military Tactics, Mounted Combat, Polearms, Shields
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Nomadic: Your character wasn’t brought up in a single place, but traveled frequently and saw much of the world as they grew up. Being part of a wandering troupe—druidic communities, nomadic herders, traveling performers, and the like—has given your character a wide and varied experience of the world and the people and places in it, though they likely don’t have strong ties to any particular location.
  • Attributes: Increase Awareness by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Medicine or Skirmish
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Comedy, Flora Identification, Foraging, Foreign Languages, Hunting, Setting Traps, Theatrics
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Pariah: Your character was brought up on the edges of society, raised by people who couldn’t or refused to conform to normative societal standards. Living outside of society—the son of a disgraced priest, or the daughter of the local woodswitch, for example—has given your character a unique perspective on what most people find normal, though it may also make it more difficult for them to integrate or pass normally when among others.
  • Attributes: Increase Awareness by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Intrigue or Medicine
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Avoiding Trouble, Heresy, Herbal Medicine, Natural Magic, Philosophy, Reading People, Witchcraft
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Privileged: Your character is a member of a wealthy and privileged family and was brought up with few expectations. Whether their family were common born leaders of a vast trade empire or monarchs of an expansive kingdom, your character was raised secure in the knowledge that they would never need to truly work, as their family’s prosperity would always provide.
  • Attributes: Increase Presence by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Authority or Diplomacy
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Dancing, Etiquette, Finances, History, Law, Negotiation, Swords, Painting, Philosophy, Politics
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Religious: Your character was brought up in an extremely religious environment, such as a monastery, where their life was oriented around their community’s religious practices and beliefs. Likely cut off from the secular world, your character grew up incredibly familiar with religious teachings and the realm of the mystical.
  • Attributes: Increase Faith by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Authority or Study
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Composure, Painting, Philosophy, Proselytizing, Religious History, Theology, Translation
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Sailor: Your character grew up on a seafaring ship, traveling the world by oar and sail. Raised as part of a crew, your character is familiar with the hard work and routine necessary to keep a ship running, and has had lots of opportunities to see new and interesting places.
  • Attributes: Increase Agility by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Skirmish or Diplomacy.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Astronomy, Meteorology, Navigation, Ropes and Knots, Ship Maintenance, Ship Rigging
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Scholarly: Your character was raised in the world of the learned and esoteric. Whether they spent most of their life in a boarding school away from home, or were tutored intensely by family or mentors, your character was brought up with a considerable amount of book-learning and the expectations of scholarly pursuits.
  • Attributes: Increase Reason by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Study or Medicine.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Alchemy, Anatomy, Botany, Cartography, History, Law, Religious History, Research, Sketching
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.
  • Urchin: Your character wasn’t raised by anyone, and instead had to depend on their own wits and skills to get by without parents or family to look out for them. After growing up alone, your character has experience with the seedier, low-belly parts of the world, and years of practice have given them the street smarts necessary to survive on their own.
  • Attributes: Increase Agility by 1, then increase a second Attribute of your choice by 1.
  • Skill: Choose one of the following Skills and increase it by 1: Skirmish or Intrigue.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus for your character that relates to the skills and practices they would have gained over the course of their upbringing. Examples Include: Athletics, Blending In, Bluffing, Charm, Lock Picking, Pick-pocketing, Stealth, Urban Navigation
  • Value: Choose whether your character accepted or rebelled against their upbringing, and then give them a Value that reflects that choice.

Step Three: Education

The quality and kind of education available to each person varies vastly across backgrounds, and is often determined first and foremost by one’s class and the wealth of their family. Though literacy is uncommon amongst commoners, for those with educated parents or connections to a wealthy patron, higher levels of education can be obtained without the need for noble blood. The level of education expected of a noble is often dependent on the person’s role and background. While it may be expected for a prince to read, write, and speak four languages as well as know how to wield a sword, a squire or a knight of petty noble heritage may not know how to read at all, while their skill with weaponry is unmatched.

In this step of the lifepath, characters gain two points to add to one or two Attributes, and one point to add to one Skill. They also gain a Focus, which should reflect the special skills that they acquired in their learning.

  • Academy: Your character was educated at a proper school or academy, where they were taught by learned professors alongside many peers. Surrounded by fellow students their age, your character had the opportunity to make friends in school, potentially with people they might not have had the chance to otherwise get to know.
  • Attributes: You gain two points that you may add to a single Attribute or split between two Attributes (increase one Attribute by +2, or increase two Attributes by +1). These Attributes are chosen freely.
  • Skill: You gain one point that you may add to a single Skill. This Skill is chosen freely.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus that relates to something your character specialized in during their education. Examples include: Canon Law, Classical Philosophy, Debauchery, Engineering, Flirting, History, Languages, Oratory, Partying, Polearms, Strategy
  • Educated Abroad: Your character was sent to be educated abroad, and they gained a formal education as they also had to learn and adapt to new languages and cultures.
  • Attributes: You gain two points that you may add to a single Attribute or split between two Attributes (increase one Attribute by +2, or increase two Attributes by +1). These Attributes are chosen freely.
  • Skill: You gain one point that you may add to a single Skill. This Skill is chosen freely.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus that relates to something your character specialized in during their education. Examples include: Alchemy, Astronomy, Botany, Ciphers, Foreign Languages, Musical Performance, Natural Magic, Negotiation, Painting, Philosophy
  • Elder Mentor: Your character was educated by a brilliant mentor, someone with great experience and with a reputation for excellence. Age has made them fade, retiring from their own exploits to teach the next generation, or maybe only you.
  • Attributes: You gain two points that you may add to a single Attribute or split between two Attributes (increase one Attribute by +2, or increase two Attributes by +1). These Attributes are chosen freely.
  • Skill: You gain one point that you may add to a single Skill. This Skill is chosen freely.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus that relates to something your character specialized in during their education. Examples include: Axes, Blacksmithing, Herbalism, Martial Arts, Music Composition, Painting, Poetry, Polearms, Singing, Swords, Tinkering
  • Family Footsteps: Your character was educated on the job, learning at the side of family members who had learned at the side of theirs, and so on for generations.
  • Attributes: You gain two points that you may add to a single Attribute or split between two Attributes (increase one Attribute by +2, or increase two Attributes by +1). These Attributes are chosen freely.
  • Skill: You gain one point that you may add to a single Skill. This Skill is chosen freely.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus that relates to something your character specialized in during their education. Examples include: Accounting, Appraisal, Carpentry, Estate Management, Haggling, Smithing, or Any Focuses listed for your Upbringing
  • On Your Own Terms: Your character didn’t have anyone else’s help to get their education. Instead, they learned as they went and taught themself all the skills they needed to know, working hard and studying alone.
  • Attributes: You gain two points that you may add to a single Attribute or split between two Attributes (increase one Attribute by +2, or increase two Attributes by +1). These Attributes are chosen freely.
  • Skill: You gain one point that you may add to a single Skill. This Skill is chosen freely.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus that relates to something your character specialized in during their education. Examples include: Axes, Bartering, Carving, Foraging, Hedge Magic, Marksmanship, Pick-pocketing, Poisons, Singing, Stealth, Unarmed Combat
  • Privately Tutored: Your character was educated by a few tutors, who personally and privately oversaw their education. Without peers or classmates, your character’s education was gained mostly in isolation, with only their tutors for company during lessons.
  • Attributes: You gain two points that you may add to a single Attribute or split between two Attributes (increase one Attribute by +2, or increase two Attributes by +1). These Attributes are chosen freely.
  • Skill: You gain one point that you may add to a single Skill. This Skill is chosen freely.
  • Focus: Select a single Focus that relates to something your character specialized in during their education. Examples include: Astronomy, Etiquette, Geography, History, Languages, Political Theory, Philosophy, Spell-crafting, Swords

Step Four: Career

Perhaps one of the most defining parts of the lifepath, this step determines your character’s career: the path that they have chosen to follow. A character’s career has a significant impact on them, narratively and mechanically, and these benefits are explained below.

  • Acolyte - Your character’s career is in service to their faith or to a religious institution, whether that may be as a priest, a holy knight, or an ascetic monk.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: The Arysian Faith Is The Way Of Righteousness; I Must Obey The Church To The Letter Of The Law.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Authority or Study—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Canon Law, Heresy, Philosophy, Religious History, Religious Rituals, Theology, Translation
  • Artisan - Your character’s career is involved in the crafting of some kind of specialized good that they sell in a shop or take commissions from patrons. They might be a baker, leatherworker, potioneer, herbalist, etc., and they’re likely also involved in the local guild associated with their craft.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: My Work Is My Life; Art Is The Highest Form Of Worship.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Study or Medicine—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Architecture, Brewing, Map-making, Painting, Sculpture, Smithing, Tailoring, Woodworking
  • Courtier - Your character has made a career out of being in a noble’s court. Whether this is as a lady-in-waiting, an advisor, or maybe an artist or scholar under contract, the character spends most of their time in service to a member of the nobility.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: Forever Indebted To My Patron; Scholarship Is Nothing Without An Audience.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Intrigue or Diplomacy—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Astrology, Counseling, Eavesdropping, Etiquette, Estate Management, Oratory, Poetry, Philosophy
  • Criminal - Your character is a criminal, and has made a career out of illegal trades like thievery or maybe even assassination.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: I Live By My Own Rules; Not All Laws Are Just.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Intrigue or Skirmish—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Brawling, Concealed Weapons Disguise, Intimidation, Lock Picking, Smuggling, Stealth
  • Laborer - Your character’s career is one of hard labor, whether that’s working in agriculture as a laborer in the field, or as a house servant doing the menial tasks that keep a household running.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: Prepare For The Worst, Hope For The Best; A Society That Mistreats Its Laborers Is Unjust.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Skirmish or Authority—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Agriculture, Animal Handling, Armor Care, Cleaning, Heavy Weights, Makeshift Tools, Mending, Riding, Sewing
  • Merchant - Your character’s career has been made in finance, and in moving money and goods from place to place.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: Sins Can Always Be Forgiven, but Opportunities Come And Go; Cultural Exchange Is Always Valuable.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Study or Diplomacy—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Bribery, Contracts, Estate Management, Finances, Haggling, Persuasion, Travel Logistics
  • Outcast - One of the more varied careers, characters who are Outcasts are marked by their time spent outside of society on the fringes of civilization. They may work as a hedgemage, someone who practices magick in the solitude of nature, or as a ranger, someone who guards the roads and forests from bandits and thugs.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
