  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Skirmish or Medicine—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Avoiding Trouble, Foraging, Hedge Magic, Herbalism, Navigation, Survival, Trapping
  • Ruler - Your character’s career has been spent learning how to rule, and presiding over a town, city, or larger territory.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: Responsibility To My People And My Kingdom; The Crown Is A Heavy Burden.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Authority or Diplomacy—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Finances, Foreign Relations, History, Law, Negotiations, Politics, Religious Doctrine
  • Soldier - Your character’s career is on the battlefield, whether as a fighter, healer, or tactician. They may be in an army that fights for the sake of one kingdom or institution (i.e. a soldier in the imperial army or a knight of the Church), or they may be a mercenary whose loyalties are only to their pay.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: I Will Do What I Must To Secure Peace For Others; The Most Honorable Death is on the Battlefield.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Skirmish or Authority—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Axes, Field Medicine, Hand-to-Hand Combat, Improvised Weapons, Military Tactics, Mounted Combat, Polearms, Swords, Shields
  • Scholar - Your character has pursued a career in study, dedicated to research and the pursuit of knowledge.
  • Value: Your character gains a single Value, which should reflect something about their career. Why did they choose this career? What does their career mean to them? How does your character perceive themself in this career?
  • Example Values: There is Always an Answer to Every Question; No Such Thing As The Unknown, Only The Hidden.
  • Attributes: Your character gains three points which may be split between two or three Attributes (increase three Attributes by +1 each, or increase one by +2 and another by +1). You may pick these Attributes freely.
  • Skills: Select between two Skills—Study or Medicine—choosing the Skill that is the most necessary for your character’s career. This Skill is increased by 2. Then, freely select two other Skills—less important to your character’s area of focus but Skills that are still relevant to their work—which are increased by 1 each.
  • Focuses: Select two focuses, at least one of which should relate to skills that your character has gained during or because of their career. Examples include: Alchemy, Anatomy, Botany, Cartography, History, Law, Religious History, Research, Sketching

Step Five: Life Events

A character’s life is made up of a mosaic of their experiences, emotions, and relationships, which together inform a character’s worldview, values, and self-image. Some of the events that a character has experienced may be more pivotal than others, and these moments in a character’s life are defined in this stage of the lifepath.

Before choosing their life events, you should decide how old your character is. Is your character still young and relatively inexperienced with much of their life still ahead; are they mature and well into adulthood; or are they older, with decades of experience under their belt, with potentially even children of their own? This decision will help you decide what life events are appropriate to choose from when making your character.

Each character should have two life events. If you want your character to have more than two, you may (with Gamemaster’s approval), as long as you do not exceed the number of Focuses or Attribute bonuses that are gained at this stage. When picking your character’s life events, you may choose from the list below or roll on the table to have them randomly assigned.

Each life event grants your character:

  • A Focus: Select one focus, which should relate to skills your character learned or used during this life event.
  • An Attribute: Your character gains +1 to an Attribute, which should reflect the lasting impact that that experience had on your character as a person.

Make sure to do this twice, once for each Life Event.

Because each character’s life and circumstances are unique, you may also choose to combine life events or come up with a new and unique life event for your character that is not listed below, so long as they still gain one relevant Focus and a +1 to an Attribute.

  1. Ran away from home: Your character—either as a child or an adult—ran away from home, forsaking their family name and potentially their titles. What drove the character away? Do they ever intend to go back?
  2. Death of a loved one: Your character, at some point in their life, has lost a loved one. Who was that person and how did your character know them? How did they die? Who (if anyone) was to blame?
  3. Serious injury: Your character was seriously hurt and needed to spend a considerable amount of time recovering. What happened when they were hurt? Who was responsible? What did recovery entail?
  4. Religious conversion: Your character has converted to a new faith. What faith did they convert to, and what drew them to it?
  5. Disowned: Your character was disowned by their family, and forced to live without their support or wealth. Why was your character disowned? Do they accept their situation, or are they still trying to fix what happened?
  6. Committed a crime: Your character has committed a crime at one point in their life and reaped the consequences of it, often viewed with suspicion if not outright distrust. What did they do and why? Were they caught? Is your character still involved in crime, or are they trying to distance themselves from their past?
  7. Lucky break: Your character happened to be in the right place at the right time, and made an impactful choice that earned them a positive reputation and potentially a real reward, such as being knighted after rescuing a queen from a bandit attack. What was the break? Who else was involved? What did they earn because of it?
  8. Won a decisive battle: Your character took charge of their forces and struck a decisive blow, winning a battle that changed the tide of a conflict, if not winning it altogether. Who were they fighting and why?
  9. Ascended a throne: Your character gained a noble title. How did they earn this title—was it inherited from a deceased relative, or granted as a reward by a monarch?
  10. Married: Your character got married! Was it an arranged marriage, or one of your character’s choosing? Does your character and their spouse get along?
  11. Took religious orders: Your character swore an oath to a religious order, taking orders as a monk or a nun and devoting themself wholly to their faith. What kind of religious order did your character join? Have they stayed true to their vows?
  12. Unknown origins: Your character doesn’t know their birth family or where they came from, and was raised by someone else. Who actually raised them? Does your character want to find their birth family?
  13. Survived an assassination attempt: Someone tried to kill your character, but they narrowly escaped death. Why was someone out to get them? How did your character manage to survive?
  14. Joined a crew: Your character has joined a band or company of people, maybe a mercenary company or a guild of artisans or even a secret society. How did your character find their crew? Does your character lead it, or do they follow someone else?
  15. Made a powerful enemy: Your character, whether through action or circumstance, has made an enemy of someone powerful who is out for your blood. Who is your character’s enemy? What did they do (or not do) in order to have earned this bitter enmity? Does your character have any hope of making things right?

Step Six: Finishing Touches

At this step, your character should be nearly complete, and in need of only a few more adjustments and minor changes before they are ready for play.

Attributes: At start, your character cannot have any Attributes above 11, and cannot have more than one Attribute at 11. For any Attribute that exceeds these limits, reduce them appropriately until they are within the limit. For each point reduced from an Attribute, increase another Attribute by one, though the stated limits must still be obeyed.

Once this is complete, you may increase three of your character’s Attributes by 1, though again, the limits must still apply.

Skills: At start, a character cannot have any Skills above 4, and cannot have more than one Skill at 4. For any Skill that exceeds these limits, reduce them appropriately until they are within the limit. For each point reduced from a Skill, increase another Skill by one, though the stated limits must still be obeyed.

Once this is complete, you may increase two of your character’s Skills by 1, though again, the limits must still apply.

Value: Your character gains one more Value. This can reflect the Life Events you chose in Step Five, or it can represent some other aspect of your character and their beliefs, like an important relationship.

Talents: Your character gains four Tier 1 Combat Talents and three Narrative Talents which may be chosen freely, so long as any Talent prerequisites are met. For a list of Talents, see Chapter Six: Talents.

Trait: Your character gains one “Defining Feature”, which is a unique Trait that you come up with that defines something important about your character. This could be something related to their unique abilities or place in the world; related to their appearance or presentation; or even something related to their beliefs or how they carry themself. Whatever you decide, your character’s defining feature should reflect something important, something defining, about them and what they’re like.

For example, a character who can see into the future might have the Defining Feature “Oracle”, a trans character might have the Defining Feature “Trans”, or a flirtatious character might have the Defining Feature “Playboy”.

Equipment: Your character gains any equipment of your choice from the equipment lists, so long as they have the inventory space and meet any prerequisites. For a list of equipment, see Chapter Seven: Equipment.

Final Scores

  • Final Check: Your character’s Attributes, added up together, should equal 56. Your character’s skills, added up together, should equal 14. Your character should have 4 Tier 1 Combat Talents, 3 Narrative Talents, 6 Focuses, and 4 Values.
  • Speed: Your character has a Speed equal to 3 + Half your Agility (rounded down). When you take the Move Minor Action, you can move a number of spaces up to your Speed.
  • Health Bar and Max Health Points (HP): When a character is damaged by an attack or a hazard, they receive an amount of damage which is subtracted from their HP. A Character has a Health Bar equal to their Brawn + Skirmish, and has three Health Bars in total, for a Max HP of  (Brawn + Skirmish) * 3.
  • Willpower: When a character is Demoralized, they take damage that is subtracted from their Willpower (see Chapter Five: Combat). A character’s total Willpower is equal to their Faith.
  • Effect Saves: Certain damage effects in this game trigger by rolling a number of effects equal to an Attribute’s Effect Save. Calculate the Effect Save for each of your Attributes with the following calculation: (Attribute/2) -1.
  • Damage Bonus: On all attacks, a character gains bonus [CD] equal to their Skirmish Skill.

Personal Details

  • Name: Your character needs a name! When choosing a name, consider your character’s social class and upbringing: where did they grow up; what is the naming scheme of the region they’re from; would their family have a tradition of passing down names; are they high class enough to even have a family/last name? Your Gamemaster can help you determine what naming conventions exist in your game’s setting, or you can use the following suggestions for inspiration:
  • Thaloran names: Aemma, Belen, Elias, Ezri, Gaelin, Lyneth, Mikel, Quinala, Yves
  • Paerdish names: Adelinde, Averil, Bridget, Cormag, Edvin, Gweir, Sigrith, Simon, Wynne
  • Oriandi names: Augustina, Callista, Daniil, Flavius, Giulio, Justinian, Loukas, Lyra, Marta, Octavian, Phaedra, Rannulfus
  • Meian names: Anja, Askr, Fulrik, Hilda, Jesper, Leif, Netta, Torrick, Tove, Vilde
  • Languages: Languages often play a large role when it comes to how a character navigates society and the environments they find themselves in, and serve as a marker of a character’s background. Characters that speak many languages often do so out of necessity though how they learned those languages (and the kinds of languages they’ve learned) differs from person to person. For example, while merchants or sailors will have likely picked up several languages thanks to frequent contact with other languages through their profession, members of the nobility are also likely to speak several languages in order to navigate the multinational world of politics, but have learned them through dedicated tutoring and study. Older languages (such as Latin, or in the case of Edhela, High Dwarrin) primarily used in scholarship aren’t very likely to be spoken colloquially, so while it may be very common for scholars and religious devotees to know these archaic languages, they’d be far less in use amongst commoners and even some nobility.
    When it comes to deciding what languages your character speaks, you’ll want to take into account each step in your character’s lifepath and what kind of access to education they had, as well as how much exposure they’ve had to different cultures and languages. For example, a character from the landed nobility who was raised in a populous city and went into the priesthood might know as many as 5 or 6 languages, while a commoner from a secluded village who was raised as a laborer might only know 1. Determine with your Gamemaster what languages exist in your game’s setting and which ones are appropriate for your character to know.
  • Appearance: What does your character look like?
  • Personality: What is your character actually like on a day-to-day? How do they behave, what’s their general demeanor? A character’s Values are often a good basis for determining a character’s personality, and vice versa.
  • Relationships: No person, and therefore no character, exists in a vacuum. While a character’s relationships can sometimes be defined by their Values, there are also many other ways that a character knows and interacts with others.
    How does your character relate to the other Player Characters? Do they know each other? Do they get along?
    This is also a good opportunity to consider your character’s relationships with people outside of the Player Characters. Who are your character’s family and friends? Do they have a spouse, or children? Do they have enemies or rivals? Who are they, and why? Details about their relationships add depth to a character, and can be helpful when coming up with Values.

Standard Array Character Creation

Standard Array character creation is a simple and fast way to make a character for Ascension, and can be particularly useful for experienced players wanting to make a character quickly or for those with character ideas that don’t quite fit the options available in the lifepath steps. In this method of character creation, you will assign your character’s Attributes and Skills from a set of predetermined ratings and determine Focuses and Values in the same step.

Step One: Attributes

Assign your character’s Attributes from the following ratings, in any order: 10, 9, 8, 7, 7, 6, 6.

Once assigned, increase your Attributes by three total points in any configuration (+1 to three Attributes, +2 to one Attribute and +1 to another, or +3 to a single Attribute). These Attributes are chosen freely. Once again, only one Attribute may be equal to 11 at start, and the rest may not exceed 10.

Step Two: Skills

Assign your character’s Skills from the following ratings, in any order: 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1.

Once assigned, increase your Skills by two total points (+1 to two Skills, or +2 to a single Skill). These Skills are chosen freely. Once again, only one Skill may be equal to 4 at start, and the rest may not exceed 3.

Step Three: Focuses, Values, and Talents

Give your character six Focuses that reflect their unique specialties and areas of expertise. Then give your character four Values that reflect their motivations, relationships, or deeply held beliefs about the world. Finally, give your character four tier 1 Combat Talents and three Narrative Talents for which they meet the prerequisites.

Step Four: Finishing Touches

Final check: Your character’s Attributes should in total add up to 56 and their Skills should add up to 14. You may not have any Attributes above 11 or Skills above 4, and may only have one Attribute at 11 and one Skill at 4.

Speed: Your character has a Speed equal to 3 + Half your Agility (rounded down).

HP: Your character has an amount of HP equal to their Brawn + Skirmish, multiplied by three. (Brawn + Skirmish) * 3.

Willpower: Your character has an amount of Willpower equal to their Faith.

Effect Saves: Certain damage effects in this game trigger by rolling a number of effects equal to an Attribute’s Effect Save. Calculate the Effect Save for each of your Attributes with the following calculation: (Attribute/2) -1.

Damage Bonus: On all attacks, a character gains bonus [CD] equal to their Skirmish Skill.

Traits: Give your character either of the traits: Commoner or Noble, and a single “Defining Feature” (see Step Six: Finishing Touches for more details). These are your character’s only starting traits.

Equipment: Give your character equipment from the lists, so long as they meet any prerequisites and have the inventory space.

Personal Details: Determine your character’s name, what languages they know, their appearance, and any other details that will help to flesh them out as a unique individual.

Example Character Creation

Seth has been invited to play in an Ascension campaign. He has a loose idea for the kind of character he wants to play—a charismatic and outgoing army commander—but wants to come up with the details as he goes, so he decides to use Lifepath Creation to make his character. He names his character Adelinde, and writes her starting stats in her character sheet (6 in every Attribute, 1 in every Skill).

First, Seth has to choose Adelinde’s social class. After reading through the options, he thinks it would be fun to play someone from the Petty Nobility, writing that down in the Social Class box on Adelinde’s character sheet and adding +1 to her Agility and Brawn. Then Seth has to give Adelinde a Value. He decides that Adelinde’s father was a famous knight for a powerful monarch before he died and that Adelinde wants to emulate his ideals, so he writes down her first Value: “The virtues of a true knight are honor, valor, and kindness.”

Next, Seth chooses Adelinde’s upbringing. Since her father was a famous knight, Seth decides that Adelinde would have had the Military upbringing as she would have squired for her father when she was young. For Attributes, Seth increases her Brawn by +1 and chooses to increase her Presence +1. For her Skill, Seth chooses to increase Adelinde’s Authority by +1. Then Seth has to give Adelinde a Focus, picking “Polearms” because Adelinde’s upbringing with her father gave her expertise in wielding all kinds of polearms. For her Value, Seth decides that Adelinde accepted her upbringing wholeheartedly and went on to pursue the same career that her father did, giving her the Value: “I will prove myself a knight worthy of the kingdom.”

Next, Seth chooses Adelinde’s education. Because her father taught her everything she knows, Seth gives her the Family Footsteps education, increasing her Presence and her Coordination by +1, and increasing her Authority by +1. For Adelinde’s Focus, Seth gives her “Battlefield Strategy”, which she learned from the years of watching her father lead armies.

For Adelinde’s career, Seth chooses Soldier. As a wandering knight-for-hire, Adelinde has spent a lot of her career doing odd jobs and helping people on a small scale, so Seth gives her the Value “It is the duty of the strong to protect the weak”, to reflect the ideals she’s gained from her experience. For her Attributes, Seth increases her Coordination, Faith, and Presence by +1. For her Skills, Seth chooses Authority as her primary Skill since she aspires to be a commander more than a melee fighter, increasing it by +2. Then he chooses to increase her Skirmish and Diplomacy by +1. Finally, Seth gives Adelinde the Focus “Mounted Combat”.

For Adelinde’s life events, Seth immediately chooses “Death of a loved one” as her first life event because of how important Adelinde’s father was to her, and how his death has driven her to work harder to follow in his footsteps. As part of this life event, Seth gives Adelinde the Focus “Leadership” and +1 to her Presence. For her second life event, Seth picks “Made a powerful enemy”, deciding that Adelinde’s commitment to truth and justice led her to exposing the crimes of a powerful duke’s son, which made her a hero of the people when the man was imprisoned, but now that duke is out for her blood. Seth gives her the Focus “Persuasion” and +1 to her Faith.

Now that Adelinde’s social class, upbringing, education, career, and life events have been chosen, Seth can do the finishing touches to make her a complete character! Adelinde has only one Attribute at 11, so Seth doesn’t need to adjust her Attribute stats. She does have one skill at 5–Authority–so Seth needs to reduce her Authority by 1 and adds it to her Study. After that, he adds +1 to Adelinde’s Brawn, Coordination, and Presence, and +1 to her Diplomacy and Intrigue. Adelinde also needs one more Value, and Seth gives her the Value: “No one is exempt from being held accountable for their actions”, as a reflection of her life event “Made a powerful enemy.”

Next, Seth has to choose Adelinde’s Talents. First, he chooses her three Narrative Talents, taking “Bolstering Word” from the Captain archetype—which he can do because Adelinde has more than 3 Authority, meeting the Talent’s prerequisites—and then taking “Chivalry” and “Bold and Brave” from the Knight archetype. For her four Tier 1 combat Talents, Adelinde takes “Cavalry Adept”, “Bannerlord”, “Tactician”, and “Demoralizing Attacker 1”.

Finally, Adelinde needs a Defining Feature. Because so much of who Adelinde is and how she carries herself in the world revolves around her role and image of herself as a knight, Seth decides to give her “Chivalrous Knight” as her Defining Feature.

After doing a final check to make sure her Attributes and Skills add up to 56 and 14 respectively, Seth can fill in the rest of her character sheet. Adelinde’s Speed is 6 (her mounted speed on a horse is 10), her Health Bar is 13 and her Max HP is 39, her Willpower is 8, and her damage bonus is +4[CD]. Seth also fills in each of Adelinde’s Effect Saves.

For her equipment, Seth gives Adelinde a lance, a shield, and a banner. He also gives her full plate as her armor, which reduces her speed by -2. Now Adelinde is ready for her first adventure!

Character Advancement

As characters are played over the course of a campaign, their experiences and hardships will cause them to grow, change, and advance. This advancement is reflected in your character’s level, and characters will have the opportunity to level up as the campaign goes on. The manner in which characters level up can be done two ways: narrative milestones; or experience points (XP), which are rewarded at the end of every session.

Leveling Up

With Lifepath Creation, Player Characters start the game at Level 0. Whenever the party completes a major story milestone or accumulates a certain amount of XP (see Experience Points), each Player Character Ascends 1 Level, to a maximum of 12.

There are also limits upon how much your character can improve until they reach certain levels. Until you reach Level 3, your character cannot have any Talents above Tier 2, and until you reach Level 5, your character cannot have more than one Attribute above 11 or Skill above 4. After reaching Level 5, you may have multiple Attributes and Skills at 11 and 4 respectively, but all characters may only ever have one Attribute at 12 and one Skill at 5.

Upon Ascending a Level, you gain the benefits listed in the Level Ascension table. You may also do any of the following:

  • Decrease one of your Attributes by 1 (to a minimum of 6) and increase another by 1 (to a maximum of 11 or 12, depending on level).
  • Decrease one of your Skills by 1 (to a minimum of 1) and increase another by 1 (to a maximum of 4 or 5, depending on level).
  • Replace a Combat Talent (that is not a prerequisite for anything else you have) with any other Combat Talent you meet the prerequisites for.
  • Replace a Narrative Talent with any other Narrative Talent you meet the Prerequisites for.
  • Replace one of your Focuses.

Experience Points

Each player gains the same amount of XP (1-4 points) at the end of every session, the number being determined by the content of the session.

Players level up every time they gain a certain number of XP, typically 4 XP, though this amount can be adjusted depending on the desired length of the campaign.

Amount

Session Events

1 XP

The characters spent little to no time pursuing the party’s Common Cause, and no Values were used or challenged.

2 XP

The characters spent some time pursuing the party’s Common Cause, and one or two characters used or challenged their Values.

3 XP

Most of the session is spent pursuing the party’s Common Cause, and at least half of the characters have used or challenged their Values. The story has been changed because of the actions taken and decisions made by characters.

4 XP

Most of the session is spent pursuing the party’s Common Cause, and almost if not all of the party has used or challenged their Values. The characters have succeeded (or failed) in achieving their goals, and the story has been changed significantly because of the actions taken and decisions made by the characters.

Part Two: Playing the Game

Chapter Three: Basic Rules

This chapter covers the core rules of Ascension, which will be used throughout the rest of the game. These rules are the foundation of this game, and will be referenced regularly in other chapters. Every player should have a basic understanding of these concepts during play.

Attempting Tasks

In both Combat and Narrative play, characters determine the outcome of their actions by attempting Tasks. Player characters are assumed to be skilled at what they do, and so do not need to attempt a Task for simple, everyday actions like opening a door or making a cup of tea. Tasks are needed when the odds are uncertain, or when success or failure would move the story forward in interesting ways, like poisoning a cup of tea, escaping from a prison cell, or convincing a king to lend you his aid.

Once the GM determines that an action a player would like to take requires a Task,  the following process for attempting a Task is used to determine the results:

  1. The GM determines which Attribute and Skill are appropriate for the Task being attempted, as well as if any of the character’s Focuses apply. If attempting a specific action listed by the rulebook, the Attribute and Skill required for the Task will be listed (this primarily affects combat). Players may also suggest an Attribute/Skill combination, but the GM has the final say. Once the Attribute and Skill have been chosen, add together the two numbers to create your Target Number.
  2. The GM sets the Task’s base Difficulty on a scale of 0 to 6 (in an extreme circumstance, this Difficulty may go higher). This Difficulty is the number of successes required in order to successfully accomplish the Task. Once the base Difficulty has been declared, the Players and/or the GM may adjust it by creating Advantages and Complications respectively.
  3. The player creates their dice pool. Each dice pool is made up of 2d20s by default, though additional dice may be added via abilities or special effects, as well as purchasing dice by spending Momentum and/or adding to Threat. Once the dice pool is created, the player rolls all their dice at once.

The maximum number of dice in a dice pool is 5d20: 2d20 from the default dice pool + up to 3d20 purchased or gained from abilities.

  1. Each die that rolls a number equal to or less than the Task’s Target Number counts as a single success. If a die rolls a 1, it is considered a critical success and generates two successes instead of one. If a die rolls a 20, it automatically generates a Complication. If a player had applied a Focus to this Task, then each die that rolls a number equal to or less than the Skill being used counts as a critical success (there is no benefit to having more than one applicable focus).
  2. If the number of successes rolled is equal to or greater than the Task’s Difficulty, the player has succeeded, and the Task is completed. If the number of successes is less than the Task’s Difficulty, the player has failed to complete the Task. Every success generated above the Task’s Difficulty rating generates a point of Momentum.
  3. The GM describes the outcome of the Task, applying the effects of any Complications created.

Task Difficulty

Before a Task is attempted, the GM must set the Difficulty. When setting the Difficulty, a GM should take into account the circumstances under which the player is attempting to take the action. High stress environments or situations where the character is lacking tools or information may indicate that a Task should be harder to accomplish, while Tasks may be easier in situations where the character is very familiar with the task at hand or they have plenty of time/tools at their disposal. Most Tasks listed as part of specific combat actions will have the Difficulty listed, so the GM does not set the Difficulty for those Tasks, though they may spend Threat to increase the Difficulty.

Players should always know the Difficulty of a Task before they attempt them; their characters are competent professionals who can easily evaluate the difficulty of their actions. This also allows Players to strategize in order to determine the best way to succeed.

Difficulty

Descriptor

Examples

1

Routine

  • Sneaking into a small residential house that you know is empty
  • Convincing a king to pay for a completed contract
  • Locating a common book in a familiar library

2

Intermediate

  • Sneaking into a noble’s house with a light guard patrol
  • Convincing a king to hire you for mercenary work
  • Locating a common book in an unfamiliar library

3

Challenging

  • Sneaking into a palace with a heavy guard patrol
  • Convincing a king to buy a very pricey piece of artwork
  • Locating a book on a niche subject in an unfamiliar library

4

Formidible

  • Sneaking into a palace with a heavy guard patrol while wearing Overt armor
  • Convincing a king who doesn’t like you to buy a very expensive piece of art
  • Locating a wildly obscure book in an unfamiliar library

5

Daunting

  • Sneaking into the palace while the guards are on high alert
  • Convincing a king to give you unlimited access to his treasury to fund a very expensive construction project
  • Locating a wildly obscure book in an unfamiliar library that has not been maintained in over a decade

6

Nearly Impossible

  • Sneaking into the palace while the guards are on high alert and know to watch for you specifically
  • Convincing a king to let you go free after you were caught trying to transport all the gold of his treasury elsewhere
  • Locating a wildly obscure book in an unfamiliar library that has been purposefully hidden

Difficulty Zero Tasks

Sometimes circumstances or special abilities might reduce a Task’s Difficulty to 0, or a Task might be so easy as to be effortless, with no possibility of failure. If a Task is Difficulty 0, it is automatically successful and characters who attempt the Task cannot outright fail. Players may choose whether or not to roll the dice to attempt a Difficulty 0 Task: at Difficulty 0, every success rolled generates Momentum, but there may be the chance to gain Complications.

Opposed Tasks

In situations where a character is attempting to overcome a direct opponent, you may attempt an Opposed Task. In every Opposed Task, there will be an active character attempting to do something (shove someone, stab them with a knife, etc.), and a reactive character who is attempting to resist.

When attempting an Opposed Task, the reactive character sets the Difficulty by rolling their dice pool. The reactive character isn’t rolling against a set Difficulty, but is just trying to generate as many successes as possible. The number of successes that the reactive character generates becomes the Difficulty rating for the active character’s roll. After the reactive character rolls, the active character attempts their side of the Task, attempting to beat the number of successes generated by the reactive character.

If the active character succeeds, they succeed in their goal and may generate/spend Momentum as usual. If the active character fails, the reactive character generates bonus Momentum for every success fewer than the set Difficulty. For example: if the reactive character’s successes put the Difficulty at 3 but the active character only rolled 2 successes, the reactive character generates 1 bonus Momentum which they may not save.

If the reactive character chooses not to resist in an opposed task, the task instead reverts to being a static Difficulty task, which has a Difficulty of 1 unless otherwise stated.

Complications

Things don’t always work out how players envision, and even when a Task is successful, it can still end up going slightly awry if the player generated a Complication on their dice roll, or because the GM has spent Threat to create a Complication. Complications don’t change the general outcome of a roll—if the roll is a success, the character succeeds in their aim regardless of the Complications—but they may create other difficult circumstances that inhibit a character from taking further action, or may create new problems that the character must now address.

Complications come in two forms: an immediate narrative consequence, or Threat. Complications that create narrative consequences will normally increase the Difficulty of the next Task the character wishes to attempt by one, or make certain actions impossible.

If the GM doesn’t want to inflict a consequence on the player, they may instead turn that Complication into 2 Threat, which they can bank or spend immediately. Similarly, for NPCs that generate Complications, they must either suffer the narrative consequence or the GM can remove 2 Threat from the Threat pool to ignore it.

Lorenz attempts a Difficulty 1 Task to pick a locked chest. His target number is 15, and he rolls a 3 and a 20. Because one of his rolls was a success, he succeeds on the Task and can open the chest. However, because of the 20, the GM creates a new Complication: now there are guards approaching Lorenz’s location, and he has to either get out fast without examining the chest in detail, or try to investigate but risk getting caught! The Difficulty of Lorenz’s next Task, to either escape or investigate without getting caught, increases by 1.

Complication Range

Sometimes the circumstances of a situation may not make a Task more difficult, but make its consequences more uncertain. In these situations, the Complication Range of a Task might increase, making it more likely for a player to generate Complications on their roll. In the same way that Focuses might increase the range of critical success, increasing the Complication Range makes it so that numbers higher than 20 can also generate Complications if rolled on the die. Every Task has a default Complication Range of 1.

Certain circumstances or abilities may increase the Complication Range of a Task, and GMs may also increase the Complication Range by spending Threat equal to the amount increased above one. When the Complication range of a Task is increased, it applies to all dice rolls on that Task, including assistants. A Task’s Complication Range can never be increased by more than 5.
