Success at Cost

Sometimes players may find it critically important or even necessary to succeed on a Task no matter what. In these circumstances, they may ask the GM (or the GM may offer) to succeed at cost. This option may be offered either before the roll is attempted or after a failed roll, but before the consequences of the roll have been described, and may not be offered for combat tasks unless explicitly listed in those rules. When a player chooses to succeed at cost, the Task is considered to have been successful, but it generates one automatic Complication in addition to any that have been generated from the Task’s roll (if applicable).

The GM may find it appropriate to increase the amount of automatic Complications generated from succeeding at cost if the circumstances call for it, though this should be made known to players before they decide to succeed at cost.

Momentum cannot be generated from or spent on a Task that has succeeded at cost.

In order to heal the king’s ill son, Adelinde needs to make a specific potion using rare ingredients. Because she only has enough ingredients to make one potion, Adelinde asks her GM if she can Succeed at Cost rather than risk failure, and the GM agrees. Adelinde successfully completes her potion, but does generate an automatic Complication; a servant spying on her thinks that Adelinde’s potion-making looks like witchcraft! Now Adelinde knows that her potion will work, but the Difficulty of convincing the king to let his son take it has increased by 1.

Assisting with Tasks

While all characters are assumed to be competent and capable in their own right, circumstances, consequences, and abilities may still make the likelihood of success unlikely or even impossible without help. Ascension provides several ways for players to improve the odds of success on their Tasks, and one of these is assistance from allies, whose dice rolls may apply to the same Task.

A character attempting a Task may be assisted by one ally at no cost, though additional characters may assist at the cost of one Momentum per character. In order to assist, a player must describe how their character is helping with the Task, and with the GM’s approval, will then roll 1d20 using their own Target Number and any applicable Focus. As long as the Task’s leader generates at least one success, all successes generated by assistants count towards the result of the Task. If the leader generates no successes, then the assistants’ successes do not count, though Complications rolled by assistants always count towards the result of the Task regardless of the leader’s roll.

Assisting characters do not have to use the same Attribute and Skill as the leading character, and cannot purchase additional dice using Momentum.

Momentum and Threat

Whenever a character generates more successes on a Task than the set Difficulty, they generate Momentum. Momentum is one of the most important resources that players have in Ascension, as it can be spent to improve their chances of success on Tasks, gain additional benefits from a successful Task, activate abilities, and so on.

Whenever a player in the party attempts a Task and succeeds, every additional success generated above a Task’s Difficulty generates a single point of Momentum, which may be spent by the player immediately or can be saved to the Momentum group pool for later use. Any member of the party may save or spend Momentum in the group pool. The group pool may have a maximum of 6 Momentum in it at once, and cannot be saved between sessions, with the Momentum in the group pool going back to zero at the start of each new session.

NPCs don’t generate or spend Momentum in this way, instead they interact with the GM’s version of Momentum, called Threat, which is explained further in the rules on Threat.

Spending Momentum

The most common use for spending Momentum is improving the odds of a Task by purchasing extra dice or reducing its Difficulty via creating Advantages. Momentum can also be spent to improve the outcome of a Task, such as by gaining additional information, or adding additional damage.

After the roll to attempt a Task has been completed, the GM will describe the outcome of that roll. If successful, the players may spend Momentum they’ve generated on that Task to improve its outcome, and any additional Momentum that goes unspent is saved into the group pool. Some Momentum spends do not depend on the outcome of a Task and may be used at any time, typically before a Task is attempted.

Momentum can be spent in the following ways:

  • Extra Dice: One of the most common and straightforward ways to spend Momentum is to add extra d20s to your roll to attempt a Task. The decision to purchase additional dice must be made before any dice are rolled. The Momentum cost for each d20 increases for each die purchased: the first die costs 1 Momentum, the second die costs 2 Momentum, and a third die costs 3 Momentum (purchasing two bonus dice would cost 3 Momentum, purchasing three would cost 6). No more than 3 dice can be bought for a single Task. If an ability or effect would grant you an additional die on a Task for free, the cost of additional dice remains the same—i.e. if you gain one extra die for free, purchasing a second die still costs 2 Momentum.
  • Create an Advantage: Players may spend 2 Momentum to create an advantageous circumstance for a character in a scene, though the Advantage must make logical sense for something that could occur in that scene (e.g. yelling at an ally to “duck!” to give them an Advantage on their Task to defend against a falling hazard). When a character uses an Advantage, they lower the Difficulty on their next Task by one. Only one character can benefit from an Advantage at a time, and once an Advantage has been used, it goes away. Players may also use a created Advantage to remove a Complication currently in play, instead of lowering the Difficulty on a Task.
  • Create a Problem: Players may spend 2 Momentum to make an obstacle or create a difficult circumstance for an opponent, increasing the Difficulty of an opponent’s next Task by 1 for every 2 Momentum spent. The decision to increase a Task’s Difficulty must be made before any dice are rolled for that Task.
  • Obtain Information: Players may spend Momentum generated after a successful Task to gain information about the situation at hand. Per 1 Momentum spent, players may ask the GM a question, though the questions must be relevant to the scene and must have answers that their characters could reasonably know or find out from that situation. The GM must answer honestly, though does not need to give complete information.
  • Special Abilities: Some special abilities from Talents may require a player to spend Momentum in order to activate their effects.

Bonus Momentum

Some abilities or situations may grant Bonus Momentum under certain circumstances. Bonus Momentum may be spent like normal Momentum, but it cannot be saved into the group pool. If it is not spent immediately, it goes away.

Bonus momentum cannot be gained on a failed Task.

Threat

In the same way that players generate and save Momentum, the GM has a similar resource called Threat, which they can use to improve the odds for NPCs and inflict challenges on the players. Threat is also a way that the game builds and maintains tension: the more Threat the GM has, the more likely that something is about to go wrong, as the GM gains more resources to create Complications.

The GM begins each session with a number of Threat equal to the number of players, and may gain more in the following ways:

  • Instead of Momentum: When using a Momentum spend, players may choose to, rather than spend Momentum, add to Threat. Every point of Threat given to the GM counts as one point of Momentum towards the player’s Momentum Spend.
  • Complications: Whenever a player rolls a Complication on a Task, the GM may choose to “buy off” the Complication instead of applying it, adding 2 to Threat.
  • NPC Momentum: When NPCs generate more successes than the Difficulty of their Task, they add the excess successes to the Threat pool, just like players do with Momentum.

The GM may also spend Threat in the following ways:

  • Extra Dice: NPCs may spend Threat to get extra dice in the same way that players spend Momentum to get extra dice.
  • NPC Complications: When an NPC rolls a Complication on a Task, the GM may spend 2 Threat to “buy off” the Complication and get rid of it.
  • Create Complication: The GM may spend 2 Threat in order to create a new Complication.
  • Increase Complication Range: The GM may spend a number of Threat equal to the range increase to increase the Complication range for a player’s Task.

Determination

In addition to Momentum, players have access to one more resource that they can use to improve their odds or unlock special features, called Determination. Determination is a special resource that reflects the special position of your characters as the protagonists in their story, allowing them to push themselves beyond their average abilities to achieve spectacular results.

Every character begins each session with one point of Determination, and may gain more Determination by interacting with their Values. Only Determination gained during a session may be saved for use in later sessions; if you do not spend the point of Determination that you gain automatically at the start of each session, it does not roll over. Characters may not have more than 3 points of Determination at a time and must discard any excess.

Spending Determination

When faced with a difficult situation, characters may spend Determination by acting in accordance with their Values in order to grant themselves an advantage. If a character’s Value would help them in a situation by driving them forward or motivating them, they may also spend Determination.

Lorenz needs to convince the king not to order his father executed. The Task is Difficulty 4, and Lorenz needs to succeed on this Task or the consequences will be dire! One of his Values is “I am loyal to my family above all else.” Lorenz asks his GM if this Value applies in this situation, and they agree that his Value would aid him in this Task, so Lorenz can now spend his Determination.

You may spend Determination in the following ways:

  • Perfect Opportunity: You spend your Determination to turn one of the dice in your pool into a 1 instead of rolling it (generating two automatic successes). You must declare this before the roll is attempted.
  • Second Chance: You spend your Determination to reroll any number of dice in your dice pool. You may do this after seeing the result of the roll, but before the GM describes the outcome.

Some Talents may grant special or unique uses for spending Determination, but you must still call upon a Value in the normal way in order to use them.

Gaining Determination

Characters gain Determination when their Values are tested and would pose challenges to them or hold them back from following through on their current course of action. When a character is about to attempt a Task or perform an action that would be in direct opposition to one of their Values, the GM may prompt them to either Comply with or Challenge their Value, gaining a point of Determination in the process.

  • Comply: Your Value conflicts with your current course of action, and you choose to comply with it. You suffer an immediate Complication, which either makes your current action more difficult, or prevents you from doing it altogether, forcing you to change course. Discuss with your GM and decide together on an appropriate Complication and how it would affect your character. Once the Complication has been played out, you gain a point of Determination.
  • Challenge: Your Value conflicts with your current course of action, and so you challenge that Value, crossing it out on your character sheet and moving forward with your current action as though you no longer have it. You gain a point of Determination, but cannot use your crossed out Value again (see Recovering Values below).

Players may also suggest to GMs moments that may be applicable for their character’s values to be tested. If the GM agrees, the character may Comply with or Challenge the value as they see fit.

During combat, characters may also gain Determination through completing bonus objectives, goals set by the GM to complete that are not part of the main victory condition.

Recovering Values

When you have crossed out Values, your character’s beliefs have grown unsteady or uncertain; they’ve challenged something fundamental that they hold dear and now must search themselves and the world in order to find some stability again.

When you recover a crossed out Value, you will rewrite or fully replace your old Value with a new one. Whether it is a small shift to your character’s beliefs, or a large change that has changed their worldview entirely, your new Value should reflect the new realization and reordering of your character’s belief system.

Lorenz challenges his Value “It is the right of monarchs to enforce justice” after he discovers that his king ordered his father’s execution knowing that he had done nothing wrong. After a long discussion with his companions around the campfire, Lorenz chooses the new Value: “It is the right of the people to hold monarchs accountable for their wrongdoing” to reflect the way his beliefs have changed after his experiences.

You may recover a crossed out Value during a session, but only after a scene in which your character does not spend or gain any Determination and contemplates their beliefs and place in the world, or discusses them with another character. Otherwise, you may recover crossed out Values in between sessions. Once recovered, new Values may be used as normal.

Common Cause

In addition to using/challenging Values in order to use Determination, characters may also appeal to their Common Cause. Each party should have a Common Cause, an agreed upon directive which defines the characters’ general goal or goals during their adventures, whether short or long term. The Common Cause can be a specific goal that changes as the goal is met, like, “Depose Duke Wainwright,” or it can be a broader or more general edict about the party’s values, like, “Defend and protect the kingdom of Thalore.”

The Common Cause can also be challenged to gain Determination in the same way as Values in order for the entire party to gain Determination. If the party agrees that the Common Cause conflicts with their current course of action, they may choose to challenge it, each crossing it out on their sheet and gaining a point of Determination. However, once the Common Cause has been challenged, it cannot be used by any character to spend Determination for the rest of the session. The players may then replace the Common Cause in order to use it again.

Chapter Four: Advanced Rules

This chapter contains several additional rules that GMs may use when players are attempting particularly difficult actions or actions that occur over long periods of time.

Group Tasks

Sometimes a circumstance may arise that would cause every character in the party to attempt the same Task as part of a communal action, like sneaking out of a prison together. When this occurs, the GM may ask the party to perform a Group Task. When attempting a Group Task, the GM sets the Difficulty and requisite Attribute/Skill combination for the Task which each party member must attempt, generating Momentum and Complications as usual. However, the success of the Group Task as a whole is determined by how many members of the party succeed on their Task. If at least half of the party succeeds, then the Group Task is successful, but with an automatic Complication generated for each party member that fails. If at least half of the party fails, then the Group Task fails, and no additional Complications are generated.

Characters may not assist each other when attempting a Group Task.

Rylan and their companions are attempting to sneak past an enemy camp without being noticed. Because all of the party members are attempting the same action together, the GM determines that this is a Difficulty 2 Agility + Intrigue Group Task. Rylan, Erik, Adelinde, and Lorenz each attempt the Task. Rylan, Lorenz, and Erik all succeed on their Tasks, with Rylan and Lorenz each generating 1 Momentum, so the Group Task is successful. Because Adelinde failed, the party suffers one automatic Complication, which the GM uses to introduce a new narrative problem for the party to address: though they sneak away successfully, the party leaves behind traces that their enemies will discover later. However, when this Complication is declared, the party decides to spend the 2 Momentum generated by Lorenz and Rylan on the Group Task to Create an Advantage that negates the Complication, stating that Rylan notices the traces they’ve left behind and doubles back to cover their trail.

Challenges

Whenever a circumstance or scenario would require significant effort from the entire party over a longer period of time in order to accomplish, it is called a Challenge. A Challenge consists of two or more Tasks, called Key Tasks, whose Attribute/Skill combination and Difficulty are determined by the GM. In a typical Challenge, the Key Tasks may be attempted in any order, but they must all be completed successfully in order to complete the Challenge. If a single character attempts more than one Key Task, the Difficulty increases by 1 cumulatively for every Key Task after the first. Characters may assist each other when attempting Key Tasks, however each character may only assist on a Key Task once during a Challenge.

Characters may also attempt Tasks other than the Key Tasks during a Challenge if they wish. These additional Tasks will not contribute directly to completing the Challenge, but may be used to contribute indirectly by generating Momentum, discovering new information, creating Advantages, or anything otherwise helpful.

The GM may introduce complications as usual during a Challenge, and they may also make Challenges more complex by requiring the Key Tasks to be performed in a specific Order, or by making Key Tasks into Opposed Tasks when the players are facing direct opposition.

Lorenz and his companions have signed up to compete in a grand tournament. There are three major events that the party will need to accomplish successfully in order to win, which the GM designates as the Challenge’s Key Tasks: jousting, a Difficulty 2 Coordination + Skirmish Task; archery, a Difficulty 2 Awareness + Skirmish Task; and the melee, an Opposed Brawn or Agility + Skirmish Task.

Because these events are happening concurrently, the party may attempt the Key Tasks in any order. Lorenz decides to attempt the joust Key Task first, and rolls 4 successes, succeeding and generating 2 Momentum which he saves to the group pool. His companion, Adelinde, doesn’t want to attempt either of the other two Tasks, but decides to help her friends by spending the 2 Momentum to Create an Advantage: Adelinde gives her favor to Erik, filling him with motivation to succeed and lowering the Difficulty of the Key Task to participate in the melee by 1. Thanks to Adelinde’s motivation, Erik’s 2 successes in the melee against his opponent’s 3 succeed on the Opposed Task and wins that event.

Before attempting the archery Key task, Rylan tells the GM they would like to attempt to sabotage their main rival in order to improve their chance at winning the event. The GM allows this, determining because of the risk involved it would be better as a task instead of a created advantage, so they ask Rylan to attempt a Difficulty 2 Agility + Intrigue task to sneak into their opponent’s tent and cut the fletching on his arrows. They roll two successes, and the GM tells them their success reduces the Difficulty of the key task by 1.

Rylan then attempts the archery Key Task, rolling a success on one die and a 20 on the other, succeeding but generating a Complication. The GM uses the Complication to introduce a new hazard in the scene: Rylan’s success in archery angered the betting ring, who had put high odds on someone else that Rylan defeated. Now that the Challenge is completed, the GM declares that the party has won the tournament, but thanks to the Complication, now the party will have to deal with a mob of angry gamblers lying in wait…

Timed Challenges

Another way a GM can add complexity and increase the tension of a Challenge is by adding time pressure in the form of intervals. The length of each interval is determined by the GM before the Challenge begins, and should be an amount of time that makes sense for the kind of actions taking place—a timed Challenge to break into a vault might have five minute intervals, while a timed Challenge to sail a ship from port to port might have intervals that are several days.

When the Challenge begins, the GM will inform the players the number of intervals that the Challenge must be completed within, and should give the players some idea of the consequences if the Challenge is not completed on time. Every Key Task attempted during a Challenge, whether it succeeds or fails, takes two intervals of time.

After successfully completing a Key Task, players may spend 2 Momentum to reduce the time taken by 1 interval. If the Task was failed, players may still reduce the time taken by 1 interval, but must give 2 Threat to the GM instead of spending Momentum.

Players may attempt additional Tasks as usual during a Timed Challenge, which may or may not take intervals according to the GM’s discretion. Any successful Tasks or Advantages made to extend the time limit increase the limit by 1 interval, and Complications may reduce the time limit by 1 interval.

Rylan and their companions are trying to rescue a prisoner from the king’s dungeons while the prison warden is distracted by the ball upstairs. There are three Key Tasks involved in this rescue—finding the secret passage into the prison, picking the lock on the prisoner’s cell, and convincing the prisoner to escape with them. The GM decides this is a timed Challenge, as the warden will be returning to check on the prison in an hour, and sets the intervals at 10 minutes each, so that each Key Task takes 20 minutes.

Rylan succeeds on the first Key Task to find the secret passage, and they generate 2 Momentum, which they spend to reduce the Task’s time by 1 interval. Rylan attempts to pick the lock, which has increased Difficulty because they’ve already attempted a Key Task in this Challenge. They still succeed but generate a Complication, which the GM decides increases the Task’s time by 1 interval. There is one Task remaining, but the party has 1 interval left before the warden returns and catches them there. Lorenz decides to try to give the party more time, and attempts a Difficulty 1 Coordination + Intrigue Task to bar the prison doors. The GM decides this will not take up an interval. Lorenz succeeds, and the barred door adds 1 more interval to their time limit, bringing them back up to two.

Finally, Adelinde attempts the last Key Task with Erik’s assistance, spending her Determination to gain a Perfect Opportunity, granting her 2 automatic successes. Adelinde and Erik succeed on the Task, generating 3 Momentum that they save to the pool. Because Lorenz gave them more time, they don’t need to reduce the time spent on the Key Task, and can escape with their freed prisoner in the nick of time.

Extended Tasks

While Challenges can be used to represent when many smaller actions are needed to achieve a single overarching goal, Extended Tasks can be used to represent when the players are facing a high pressure situation in which accomplishing a single action is too complex to be achieved in a single Task, and instead must be worked on over a period of time.

Every Extended Task has a Progress Bar, which is the measure of how much Progress is required in order to successfully accomplish your goal. During an Extended Task, characters will attempt multiple tasks called Progression Tasks, with each successful Task allowing them to roll [CD] to generate an amount of Progress, similar to how damage is rolled after a successful attack in combat. An Extended Task is completed when players generate enough Progress to fill the Progress Bar.

Extended Tasks will always have a set Difficulty that determines the Difficulty of every Progression Task attempted as part of it. This Difficulty may be further modified by Advantages, Complications, and special abilities or effects. Not all Progression Tasks in the same Extended Task need to be the same activity, nor do they need to use the same attribute + skill combination. The GM should evaluate what attribute and skill they feel is most applicable to each individual Progression Task.

Though not all Extended Tasks will have a time limit that denotes failure if it is not completed within the timeframe, Extended Tasks always use intervals (see Timed Challenges above) as a means of representing the passage of time during the Extended Task. Before beginning an Extended Task, the GM should determine how much time each interval represents. All Tasks attempted as part of an Extended Task take 2 intervals of time.

If an Extended Task will be particularly challenging to overcome, the GM may also add Resistance, which reduces the Progress generated after each successful Task by the amount of Resistance.

For GM guidance on using and creating Extended Tasks, see Chapter Twelve: Running the Game.

Attempting an Extended Task

Whenever a character attempts a Progression Task as part of overcoming an Extended Task, they follow the following steps:

  • Attempt the Task. The player attempts a Progression Task as normal, rolling against the Extended Task’s set Difficulty.
  • Roll Progress. If successful on the Progression Task, the player rolls 2 [CD] plus additional [CD] equal to the Skill they used. The amount rolled is the amount of Progress generated.
  1. If the Extended Task has any Resistance, reduce the Progress by 1 for each point of Resistance.
  2. The player gains +1 [CD] for every assistant on their Task.
  • Apply Progress. Add the Progress generated from your roll to the Progress Bar. If this fills the Progress Bar, then the Extended Task is successfully completed.

Extended Tasks and Momentum

Momentum generated during an Extended Task can be saved or spent as normal. There are also two additional ways to spend Momentum as part of an Extended Task:

  • Additional Progress: A character can increase the Progress generated from their Progression Task. Each point of Momentum spent adds +1 Progress.
  • Reduce Time Cost: A character may spend 2 Momentum to reduce the time a successful Task takes by 1 interval, to a minimum of 1. To reduce the time taken for a failed Task, they must instead give the GM 2 Threat.
  • Reroll Progress: A character may spend 1 Momentum to reroll any number of [CD] from their current Progression Task.

Extended Tasks and Complications

In addition to the standard ways to use Complications, there are two other ways a GM may employ Complications during an Extended Task:

  • Dead End: Remove 4 Progress from the Progress Bar. This is resolved after applying all Progress generated from a Progression Task.
  • Extended Time Cost: A character’s task takes an additional interval.
  • Unforeseen Problem: The Extended Task gains an additional +2 Resistance (to a maximum of 4) that applies to the next Progression Task attempted against it. This extra Resistance goes away after that Progression Task is resolved.

If the characters decide to abandon an Extended Task, or if they fail to accomplish it within the set amount of time, then they suffer the consequences of failure as well as one additional, immediate Complication.

Example Extended Task

Adelinde and her companions have raised an army to besiege the king’s city. Because a city siege is a long and arduous endeavor that will take an army weeks or even months and cannot be accomplished in a single Task or Challenge, the GM decides that this should be an Extended Task. The king’s city has strong fortifications, and the people inside are fiercely loyal to their overlord, so the GM sets the Extended Task’s base Difficulty at 3 with 2 Resistance and a Progress Bar of 20, and sets the interval length at one week.

Rylan attempts the first Task, a Difficulty 3 Awareness + Intrigue Task to scout out the city to find its weak points and any hidden supply lines. They use 1 Momentum from the group pool to buy an extra die and then attempt the Task. They succeed without generating any Momentum, and then roll 2[CD] + 4[CD] from their Intrigue for 6[CD] total, generating 7 Progress which is reduced to 5 by Resistance. They add 5 to the Task’s progress bar, and take note that two intervals have passed. The GM then describes the results of Rylan’s scouting, how they discovered hidden sewer tunnels leading out of the city that its citizens were using to smuggle weapons and food inside.

Erik attempts the next Task assisted by Adelinde, using the new information about the sewers to order an encampment around the sewers’ entrances, preventing anyone from getting in or out. This is a Difficulty 3 Brawn + Authority Task, assisted by Adelinde’s Presence + Authority. Together, Erik and Adelinde generate 4 successes, gaining 1 Momentum, which they bank in the pool. Erik then rolls 2[CD] + 4[CD] from his Authority + 1[CD] from Adelinde’s assistance for 7[CD] total, generating 6 Progress reduced to 4 by Resistance. He adds 4 to the Progress Bar, which is now at 9 total, and takes note that two more intervals have passed. The GM describes the result of Erik and Adelinde’s successful encampment, which has prevented the people of the city from being able to resupply, and as a result, have started to run out of food, fomenting resentment against the king.

Lorenz attempts the next Task to order the army to fire projectiles at the city walls, assisted by Rylan, who joins the soldiers in the attack. This is a Difficulty 3 Presence + Study Task, assisted by Rylan’s Awareness + Skirmish. As their army has Mages in their ranks, granting the party a Trait, Rylan uses this to spend 1 momentum to create an Advantage to have the mages create powerful projectiles, lowering the difficulty of the task by 1. Lorenz and Rylan generate 4 successes, gaining 2 Momentum. Lorenz rolls 2[CD] + 5[CD] from his Study +1[CD] from Rylan’s assistance for 8[CD] total, generating 9 Progress. Lorenz spends 1 Momentum to reroll his two blank [CD], gaining an additional 2 Progress, and spends 2 more Momentum (1 that he generated, 1 from the pool) to add +2 Progress for a total of 13 Progress, reduced to 11 by Resistance. He adds 11 to the Progress Bar for a total of 20, which fills it completely, ending the Extended Task. The GM describes the result of Lorenz’s Task as the walls of the city begin to come down, granting the army access into the city and ending the siege after 6 weeks.

Negotiation

While most narrative scenes in Ascension will have little structure to define what players can or cannot attempt, allowing for players to attempt Tasks only when they or the GM feel it is necessary, Ascension also has an additional set of rules for when a social conflict scene feels significant enough to warrant more structure, called Negotiation.

Negotiation is one of the most important Challenges that players might engage in. While a battle might tip the balance of a war, a successful negotiation might avoid the need for a battle altogether. If the players need to get an important NPC—oftentimes a lord or other sort of leader—on their side, a Negotiation Scene might be necessary. Negotiation scenes are not real time conversations, but representative of scenarios where characters are spending a long amount of time negotiating with an NPC or NPCs, from negotiations over dinner to several days of peace talks. Each turn that players take and the actions they attempt during those turns are glimpses into these extended periods of time, more like a montage of smaller scenes than one continuous conversation.

Negotiation scenes function similarly to a round of combat: each player has a turn, during which they may perform a single Major Action from a list of actions available to them with the goal of swaying the target NPC(s) to their side. The GM also has a number of turns equal to half the number of players rounded down, which they may take in between player turns. Each round always concludes when the players attempt the Persuade Task.

Starting Negotiation

Favor represents how much an NPC agrees with the players’ position. Favor starts at 0, and it is the players’ goal to increase the favor as much as possible before the scene ends. After successfully completing a Persuade Task, players roll a number of challenge dice equal to their Diplomacy Skill to determine how much Favor they’ve earned this round. Players can gain additional Favor dice to their roll by attempting to Appease Companions or any abilities or effects they have from their Talents.

NPC Companions. In some negotiations, the target of your Persuasion Tasks may have allies or companions who may help or hinder your attempts to sway your target. Each allied companion present during a Negotiation gives +1 [CD] Favor (to a maximum of +3 [CD]). Neutral companions do not provide any automatic bonuses or penalties but can be influenced via the Appease Companion action in order to bring them over to your side, though whether they are permanently swayed or temporarily appeased is up to the GM. Companions that are opposed to you and/or your cause can create obstacles or work directly against you, as detailed in the NPC Negotiation Tasks.

Values. NPCs that are a part of a Negotiation scene, particularly the target of your Negotiation and their notable companions, will always have Values. While you may know enough about a character to be able to guess at their Values, the explicit wording of an NPC’s values are always hidden from players at the start of a Negotiation. If a player makes a promise or an offer as part of the Persuade Task that appeals to one of the target’s Values, they may add +2 [CD] Favor to all subsequent Persuade Tasks (including those attempted by a different player), and this effect stacks. If a player makes a promise or an offer that violates one of their Values, they lose -2 [CD] Favor from all subsequent Persuade Tasks (including those attempted by a different player), and this effect also stacks.

Difficulty. The Difficulty of a Persuasion Task starts at 2 and increases by 1 at the end of each round. The Difficulty of all other tasks made in the negotiation also starts at 2, and increases by 1 each time the same character attempts the same Task an additional time. For example, the first time a character attempts to Read in a negotiation scene, it will be at Difficulty 2, but if they try it again, regardless of whether the previous attempt succeeded or failed, it will be at Difficulty 3. If a different character tried the Read Task for the first time, it would be Difficulty 2 for them, and only increase if they attempted it a second time.

At the beginning of a negotiation, if the GM has 0 threat, they gain Threat equal to the number of players.

Negotiation Major Actions

Once a Negotiation begins, all players have a chance to perform a single Major Action from the list below, though some actions cannot be performed more than once in the same round. Some Major Actions will call on a specific Attribute and/or Skill in order to be performed, though others may not. Tasks that do not have specific Attributes or Skills listed may be performed using any Attribute + Skill combination as is relevant to the Task and how the PC is attempting to do it, and is ultimately subject to the GM’s ruling.

Persuade. The most straightforward task, although this can only be used by the Player’s entire side once per round. This is a Diplomacy task; the Attribute used in this task is determined by the GM depending on how the player takes this action—most commonly Presence, though other Attributes may apply. For example, an appeal using the PC’s deeply held convictions might be a Faith + Diplomacy task, or an appeal using logic and/or historical precedent might be a Reason + Diplomacy task. On a success, roll [CD] Favor equal to your Diplomacy. As a momentum spend, you can create additional Favor for each Momentum spent. Additionally, you may spend 1 momentum to re-roll any number of [CD] for this task.

Read. You attempt a Task using a relevant Attribute + Skill in order to glean or recall information about the NPC or one of their companions. On a success, you learn 1 of your target’s values that has not yet been invoked in the scene.

Excuse. You attempt a Task using a relevant Attribute + Skill in order to correct a blunder made by one of your allies. On a success, you can negate the effects of a single Complication created by an ally of yours (but not yourself).

Chit-Chat. You attempt a Task using a relevant Attribute + Skill in order to capture your target’s attention by discussing things unrelated to the topic of the negotiation. On a success, the Difficulty of the Persuade Task will not go up at the end of this round. On a failure, the Difficulty of the Persuade Task increases by 2 instead of 1 at the end of the round. This Task may only be attempted once per scene.

Assist. You can always assist during a Negotiation.

Sway a Companion. You attempt a Task using a relevant Attribute + Skill in order to sway one of your target’s neutral companions. On a success, you gain +1 [CD] Favor to be added to your next roll on a Persuade task. If you managed to appeal to one of their Values as a part of this Task, you gain an additional +1 [CD]. This action may only be attempted once per round.

NPC Negotiation Tasks

The following actions may be taken by NPCs on GM turns. Some actions require spending Threat in order to attempt, and their cost is listed next to each action’s title. Each action can only be attempted once per round.

Make Demands (0-5 Threat). The NPC demands a concession, with severity roughly equivalent to the amount of threat spent. If the players agree, they gain 3 + X favor, where X is the amount of threat spent. If they refuse, the GM instead gains double the amount of threat spent.

Counter-offer (3 Threat). The NPC makes a counter-offer. Lower the Favor cost of Small and Large Requests, Changing Attitudes, and Forging a Permanent alliance by 5, and raise the Favor cost of Above and Beyond by 10.

Hedge Bets (1-3 Threat). The NPC seems reluctant to commit to a deal. Create an amount of Resistance on the players’ next Persuade Task equal to the amount of Threat spent.        

Search for True Motives (No Cost). One of the NPCs, either the target or one of their companions, attempts to uncover whether the players have lied to them, or if they are concealing their true motivations. Choose one PC and attempt an opposed Task against them using Presence/Awareness + Diplomacy/Intrigue, opposed by their Presence/Faith + Diplomacy/Intrigue. On a success, the NPC may ask that PC one question which they must answer honestly. If their answer offends, or negatively conflicts with one of the NPCs’ Values (including NPCs not making the active roll), the players subtract -2 [CD] from their Favor dice pool on their next Persuade Task.

Whisper Poison (No Cost). One of the companions opposed to the players attempts to sway the target NPC back to their side. Make a Difficulty 2 Presence + Diplomacy Task. On a success, roll [CD] equal to that companion’s Diplomacy and reduce Favor by that amount.

Negotiation and Complications

In addition to the GM’s normal use of Complications, there are additional ways a GM may employ Complications during a Negotiation, representing setbacks that occur during a scene as a result of player action or circumstances created by the GM.

  • Annoyed a Companion: Turn an allied companion into a neutral companion. If the companion is already neutral, they may no longer be swayed, and players cannot attempt the Sway a Companion Task on this NPC.
  • Conversational Blunder: Remove 3 Favor from the current total.

Ending a Negotiation

A Negotiation ends when the Difficulty of a Persuade Task would exceed Difficulty 6, when every Player Character decides to end it, or when the party’s goal has been reached and the GM decides that no further progress can be made. The amount of Favor is finalized, and the players may spend it on Goals, the available Goals and their Favor cost determined by the GM roughly aligning to the following template:

Small Request (costs 15 Favor). The NPC grants a small request of the Players that they were unwilling to grant before the negotiation. A small favor request usually can give a small benefit in an upcoming battle, but is never enough to completely change the terms of a battle.

Large Request (costs 20 Favor). The NPC grants a request that involves some amount of risk on the NPC’s part to the Players that they were unwilling to grant before the negotiation. A risky request might be allowing the Players’ army to march through the NPC’s territory, or to pull some political strings on the Players’ behalf.

Change Attitude (costs 25 Favor). The NPC changes an attitude that they have had up until this point, as long as it does not conflict with any of their values. This can be something such as giving the party a division to join their army, to not oppose them in an upcoming battle with a tenuous ally of theirs, or to perform a single action that poses a large risk for the NPC.

Forge Permanent Alliance (costs 35 Favor). The NPC completely changes their loyalty to be fully allied with the Players, as long as they do not have to oppose any of their own values to do so.

Above and Beyond (costs 50 Favor). The NPC becomes not only loyal to the party, but changes their mind on something significant, or agrees to provide a massive boon to the party on goodwill alone, without needing the party’s fulfillment of their agreement upfront first.

When a Negotiation ends, that NPC usually cannot be negotiated with again unless there has been a major change in circumstances since the last negotiation (such as the party gaining a more powerful army or some crucially important leader has died since the last negotiation).

Example Round of Negotiation

As Erik and his companions fight their war against the king, they decide to visit the nearby castle of a duchess to convince her to join their cause. From what they already know, Duchess Marcella is already somewhat favorable to the party’s position against the king, so they only need to achieve enough Favor for a Large Request in order to get her on their side, though they’re hoping to get enough to Forge a Permanent Alliance.

Once Duchess Marcella agrees to meet with the party over dinner in order to negotiate, the GM begins by describing the scene as the party enters the dining room. As they sit down, Duchess Marcella greets them, introducing her spouse next to her, and there is a bit of small talk before the duchess finally gets to the point, saying: “I know exactly why you’re here, you know. What I’m curious about is what you think you can offer me to get me to turn against my sworn liege lord.”

With that, the Negotiation rounds start, with Rylan taking the first turn. They decide to use the Read major action on Duchess Marcella’s husband, Lord Talbot, making a Difficulty 2 Awareness + Diplomacy Task. They generate 3 successes, succeeding on the Task and gaining one Momentum. Rylan isn’t very good at talking, but they are very good at noticing things, and the GM describes how Rylan picks up on Lord Talbot’s attitude as the others begin to discuss the king and his tyranny—it seems that Lord Talbot also dislikes the king, but is so afraid of the consequences of rebellion that he doesn’t want to help. Rylan learns Lord Talbot’s Value: “Rejecting the social order is what gets people killed.”

After Rylan, it is the GM’s turn, and they decide to have Duchess Marcella take the Search for True Motives action against Lorenz. She makes a Presence + Diplomacy Task, opposed by Lorenz’s Presence + Intrigue. Marcella generates 2 successes, and Lorenz only generates 1, so Marcella succeeds and gains 1 Threat that the GM banks in their pool. She then gets to ask Lorenz one question he must answer honestly.

Duchess Marcella: The kingdom has been violently corrupt for decades. Why bother trying to fix it now?
Lorenz: Because the king imprisoned my father, and tarnished my house’s good name. I admit, I probably would have stood by and continued to watch the kingdom devolve into tyranny and corruption as so many have before me, as my father was content to do as well. But the king took him from me, and in doing so opened my eyes to the truth of my circumstances: that my family and I were not free but in bondage to a cruel master.

Duchess Marcella seems lost in thought after hearing Lorenz’ answer, and Rylan notices that both she and her husband seem emotionally affected by Lorenz’ story.

Next it is Erik’s turn. He decides to take the Chit Chat action and begins telling Duchess Marcella and Talbot all about his exploits in his latest battle. Because he’s talking about his combat prowess and using his axe to gesticulate and explain, the GM allows Erik to attempt the Difficulty 2 Task using Brawn + Diplomacy. Erik succeeds but rolls a Complication, and the GM describes that as Erik brandishes his axe to recreate cutting off an enemy’s head, Lord Talbot leaps back, afraid that Erik is trying to attack him. Though the party does their best to explain, forcing Erik to sit back down and put his axe away, the Difficulty of the party’s next attempts to sway Lord Talbot increases by +1.

It goes back to the GM’s turn, and they spend 3 Threat in order to have Duchess Marcella take the Make Demands action. Duchess Marcella beckons for a servant to bring out a portrait, displaying a comely young woman with curly hair and a bashful smile. Marcella explains that this is her eldest daughter, who she is looking for a spouse for. She eyes the party, before making an offer.

Duchess Marcella: If I decide to help you, and that’s a big if, I would like one of you to marry my daughter. She is in need of a spouse, and if you win this war, any one of you will prove important and noble enough to be worthy of her hand.
Adelinde: Does she…want to be married off, Your Grace?
Duchess Marcella: No, which is why she has been doing her utmost to scare off every other suitor up to this point. But surely none of you could be scared away with your rebellion against the king so dependent on my own efforts to aid you, yes?
Erik: Well, to be honest I’m pretty sure we don’t need your help that badly—
Adelinde: We’ll consider it. She certainly looks very pretty, and my own mother has been urging me to get married. If a wedding is what it takes to win you to our side, Your Grace, I would be willing to offer myself to be your daughter’s bride.

Though Erik is disgruntled, Adelinde’s acceptance of Duchess Marcella’s offer gives the party 6 Favor, and both the duchess and her husband look pleased.

On Lorenz’s turn, he decides to mend bridges with Lord Talbot, taking the Excuse action to try and fix Erik’s blunder. Lorenz attempts a Difficulty 2 Presence + Diplomacy Task and succeeds, generating 1 Momentum. He apologizes profusely to Lord Talbot and compliments him on the castle’s beautiful architecture and decoration. Thanks to Lorenz’s good manners, Lord Talbot starts to relax again, agreeing to forget the whole incident with the axe and offering to show Lorenz around the rest of the castle later. Lorenz spends the 1 Momentum he generated to Obtain Information, asking the GM the following question: “How much influence does Lord Talbot have over his wife?” The GM informs Lorenz that throughout the dinner, he would have noticed that while Duchess Marcella is very forceful and independent in her opinions, she does seem to care deeply for her husband, so while Lord Talbot would never be able to fully convince her to do or not do anything, she would be more willing to do something that would make him happy than something that wouldn’t.

Because there are four player characters in this Negotiation, the GM only has two turns, so after Lorenz goes, Adelinde gets to take the last turn of the round. Since she has the best Presence and Diplomacy in the party, she has been saving her turn until the end so she can take the Persuade Task. Before she attempts the roll, however, Adelinde addresses Duchess Marcella directly. Because Rylan noticed that Duchess Marcella was emotionally affected by Lorenz’s story about his father, and because the duchess made a point about asking for a marriage for her daughter, Adelinde theorizes that the duchess has a Value about the importance of family.

Adelinde: Your Grace, we know that what we are asking of you may seem costly and with great danger to you and your noble house. And it is true, the path we walk is not without risk, and we will no doubt suffer some loss in the course of this rebellion. But we are not doing this for our own gain or ambition. We are doing this for our families and for their futures, and so long as the king is in power, our families are not safe, their futures not preserved. Think of your children, and your lovely daughter: do you want them to live their lives hampered by fear and cowering under the tyranny of this wicked king? Or will you take a chance on giving them the lives of happiness and security that they deserve?
GM: Duchess Marcella nods and glances at her husband, taking his hand in hers. Both of them look at the portrait of their daughter and conflicted emotions war on their faces, as though you have touched on something important to them…

Because Adelinde successfully appealed to one of the Duchess’ Values, the party gains +2[CD] on all future Persuade Tasks. Then Adelinde attempts the Difficulty 2 Presence + Diplomacy Task and succeeds, generating 3 successes and gaining 1 Momentum. Because it was a success, Adelinde rolls 7[CD], generating only 3 Favor, so she spends the 1 Momentum she generated earlier to reroll her 5 blank dice. Her reroll generates 4 more Favor, creating 7 Favor total.

Once Adelinde’s turn is over, the round ends. The party has accumulated 13 Favor over the course of the round, which isn’t enough for what they need—a Large Request—so they decide to continue the negotiation and a new round begins. Because Erik successfully accomplished the Chit Chat action, the Difficulty of the Persuade Task in this next round won’t increase, but all characters will suffer a +1 Difficulty Increase if they attempt the same Tasks in this round that they did the previous round.

Part Three: Going to Battle

Chapter Five: Combat

Sometimes circumstances will arise in which characters must take violent action in order to accomplish their goals. When these scenarios arise, characters enter combat.

Combat often involves many moving pieces, including unique rules and abilities that sometimes change the way specific rules are written, or allow characters to subvert the rules when they take certain actions. In addition to the normal Golden Rules of play, there are some combat-specific Golden Rules that always apply:

  • Any effect granted by an ability, talent, or action does not stack with itself unless explicitly stated. If an effect is granted again by the same ability, it replaces the first instance of the bonus. This includes effects from the same ability provided by different characters.
  • If a character succeeds in defending against an attack, the counterstrike damage they deal as a result is not a standard attack, and so cannot be affected by any abilities or reactions that may trigger on a successful attack. Bonus momentum may still be spent to Reroll Damage or add Bonus Damage on a counterstrike.
  • When halving damage, always round down to a minimum of 1.
  • Any modifications to damage (e.g. halving damage from an effect) are applied to the damage before subtracting for resistance.

Turn Sequence

During a conflict scene, characters (also referred to as “units”) perform actions in a specific order. Each character takes a turn, during which they may take a Major Action and a Minor Action (and maybe more). Once each character in the conflict has taken a turn, a single round is completed, and a new round begins. This repeats until the conflict ends.

Players always have the initiative at the start of each round of conflict, letting them act first. At the start of the round, the players nominate one Player Character to take their turn. Once that turn is completed, the GM nominates an NPC to take their turn, and this is followed by another PC turn, and then an NPC turn, and so on until every character on both sides has acted. If all the characters on one side have acted, the remaining characters can take their turns in any order.

Once the round is complete, a new round begins. No character may take more than one Turn per round.

Momentum in Combat

Unlike in narrative play, players no longer bank Momentum in or spend Momentum from their collective pool while in combat, nor may the GM gain, spend, or be given Threat. When a combat encounter begins, the players and GM note down the present totals of both the Momentum and Threat pools and set them aside until the encounter is complete.

Instead of generating Momentum after rolling surplus Successes, players gain bonus momentum, which cannot be saved and must be spent immediately. Players may also generate bonus momentum as a result of talents and abilities.

The standard momentum spends (such as Extra Dice, Create an Advantage, and Gather Information) are unavailable during combat. Bonus Momentum may be spent on a player’s turn to gain the following combat-specific effects:

Name

Cost

Effect

Bonus Damage

1

A character can increase the damage inflicted by a successful Attack, regardless of the type of Attack. Each Momentum spent adds +1 damage.

Extra Minor Action

1

Take an additional Minor Action.

Reroll Damage

1

The player may re-roll any number of [CD] from the current Attack

Swift Task

2

The character may attempt one additional Task (This may only be done once per turn).

If you are rolling [CD] for a reason other than damage during combat, such as for healing during the First Aid task, you may spend momentum to increase the total or reroll blanks using the Bonus Damage or Reroll Damage momentum spends.

Bonus Dice

During combat, bonus dice on Tasks may not be purchased with bonus momentum during combat. However, there are several different ways to add additional dice to your dice pool when attempting a Task in combat. Most bonus dice will come from abilities granted by Talents, though you may also receive bonus dice from actions taken by your allies.

If a character would receive bonus dice from multiple abilities, these instances will stack together, allowing you to add several dice to your pool to a maximum of 5.

Complications

When players or enemy units would generate a Complication during combat, the effect is always the same: the unit suffers +1 Difficulty on their next Task. The Complication goes away after it has affected a Task in this way.

Determination in Combat

During a combat encounter, players may utilize Determination in the same ways as during narrative play, and they also gain two additional ways to spend their Determination: Burst of Effort, and Avoid Injury.

  • Burst of Effort: You spend your Determination to immediately take an additional Major and Minor action on your turn. If you have already taken a Minor action on your turn, you may take that same Minor action again.
  • Avoid Injury: If you are dealt damage that would reduce your HP to 0, you may instead return to 1 HP, ignoring the damage.

In order to spend Determination during combat, players must still trigger their relevant Values or call upon the Common Cause. Players may also still Challenge or Comply with their Values in order to gain Determination during combat, however they are still limited to 3 Determination held at once.

Actions in Combat

On any given Turn in combat, a character can attempt a single Major Action, two Minor Actions, and any number of free actions.

Minor Actions

Minor Actions are actions that characters can take in combat that are small enough to not require a Task. Minor actions are often used to set up Major Actions, such as aiming before making an attack. Characters may perform two Minor Actions for free during their Turn, and may take unlimited additional Minor Actions at the immediate cost of one Bonus Momentum each.

Each Minor Action can only be performed once per Turn. Unless otherwise stated, any bonus from using a Minor Action (such as the re-roll from Aim or the temporary HP from block) lasts until the end of your next turn or until you retake the same Minor Action, whichever comes first. Characters may use the following Minor Actions, as well as any they gain from their talents, when in combat:

  • Aim: You may re-roll a single d20 made on your next attack, keeping the second result.
  • Block: You protect yourself or an ally within Reach from attack. You or the ally you are blocking gain +2[CD] Temporary HP.
  • Brandish: You may roll an +1[CD] on the damage roll of your next weapon attack.
  • Climb: You scale an object or area of terrain that is 1 level of height above or below you. You may not take this action if you are mounted. This counts as Voluntary Movement.
  • Dismiss Mount: You send your mount to safety, away from the battlefield. You cannot be riding your mount when you take this action.
  • Draw Item: You may draw an item carried on your person or pick up an item within the same or an adjacent space as yourself. If an item does not require a Major Action to use, it can be used immediately, allowing you to draw and use the item with a single Minor Action.
  • Interact: You interact with an object in the environment. Particularly complex actions may require a Major Action instead.
  • Move: You move a number of spaces up to your Speed. You may not take this action if you used the Sprint Major Action this turn. This counts as Voluntary Movement.
  • Mount/Dismount: You immediately dismount from the creature you are riding, or climb onto it. This counts as Voluntary Movement.
  • Stand: You stand from being prone, removing all effects from the status. You may not Drop Prone and Stand in the same Turn.

Major Actions

Major actions are significant, effort intensive actions that often require attempting a Task. Characters may attempt a single Major Action for free during their turn, and may spend Momentum or their Determination in order to attempt a second Major Action (see below).

The following Major Actions are available during Combat:

  • Assist: You perform some activity that will grant an ally an advantage. You nominate a single ally you can communicate with, and declare how you are giving aid, including which Attribute, Skill, and Focus (if any) you are assisting with. During the nominated ally’s Task, you use a reaction to assist using the chosen Attribute, Skill, and Focus, as normal for assisting on a Task.
  • Attack: You attack an enemy or other viable target, and attempt to inflict harm. See Making an Attack for a full explanation.
  • Cast a Spell: You cast a magickal spell. See Chapter Eight: Magick for a full explanation.
  • Console: Your words inspire a demoralized Ally within Range 10 of you. Make a Difficulty 1 Presence + Authority check. On a success, your target regains all Willpower.
  • Demoralize: You attempt to demoralize an enemy within Range 10 of you and deal damage to their Willpower. Make a Presence + Diplomacy check contested by Faith + Skirmish. On a success, you deal 2 + Diplomacy [CD] Willpower damage.
  • Disengage: You get yourself out of harm’s way. Until the end of your turn, your movement does not provoke opportunity attacks.
  • Direct: [Requires the Commander or Tactician Talents] You nominate a single other character within range equal to your Presence, and the nominated character may immediately use their reaction to attempt a single Task ordered by you, assisted by your Presence + Authority. If they succeed, you may grant them any bonus momentum you currently have to spend on the result. You may use this action a number of times per scene equal to your Authority.
  • First Aid: You attempt to give yourself or a friendly target some quick healing. In order to attempt this Task, you must be able to touch your Target. This is a Reason + Medicine Task with a Difficulty of 1. On a success, roll [CD] equal to Medicine. The target regains HP equal to the result.
  • Grapple: You attempt to grab an adjacent opponent and overpower them. This is an Opposed Task using Brawn + Skirmish, opposed by the defender’s Brawn + Skirmish.

On a success, the target is Immobilized, and only moves when the attacker moves. Neither character can take reactions while engaged in a grapple, and cannot deal damage from counterstriking. A grapple ends when the attacker ends the grapple as a free action on their turn; the attacker or defender is moved to be no longer adjacent to the other, such as if they are knocked back by an effect; or if the defender succeeds on a Task to escape as a Minor Action on their Turn, using either Agility, Brawn, or Coordination + Skirmish and opposed by the same Attribute + Skirmish from the defender. Only one character may be grappled by you at a time. When grappling creatures that are larger than Size 1 (Size 1 + X), the Difficulty of the Task increases by X.

  • Guard: You put yourself between an ally and a source of danger. Choose one ally within your Reach and attempt a Faith + Skirmish Task with a Difficulty of 1. On a success, the Difficulty of any attacks made against your chosen ally increases by +1 until the start of your next Turn. Your ally can only benefit from the effects of Guard so long as they remain within your Reach and you are not incapacitated or unconscious.
  • Hide: You attempt to find a position where you are hidden or obscured from an enemy’s view. This is a Difficulty 2 Agility + Intrigue Task (this Task cannot be attempted while engaged with an enemy).

On a success, you are hidden from sight and cannot be targeted by attacks unless the enemy uses a Search action to discover you or until you take any hostile action against another character. You can only attempt to Hide if you have Cover from an enemy (Cover granted by items like shields does not count).

  • Pinpoint: You target an enemy on the battlefield, highlighting their weaknesses. You choose an enemy on the battlefield within Range equal to your Reason, and create an Advantage for you or an ally to use, lowering the Difficulty of any Task made against the target. This Advantage remains on the target until it is used.
  • Ready: You declare that you are waiting for a specific situation or event to occur before attempting a Task. This situation or event must be chosen when Ready is declared, as well as the specific Task being attempted when that situation occurs. When this triggering situation occurs, you may use a reaction to temporarily interrupt the acting character’s Turn to resolve your readied Task. If the triggering situation is another character’s Major Action, the readied Task is resolved before any dice are rolled for the inciting action. Once the readied Task has resolved, events continue as normal. You cannot use any other reactions until your readied Task has been resolved, and if the triggering situation does not occur before your next Turn, the readied Task is lost. Characters who use the Ready Action can still perform Minor Actions during their Turn as normal, but cannot take a second Major Action.
  • Recall Mount: If you have a mount that has been dismissed from the battlefield, you may recall it to your side.
  • Refocus: You pause to catch your breath. You regain full Willpower.
  • Search: You attempt to find a Hidden character on the field. This is a Difficulty 2 Awareness + Intrigue Task with a range equal to your Awareness. On a success, you detect your target and they no longer gain the benefits of being hidden from you, but only if they are within range.
  • Shove: You attempt to shove an adjacent character. This is a Brawn + Skirmish Task of difficulty 1, opposed by the defender’s Agility + Skirmish if they choose to resist. On a success, you move your target 1 space away from you, in a direction of your choice. This counts as involuntary movement and does not provoke opportunity attacks.
  • Sprint: You move a number of spaces up to three times your Speed. You may not take this action if you have already used the Move Minor Action on this turn. This counts as Voluntary Movement.

A character can attempt a single Task during each Turn, though you may also use the following ways to attempt a second Task:

  • Determination: You can spend a point of Determination in order to take another Major and Minor Action on your turn.
  • Swift Task (Momentum Spend): You can spend 2 points of bonus Momentum in order to take a second Major Action on your turn.

Regardless of the method used, a character cannot attempt more than two Tasks in a round.

Free Actions

Free actions are special actions that a character can take on their turn that are neither Minor or Major actions and do not count against the number of those actions that a character can take. A character may take an unlimited number of free actions on their turn. Most free actions come from special abilities granted by a character’s Talents or equipment, though falling prone and stowing or dropping a held item is always a free action.

  • Fall Prone: You drop to the ground.
  • Stow/Drop Item: You stash an item on your person, or drop it on the ground.

Reactions

In addition to their own actions taken on their Turns, characters can use reactions, special actions that characters can take outside of the turn order in response to actions taken by other characters.

You may take one reaction each turn, but you cannot take the same reaction more than once per Round unless otherwise specified. You cannot use reactions during your own Turn.

Reactions have a specific condition or circumstance that allow them to be used, and they must be declared immediately as soon as that condition applies. If responding to an action taken by another character, reactions resolve after the action resolves, unless otherwise specified. By default, each reaction may be used 1/round, and uses reset at the start of your turn.

There is one default reaction that all characters may use, though they may gain other reactions from Talents or other special abilities:

  • Opportunity Attack: When an enemy takes any Voluntary Movement while inside of your Reach without taking the Disengage Major Action, you may use a reaction to make a single melee weapon attack on the enemy target. This attack is an Opposed Task, but only the attacker deals damage on a success.

Making an Attack

There are two types of attacks in Ascension: melee attacks and ranged attacks. Characters make attacks by using weapons or spells to attempt Opposed Tasks against their target, using Attributes determined by the weapon or spell being used.

The process of making an attack is outlined in the steps below.

  1. Attacker declares attack: The attacker decides they wish to make an attack and chooses how.
  1. If a melee weapon or spell is chosen, the attack is a melee attack.
  2. If a ranged weapon or spell is chosen, the attack is a ranged attack.
  1. Attacker chooses target: The attacker chooses a target for the attack. This can be any creature or object which can be damaged by the attack.
  1. A melee attack can be used against a target within Reach of the attacker.
  2. A ranged attack can be used against any target within range and in line of sight of the attacker.
  • Ranged attacks have +1 Difficulty if the attacker is adjacent to any enemies.
  1. Skill Test: The attacker makes an Opposed Task against their target. Both the attacker and the defender use an Attribute determined by the attacker’s weapon or spell. Unless otherwise stated, both always use Skirmish for the Skill. Like any Opposed Task, the defender rolls first, followed by the attacker’s roll. Any increases or reductions to the Difficulty by effects or abilities are then applied.
  1. If the target is unable or chooses not to defend themself (such as if they were Incapacitated), this becomes a Difficulty 1 Task to determine if the attack hits.

[Insert Weapon Triangle Diagram here]

  1. Outcome: If the attacker succeeds on the Task, they get to inflict damage on their target. If the defender wins the Opposed Task, they may inflict damage on the attacker as a Counterstrike if they are able.
  1. The defender may only counterstrike when defending against a melee attack and if they are also wielding a melee weapon.
  1. Calculating Damage: Damage is calculated in the following order:
  1. A number of challenge dice [CD] are rolled equal to the weapon’s base damage + the wielder’s Skirmish.
  2. If there are relevant effects that would reduce or increase the damage, these are applied now (e.g. -2 damage from Fire spells from Pyromancer 2). When halving, round down to a minimum of 1.
  3. The target’s Resistance is subtracted from the damage.
  4. Remaining damage is inflicted on the target, subtracting from their HP.

Multiple Targets and Bonus Momentum

If any Task calls for a contested check against more than one opponent, the reactive characters each roll first, followed by the active character who only rolls once. Any reactive characters that rolled equal to or below the active character’s number of successes fail the Task, as usual, but the effective Difficulty for determining how much bonus Momentum is generated is the single highest number of Successes made by any of the reactive characters.

In other words, if you cast Fireball and roll 3 Successes on your Magick + Skirmish task, and the 2 Characters in the area of effect roll 4 and 2 Successes respectively, then no bonus Momentum is generated because the highest number of successes from a reactive character (4) is higher than the number of successes the active character generated (3)—which also means that enemy unit isn’t dealt any damage by the attack—while the lowest number of successes (2) is lower than the active character’s (3). However, if both of the reactive characters roll 2 successes each, 1 bonus Momentum is generated.

[Sidebar] Focuses in Combat

When in combat, litigating whether a character’s Focuses might apply to the situation can slow down the flow of battle. In order to streamline this, here is an optional rule for how to use Focuses during combat scenarios:

Combat Focuses. During character creation, characters may choose two Skills that they have specialized in as their “Combat Focuses.” Instead of relying on their written Focuses to gain an expanded crit range during combat, any time a character attempts a Task using one of their specialized Skills they gain an expanded crit range based on that Skill. You may also swap which Skills you are specialized in when you level up. You may choose a third Skill at level 6.

Damage and Injuries

Beneath their armor and behind their courage, characters can withstand a degree of punishment before any lasting injury is caused. This ability to endure is represented by the character’s amount of Health Points (HP), a total equal to Three Health Bars, each being Brawn + Skirmish, for a Max HP of (Brawn + Skirmish) * 3. Characters may be able to increase the maximum of a Health Bar and thus their Max HP through other means, such as Talents.

When a character takes damage, they first subtract any Resistance they have from the damage total (see Resistance and Cover), and any damage remaining affects the target, subtracting from the character’s total amount of HP. Each point of damage on the damage roll, after reductions, removes a single point of HP.

When a character’s HP is reduced to certain amounts, they suffer Wounds. Wounds are temporary harms that a character suffers as they take more and more damage during a fight. Characters suffer a Wound when their HP is reduced by 1 and 2 Health bars, and they can get rid of these Wounds when their HP is restored above those totals.

  • Wound 1: When a Character’s HP is reduced by at least 1 Health Bar (in other words, is at or below ⅔ of their maximum HP) they suffer Wound 1, causing their speed to be reduced by 2.
  • Wound 2: When a Character’s HP is reduced by at least 1 Health Bar (in other words, is at or below ⅓ of their maximum HP) they suffer Wound 2, causing them to be unable to take Swift Tasks (the penalty of Wound 1 continues to apply).

Injuries

When a character’s HP is reduced to zero, they become Incapacitated and fall Prone. If a character is healed and their HP restored, they are no longer Incapacitated but remain Prone until they take the Stand Minor Action. Characters at 0 HP cannot take further damage but may still suffer Statuses inflicted by attacks.

Characters that have been reduced to 0 HP may also choose to die rather than become Incapacitated. If a player chooses for their character to die, they immediately gain a point of Determination which they may spend or grant to an ally, and they may immediately take a turn, acting as if their character had full HP (they do not suffer from the consequences of Wounds). Once that turn ends, the character is permanently dead and cannot return to play.

At the end of battle, characters that have been reduced to 0 HP suffer their Injuries. Injuries are permanent harms that may last until a character receives careful treatment from a medic or healer. Once battle is concluded, all characters who have been reduced to 0 HP one or more times must make an Injury check to determine the results of their Injury. In order to make an Injury check, roll a d20 for every time your character has been reduced to 0 HP during the battle (1d20 for only one reduction to 0 HP, 2d20 for the second, and so on). You must take the highest result rolled and check the corresponding number on the Injury chart to determine the outcome.

Ascension provides levels of lethality of injuries: Noble, Deadly, and Brutal. With noble injuries, player characters will not die from their injuries, but may suffer serious narrative consequences from them. Players and the GM should agree on what level of lethality at the start of the campaign, and may adjust the table as they feel is appropriate for the desired tone of the campaign, and then roll on that version of the table when determining injuries after a battle.

Treat Injury: A character attempts to treat an injury on themselves or an ally. This is a Difficulty 3 Reason + Medicine Task to treat an ally and Difficulty 4 to treat themself. The Difficulty is increased for every additional number of times the affected character rolled on the injury effect table.

Unless agreed upon by the players and GM at the start of the campaign, all Treat Injuries tasks may Succeed at Cost.

Avoid Injury: Once per scene, a character may spend their Determination to Avoid Injury. If a character is dealt damage that would reduce their HP to 0, they may instead return to 1HP, ignoring the damage.

Injury Traits

Lasting injuries are sorted into three categories that shape the degree to which they affect the character. The affected player and the GM should collaborate to determine the appropriate injury for the character to suffer and how it might affect them based on the category of injury they suffered.

Temporary Injuries: A temporary injury is an injury that creates a lasting impact on the character for weeks as it takes time to heal and is certain to leave a scar.

Minor Permanent Injuries: A minor permanent injury is an injury that creates a long term impact on the character for years or longer. Examples may include a temporary limp, chronic pain, or losing hearing in an ear.

Major Permanent injuries: A major permanent injury is an injury that massively affects the life of the inflicted character. Examples may include losing a limb or an eye or losing the ability to move a body-part.

By default, Ascension assumes that injury traits do not ultimately hamper the functioning of the character, instead affecting them on a story level. A character who loses a limb may gain a prosthetic that allows them to keep fighting, but may suffer phantom limb pain. A character who loses an eye may learn to fight without depth perception, but may be looked at differently by strangers than they were before.

When handling injuries, they should be used to expand the narrative and development of the affected character instead of being treated as purely a mechanical debuff, in narrative or combat play both. Ascension does not define any mechanical consequences for injuries; any mechanical complications should be agreed upon by the player and GM both, and are recommended not to be any worse than the effect of a wound.

Temporary HP

Some abilities or spells may grant temporary health points (temporary HP), which is a special type of HP that goes away completely once a condition has been met, it is replaced, or when it has been depleted. Temporary HP does not add to your maximum HP total, but is a separate pool of HP that buffers you against damage to your actual HP. When taking damage, you subtract from your temporary HP first if you have it, and only take damage to your HP total when you no longer have any temporary HP.

Once lost, temporary HP cannot be restored, so any abilities or spells that heal HP cannot restore temporary HP. Temporary HP also cannot stack, so once an instance of temporary HP is granted, granting a second instance of temporary HP would replace the first, not add onto it.

Willpower

Though physical damage is the only thing that can kill a character, the stress of battle and the cries of their enemies can also affect a character’s will to keep fighting. This resolve to keep going is represented by a character’s Willpower, which is equal to their Faith.

When a character receives damage from a Demoralize Task, they subtract the damage from their Willpower. Willpower is not affected by Resistance, and unless stated otherwise, Willpower Damage is not considered Damage for any rules that refer generally to Damage.

If a Character’s Willpower reaches 0, they are Rattled, and all tasks increase in Difficulty by 1. A character can clear Rattled as soon as any amount of Willpower is restored, such as with the Console Minor Action.

Statuses

When in combat, certain attacks, abilities, circumstances, and weapon qualities may affect a character with one of the following Statuses.

  • Blinded: While Blinded, you cannot see (you have +1 Difficulty on Tasks that target or are contested by characters you cannot see, such as Attacking or Defending. See Visibility and Hidden Characters below).
  • Dazed: When Dazed, you can only take one Major Action or one Minor Action on your turn. You may still use the Burst of Effort Determination spend to gain extra actions.
  • Enraged: When Enraged, the Difficulty of Attacks made against all creatures except the source of your Rage increases by 1.
  • Exposed: While Exposed, you gain no benefit from Resistance.
