Some of the following structures listed operate on the assumption that you will be using segments and have rules accordingly.

  • Walls are sheer structures of 1 or more Height built to defend a location and block passage through an area. Walls often serve as the border of zones. If a wall stands as the border between two zones, then divisions cannot pass into that zone without an open gate until the wall is destroyed or unless they take a different route. There are three types of walls:
  • Weak walls are cheaper fortifications made of wood, mud, or brick. These include walls around simple forts and small villages. Weak Walls have between 4-7 health.
  • Moderate walls are made of more durable material such as stone or concrete. These include most buildings, town walls, palaces, and simple castles. Moderate Walls usually have between 8-14 health.
  • Fortified walls are heavily reinforced defenses of cities, mighty castles, and fortresses. They are often 2 spaces thick and allow for officers to walk atop their battlements. Fortified Walls usually have between 15-21 health.
  • Gates are entrance ways used to pass through walls or other fortifications. They usually take up one or two tiles. Gates are usually constructed out of wood and will have half the health of the adjacent walls. A gate made of metal will have the same health as the walls it is attached to.
  • A gate may also be opened or closed as a Minor Action from inside its walls.
  • Turrets are high towered structures from which ranged weapons can be fired. They are usually 1-3 tiles wide and often are part of or atop walls. Turrets use the same health ranges as walls do.
  • Bridges are structures over water or above a great height difference. They are between 1-4 spaces wide. When destroyed, they generally leave the area between two locations impassable.
  • Wooden bridges usually have 6-12 health.
  • Stone bridges usually have 13-18 health.
  • Dams are stone structures designed to hold back the flow of water, preventing a region of the battlefield from being flooded. When destroyed, some specified area on the battlefield will get flooded with Deep or Perilous Water. Dams usually have 15-20 health.
  • Unstable Slopes are sides of mountains, cliffs, or hills that are on the verge of collapse. When one segment is destroyed, every segment of the structure collapses in a landslide and for every level of height the landslide falls deals 4[CD] piercing damage to an adjacent area below. Unstable Slopes usually have between 5-15 health.
  • Pathways are usually 1 wide walkway at an elevated height providing a walkway around the side of a sheer cliff or wall. When destroyed, the pathway is rendered unusable. Pathways use the same health ranges as walls or unstable slopes.
  • Other Structures such as houses, windmills, churches, or any other objects or buildings on the battlefield that may be targeted can have between 4-12 health, at the GM’s discretion.

Structures can only be damaged by certain divisions (such as trebuchets or mangonels) and cannot be damaged by players and NPCs. If a structure being targeted by an attack has multiple segments, the ordering officer must choose one of the segments as the target of the attack. Each segment of the structure accumulates damage separately.

Destroyed structures (or segments of structure) are replaced with appropriate terrain. Any character on top of the destroyed structure immediately takes the applicable fall damage and is knocked Prone.

Destroying segments of a structure can take different forms depending on the structure and the terrain around it. For example:

  • When a wall segment is destroyed, it may be replaced with difficult terrain that officers and divisions may move through.
  • When a gate is destroyed, it may be replaced with normal terrain, allowing easy passage through the wall.
  • When a bridge segment is destroyed, the spaces where that segment was may be replaced by Perilous Water.
  • When a segment of a dam is destroyed, water may flow from the spaces out across the battlefield, replacing all spaces along its path with Deep or Perilous Water.

The consequences of destroying segments of a structure are ultimately up to the GM.

Special structures may have resistance or provide certain buffs or debuffs to characters on the battlefield, at the GM’s discretion.

Example Round of Mass Combat:

The party of Lorenz, Adelinde, Erik, and Rylan and their army have chosen to take a stand against the king’s formidable army at a strategically important bridge. Before the combat scenario begins, the party and the GM make note of the current totals in their Momentum and Threat pools in order to remember them for later, but these currencies will not be relevant during combat itself and are set aside. Each party member also checks their equipment, and Lorenz his spell list, to make sure that they have everything equipped that they want to use before combat begins.

The party then determines which stratagems they want to have their divisions prepare. Rylan suggests they take Longbows for their bowmen to have extra range against their enemies. Lorenz insists on giving their mages Siege Magic so that they can attempt to destroy the bridge to prevent the king’s army from crossing it. For their Light Footmen, they choose the stratagem Push In.

When the GM presents the battle map, the party takes note of the battlefield’s division into five zones: the west riverbank containing their deployment area, the east riverbank with the king’s army, the stone bridge and the land at its entrances, and two zones of river water—perilous to the north of the bridge and only deep water to the south. The enemy army’s officers are a crusher, a warrior, a banneret, a bladesman, two cavaliers, and a pegasus knight commander. While the king’s army is scale 4, the GM chooses to only deploy 3 enemy divisions: a heavy infantry division, a light infantry division, and a pegasi cavalry division. Because the enemy army has fewer divisions than its scale, each of its divisions gains an extra 1[CD] to its attacks and 1 point of total morale.

The GM declares the party’s battle objective is to Holdout and defend their deployment area for 5 rounds, while also stating that Lorenz’s goal to destroy the bridge is a bonus objective that, if achieved, will grant a point of Determination for each party member. Once the PCs have placed their tokens in the deployment area, the combat can begin.

Wanting to ensure the enemy army is unable to force its way across the bridge, Adelinde chooses to go first. She starts by, as a free action, ordering the footmen division to use its Free Move into the bridge zone. To swiftly cross the bridge on her horse, she takes the Sprint major action to move 24 spaces into the east river bank zone beside the enemy officers. Next, she takes advantage of the Light Footmen’s ability to be ordered as a minor action to order them to Reposition and move into her current zone. She rolls 3 successes, earning 2 bonus momentum and successfully bringing the light footmen into the zone with her. Hoping to defeat the army’s leader early, she uses her Willbreaker minor action then uses both of her bonus momentum to perform a Swift Task and attack the pegasus knight commander, taking advantage of the knight’s weaker Brawn. Both she and the knight have infantry at their side providing the To Arms buff, giving each of them an Advantage on the attack/defense and effectively canceling each other out. Adelinde and the pegasus knight both roll 1 success, which means Adelinde succeeds but only earns 1 bonus momentum from Cavalry Adept. She rolls 4 damage and 2 effects, spending her momentum to reroll 2 blank dice to get a total of 6 damage and 3 effects, inflicting 5 damage after the knight’s Resistance and 3 Will damage.

Because of the presence of Adelinde’s footmen, the enemy infantry are unable to leave the east bank zone without provoking a Mass Opportunity Attack. Thus in an effort to drive Adelinde’s footmen back, the GM decides to have the banneret go. As his major action, the banneret immediately orders the enemy heavy footmen division to make an attack against Adelinde’s light footmen division. As a reaction, Adelinde chooses to order a Brace, allowing her to turn the attack roll into a contested check. Each of them roll a Presence + Authority task and each earn 2 successes. Succeeding on his order, the banneret rolls 7[CD]—based on the footmen’s base damage, his Authority, and the +1 bonus damage from the king’s army’s scale—generating 6 damage, subtracting 1 from Adelinde’s footmen’s Resistance and reducing them to 3/8 morale. With no bonus threat, the banneret uses a minor action to Move in order to get further from Adelinde while still staying in the zone. With his second minor action, the banneret takes the Block minor action, generating 1 point of temporary HP for himself.

On Rylan’s turn, they first take the Move minor action to advance forward to shoot at the enemy soldiers on the opposite bank. The pegasus knight is still just out of Rylan’s range, they instead decide to try and fire at the crusher. Rylan takes the Aim minor action first, then takes the Attack major action, generating 3 successes against the crusher’s 1. Because of the bowmen division’s buff Projectile Cloud, Rylan’s attack gains the Startling damage effect. They roll 7 damage and 2 effects, dealing 5 damage after the crusher’s Resistance which reduces them to 5/10 HP, and thanks to the crusher’s Awareness effect save of only 2, also inflicts the Off-Guard status. With 2 bonus momentum, Rylan decides to use Swift Task to make another attack to try and finish off the crusher. Rolling without Aiming this time, they only generate 2 successes against the crusher’s 1 success. Rylan rolls 4 damage and spends their single generated bonus momentum for 1 extra damage. Because the crusher is Off-Guard, they don’t benefit from resistance, so they take all 5 points of damage and are defeated.

The GM has one of the cavaliers go next. Hoping to leave Adelinde vulnerable without her footmen, they have the cavalier use a minor action to order the king’s light footmen to attack Adelinde’s own light footmen. Because she has already used the Brace reaction this round, she is unable to do so again, so the cavalier instead rolls against a Difficulty of 1. With a target of 10, the cavalier only manages to roll 1 success, but that is just enough to succeed. With only 2 Authority, the cavalier rolls 5[CD], generating 4 damage which is just enough to defeat Adelinde’s light footmen and leave them Broken. As the GM gets to choose where the division retreats to, they choose to send it into the deep water zone south of the bridge as the king’s forces cut off the division’s attempt to flee over the bridge. The division now cannot be issued any orders until it is Regrouped. As the cavalier still has a major action, they first Move as a minor action to ride within range of Adelinde and make an attack. Adelinde defends with her Brawn, rolling 3 successes from 3 dice thanks to her shield against the cavalier’s own 2 successes. But because the cavalier has an Advantage from their infantry’s To Arms buff and Adelinde does not, the Difficulty of their attack is reduced by 1, meaning the cavalier’s attack succeeds. As the GM gave the cavalier the Charge optional feature, they roll an additional CD and gain the Knockdown damage effect. The cavalier rolls 6 damage and 3 effects, which thanks to Adelinde’s full plate armor is reduced to only 1 damage, bringing her to 38/39 HP.  Despite meeting her Brawn effect save, this roll does not knock Adelinde Prone because the Plate quality of her armor increases her effect save against the Knockdown effect by +1. Now that Adelinde’s light footmen are gone, the cavalier could command one of the king’s infantry divisions to move onto the bridge, but since there are no allied officers on the bridge yet, the GM chooses not to in order to avoid letting the infantry division be attacked without an ally to Brace.

Lorenz goes next. Hoping to help Adelinde and work on destroying the bridge, Lorenz first orders the Mage division into the bridge’s zone as a free action. In order to be able to give them another order, he must follow them inside, so he takes the Move minor action to move up to his speed, just barely making it into the edge of the bridge zone. Hoping to generate enough momentum to cast a spell and issue an order, as his major action, Lorenz casts Firebolt against one of the bladesmen. He declares he is using the mage division’s buff Arcane Expertise to treat his Skirmish as one higher for this task, increasing his target to a 16 and his crit range to a 5. Rolling a 12 and a 5, he generates 4 successes against the bladesman, generating 2 bonus momentum from the successes and an additional point from his spell implement for a total of 3 bonus momentum. He rolls 6[CD] Piercing for his damage--his Skirmish is still increased by the division which gives an extra [CD]--rolling 3 damage and then spending a bonus momentum to reroll his blanks for another 4 damage, which defeats the bladesman. With 2 bonus momentum left, he has enough to Swift Task, so as a second major action he orders the Mages to make an attack against the bridge structure. Because the bridge cannot Brace, he rolls his Presence + Authority against a Difficulty of 1, generating 1 success. Lorenz adds together the mage’s 2[CD] base damage, his authority of 2, and the additional 2 dice from Siege Magic for a total of 6[CD] damage, getting 6 damage as the result. The bridge has 14 health and no Resistance, so it is reduced to 8 HP.

The GM then has the pegasus knight commander take her turn. Content that her other officers will be able to handle Adelinde without her footmen, she chooses to go after Lorenz’s mages. Thanks to the buff from the Pegasi Cavalry, she is able to take the Move minor action and get out of Adelinde’s range without provoking an opportunity attack and onto the bridge right beside Lorenz. She then uses a free action to order the pegasi cavalry’s Free Move to follow her into the bridge zone and a major action to order them to attack Lorenz’s Mage Division. Lorenz chooses to Brace as a reaction. As a commander, the pegasus knight has 4 Authority, so she rolls against a target of 11. She generates 1 success, while Lorenz manages to roll 2, allowing his mages to Counterstrike against the melee attack. He rolls his mage’s damage of 5[CD], generating 7 damage, reduced to 6 after the pegasi cavalry’s Resistance, reducing them to 2/8 Morale. Because of her Commander Feature Tactician, the Pegasus Knight is able to take another major action after giving an order, and she chooses to attack Lorenz. Lorenz’s Skirmish is no longer increased by the mage division now that he has finished the task for the spell, so he only has a target of 10 when defending. The pegasus knight rolls 3 successes against his 1 then rolls 6[CD] for 6 damage, increased to 8 from her bonus momentum. Lorenz has 1 Resistance and so takes 7 damage, leaving him at 23/30 HP. The pegasus knight then uses her feature Darting Blow to move 5 spaces without provoking an opportunity attack. She enters the perilous water zone to the north, and because of the division’s special feature, can use another free action to command the pegasi cavalry to use a second Free Move to follow her.

Erik is last member of the party to act, and considers his options carefully. He wants to charge across the bridge to fight the enemy officers, but he knows that if the enemy infantry divisions move onto the bridge, the enemy officers will have an Advantage against him and his allies because of the infantry’s To Arms buff. He also knows that if the pegasus knight can hold onto her pegasi cavalry, she will keep escaping over the water and remaining out of reach. First he decides to attempt to deal with the pegasi cavalry, using a Major Action to order their bowmen division to attack the pegasi cavalry. The pegasi cavalry are in an adjacent zone, but the bowmen’s Longbows stratagem allows them to attack anyway. While Erik has a Leadership focus and Authority of 3, his 8 Presence only gives him a target of 11, so he decides to spend his Determination to set one of the dice in his pool to a 1, generating 2 successes automatically. The Pegasus Knight Braces, rolling an extra die from her Braced optional feature as a commander. Erik rolls another success, and the Pegasus Knight rolls 2, leaving Erik successful and generating 2 bonus momentum because of the decreased Difficulty of attacking a Flying division with a Projectile division. He rolls the bowmen’s 5[CD] damage and gets 4 damage, enough to defeat the pegasi and leave them broken. Since the only adjacent zone that doesn’t have one of his allied divisions in it is with the rest of the army, he decides not to have it retreat. He then moves into the edge of the Deep Water zone and uses his bonus momentum to order the Light Footmen to Regroup, which he can do even though they have already been given an order this round because they are Broken. With 10 Faith and 3 Authority, Erik’s target is 13 with a Difficulty of 2 because the division is Broken. He generates 2 successes and rolls 5[CD], generating 4 restored morale. Because they are in the water and thus all the zones borders are hazardous, he will have to use a Reposition order next round to move them onto the shore again.

After Erik’s turn, the rest of the enemy units may go. Of the units still standing, the warrior and the other cavalier haven’t gone yet. The warrior goes first, moving immediately to attack Adelinde. They roll 2 successes against Adelinde’s 1 success, then gain an additional success because of the Advantage from To Arms. The warrior rolls 9[CD] damage thanks to its great axe, generating 10 damage which is increased to 12 with their 2 bonus momentum, reducing Adelinde to 31/39 HP after Resistance. Next the cavalier goes, first using a Free Move to command the Heavy Footmen to move onto the bridge, then taking a minor action to move onto the bridge. Once in position, the cavalier makes a successful attack on Lorenz, dealing another 6 damage reduced to 5, leaving Lorenz at 18/30 HP and inflicting a Wound.

After that, all of the enemy units have taken their turns or been defeated, and each army has the option to make any division that has not taken a Free Move do so. The players have no divisions able to, but the GM decides to have the king’s light footmen use a Free Move to get onto the bridge after the heavy footmen. After that, a new round begins.

Chapter Eleven: Building Blocks of an Army

This chapter includes all of the pieces you need to build an army: Divisions and their Stratagems, and your army’s Talents.

Divisions

Divisions each have their own set of features and abilities specified in their description. Each division will also have at least one Type listed, which describes its role on the battlefield and any strengths or weaknesses it may have.

  • Infantry: Infantry divisions are the foot soldiers of your army, and often will make up the bulk of an army’s fighting force. They provide buffs to an army’s melee attackers, making them quite strong when unchallenged in a zone.
  • Cavalry: Cavalry divisions are made up of mounted soldiers, ideal for extra mobility or extra damage.
  • Projectile: Projectile divisions can attack enemy divisions at a distance, preventing counterstrikes from an enemy division so long as they are not also the Projectile type.
  • Flying: Flying divisions are swift and agile in the air, but vulnerable to arrows and projectile weapons. Projectile Type divisions gain -1 Difficulty on attacks against Flying Type divisions.
  • Magick: Magick divisions deal punishing blows to enemy divisions at range, while being more vulnerable to physical attacks.
  • Support: Support divisions grant bonuses not only to the army’s officers, but also to the army itself.
  • Siege: Siege divisions excel at bringing down Structures. You may only attack Structures with Siege Type divisions.

Officers may only benefit from two of the same buff at any given time. (E.g. an officer may not benefit from two light footmen’s buff or from one light footmen and one heavy footmen, as they provide To Arms).

Light Footmen

Easy to train, quick to field.

Type: Infantry

Resistance: 1

Attack Damage: 2[CD]

Buff: To Arms - When an allied officer in the same zone makes or is targeted by a melee attack, they gain an advantage on their roll to attack/defend.

Features: 

  • This division may be issued an order as a Minor Action while unbroken.
  • If there is at least one allied officer in this division’s zone, whenever an enemy division moves out of this zone, the border is considered Hazardous unless the division is flying.

Heavy Footmen

Tougher soldiers for intense skirmishes.

Type: Infantry

Resistance: 3

Attack Damage: 2[CD]

Buff: To Arms - When an allied officer in the same zone makes or is targeted by a melee attack, they gain an advantage on their roll to attack/defend.

Features: 

  • If there is at least one allied officer in this division’s zone, whenever an enemy division moves out of this zone, the border is considered Hazardous unless the division is flying.

Bowmen

Archers ready for battle.

Type: Projectile

Resistance: 1

Ranged Attack Damage: 2[CD]

Buff: Projectile Cloud - Whenever an allied officer in the same zone makes an attack with a ranged weapon, they gain the Startling damage effect.

Features: 

  • When this division attacks divisions with the Flying type, the Difficulty is reduced by 1.

Ballista

Massive crossbow-like projectile weapons.

Type: Projectile

Resistance: 0

Ranged Attack Damage: 4[CD]

Buff: None

Features: 

  • When this division makes an attack, the ordering officer uses their study instead of authority for the task.
  • This division may attack any division in an adjacent zone, increasing the Difficulty of 1.
  • All zone borders are considered Hazardous for this division.
  • When this division attacks divisions with the Flying type, the Difficulty is reduced by 1.

Light Horse Cavalry

Horseback riders, good for scouting ahead.

Type: Cavalry

Resistance: 1

Attack Damage: 3[CD]

Buff: Gallop - A mounted allied officer that starts their turn in the same zone may take the movement Minor Action for free.

Features: 

  • This division can make two Free Moves every round. An officer may order this division to Free Move even if they have already ordered a Free Move this turn.

Heavy Horse Cavalry

Horseback riders, good for breaking enemy ranks.

Type: Cavalry

Resistance: 2

Attack Damage: 3[CD]

Buff: Chargers - If a mounted allied officer starts their turn in the same zone, they gain an additional 2[CD] on the first melee attack they make.

Features:

  • When this division makes an attack the same turn it enters a zone, it deals an extra 2[CD] damage and gains the Startling damage effect.

Horse Archers

Talented riders able to fire bows from atop a steed.

Type: Projectile, Cavalry

Resistance: 1

Ranged Attack Damage: 2[CD]

Buff: Gallop - A mounted allied officer that starts their turn in the same zone may take the movement Minor Action for free.

Features: 

  • This division can make two Free Moves every round. An officer may order this division to Free Move even if they have already ordered a Free Move this turn.
  • When this division attacks divisions with the Flying type, the Difficulty is reduced by 1.

Mages

Spellcasters with powerful magic.

Type: Magick

Resistance: 0

Ranged Attack Damage: 2[CD] Piercing

Buff: Arcane Expertise - Once per round, when an allied officer in the same zone casts a spell with arcane magick, they may treat their relevant skill as one higher, to a maximum of six, for the task.

Features: 

  • Officers may use Reason instead of Presence when issuing Orders to this division.

Pegasi Cavalry

Flying riders, great for scouting.

Type: Cavalry, Flying

Resistance: 1

Attack Damage: 2[CD]

Buff: Free Flying - When an allied officer with a flying mount takes the Move or Sprint actions while in the same zone as this division, their speed is increased by 1 and they do not provoke opportunity attacks until the end of their turn.

Features: 

  • This division can make two Free Moves every round. An officer may order this division to Free Move even if they have already ordered a Free Move this turn.
  • This division is not affected by difficult terrain.

Griffin Cavalry

Aerial riders, great for swooping.

Type: Cavalry, Flying

Resistance: 1

Attack Damage: 3[CD]

Buff: Swoopers - Whenever an allied officer with a flying mount in the same zone makes a melee attack, they may roll an additional die.

Features: 

  • This division is not affected by difficult terrain.

Medical Unit

Trained Medics capable of revitalizing injured soldiers.

Type: Support

Resistance: 0

Attack Damage: 0[CD]

Buff: Triage - When an allied officer in the same zone takes the First Aid task, they may target any officer in the same zone regardless of distance.

Features: 

  • Officers in the same zone as this division may issue the Regroup order as a Minor Action.

Military Band

Musicians playing to inspire soldiers in battle.

Type: Support

Resistance: 0

Attack Damage: 0[CD]

Buff: War Drums - Allied officers in the same zone roll an extra die on console and demoralize tasks.

Features: 

  • At the end of each round, all unbroken allied divisions in the same zone as this division regain 1 morale.

Tactical Corps

Strategic thinkers who help analyze the battlefield.

Type: Support

Resistance: 0

Attack Damage: 0[CD]

Buff: Order Runners - Officers within the same zone as this division may issue orders to divisions in adjacent zones as if they were in that zone.

Features: 

  • When this division enters a zone with an enemy division, the ordering officer may ask one question about the opposing army as if using the Obtain Information momentum spend.

Mangonel

Shorter ranged but more flexible catapults.

Type: Siege

Resistance: 0

Ranged Attack Damage: 4[CD]

Buff: None

Features: 

  • When this division makes an attack, the ordering officer uses their study instead of authority for the task.
  • This division may attack structures within or along the border of its current zone.
  • This division may attack any division in an adjacent zone, increasing the Difficulty by 1.

Trebuchet

Siege weapons capable of striking from afar.

Type: Siege

Resistance: 0

Ranged Attack Damage: 5[CD]

Buff: None

Features: 

  • When this division makes an attack, the ordering officer uses their study instead of authority for the task.
  • When making an attack, this division can target any division in an adjacent zone, or a structure in or along the border of any adjacent zone. This division cannot attack targets in the same zone.
  • All zone borders are considered Hazardous for this division.

Stratagems

Each division gets 1 stratagem. Most stratagems can only be applied to divisions of a particular type, though there are some that can only be utilized by a specific division.

Surrounding Tactics

Applicable Divisions: Infantry

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose an enemy officer within Range 8. The officer is Slowed and Off-Guard until the end of their next turn.

Fortify

Applicable Divisions: Infantry

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. Until the start of your next turn, all borders of your current zone are considered Hazardous to enemy divisions, if they were not already. The first opportunity attack you make before your next turn deals 3[CD] additional damage.

Stand Your Ground

Applicable Divisions: Infantry

3/scene, you may issue this as an order. Until the end of your next turn, enemy divisions in the same zone may only target this division. This ends if this division is broken.

If you have taken the Guard Major Action this turn, the Bonus Momentum cost to take a Swift Action to issue this order is reduced by 1.

Battering Ram

Applicable Divisions: Infantry

You may issue this as an order. Choose a gate or door space on the battlefield. Make a Presence + Authority task of Difficulty 1. On a success, deal damage to the target equal to the division’s normal attack + 2[CD].

Push In

Applicable Divisions: Light Footmen

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. While you are in the same zone as this division, any melee attacks you make this round cannot be defended against. Immediately take the Attack Major Action and roll an additional die on the attack.

Mounted Infantry

Applicable Divisions: Infantry, Bowmen

This division starts the battle mounted. While mounted, this division can make two Free Moves every round. An officer may order this division to Free Move even if they have already ordered a Free Move this turn.

This division may not be issued any non-movement orders while mounted, but may be ordered to dismount as a free action. Once this division has dismounted, it may not become mounted again for the rest of the scene.

At Guard

Applicable Divisions: Heavy Footmen

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose up to three allied characters in this zone. They gain 2 temporary HP until the end of your next turn.

Siege Tower

Applicable Divisions: Infantry

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose a free space in the same zone. A ladder is placed there. If the ladder is adjacent to walls along the border between two zones, allied divisions are able to cross the border as Hazardous Terrain. The ladder is destroyed if this division is Broken.

As a Minor Action, you may order the division to pick up the ladder. The ladder is removed from the field and this division regains its use of this stratagem.

Missiles into Ranks

Applicable Divisions: Projectile

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. This division may make an attack against a targetable division. On a success, all other enemy divisions in the same zone take 3[CD] damage.

Cover Fire

Applicable Divisions: Bowmen, Horse Bowmen

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose an allied officer in the same zone. Until your next turn, all attacks against the target officer have +1 Difficulty and they cannot be targeted by opportunity attacks.

Pin Down

Applicable Divisions: Projectile

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose an enemy officer within Range 7 of you and perform a Difficulty 1 Presence + Authority task. On a success, they are Immobilized and Exposed until the end of their next turn.

Longbows

Applicable Divisions: Bowmen

Your bowmen are equipped with longbows. If this division has not moved this round, they may attack a division in an adjacent zone. They may not move for the rest of this round.

Anti-Cavalry Barrage

Applicable Divisions: Projectile

2/scene, you may issue this order as a reaction when an enemy cavalry division enters the same zone as this one. Immediately make an attack with an advantage.

Hail of Arrows

Applicable Divisions: Projectile

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. For the rest of the round, every army attack made by an ally in the same zone gains an extra 1d20.

Mounted Withdraw

Applicable Divisions: Cavalry

When this division crosses a Hazardous border, it does not provoke Mass Opportunity Attacks from divisions in the zone it is leaving.

Cavalry Charge

Applicable Divisions: Cavalry

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. This division charges into an adjacent zone. All enemy divisions in the target zone take 2 Piercing damage.

Ride Along

Applicable Divisions: Cavalry 

2/scene, you may move half your speed when you order this division to make a Free Move. You may only do so once per round.

Shock into Submission

Applicable Divisions: Cavalry 

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose any number of enemy divisions in the same zone. Perform a Presence + Authority task with a Difficulty equal to the number of divisions you chose. On a success, each of those divisions cannot provide its buff or take advantage of its stratagem until the start of your next turn.

Trampling Rush

Applicable Divisions: Cavalry 

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. This division charges at enemy officers. All enemies in a four space line from the ordering officer take this division’s regular attack damage.

Strike with the Pack

Applicable Divisions: Heavy Cavalry, Griffin Cavalry

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Order this division to make an Army Attack, then make an attack. Your attack gains the Startling effect.

Barrel In

Applicable Divisions: Cavalry

1/scene, this division can be ordered to make an army attack after making a Free Move.

Arcanum Unbound

Applicable Divisions: Mages

When you order this division to make an attack, you may increase its damage by 2[CD]. After you do, this division is Off-Guard until the end of your next turn.

Bursts of Magick

Applicable Divisions: Mages

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose a space on the battlefield within Range 6 of you. This division makes an attack on that space with the Burst 2 damage effect.

Defensive Warding

Applicable Divisions: Mages

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose up to three allies in the same zone, officers or divisions. Until the end of your next turn, they gain 3[CD] temporary HP.

Arcane Reserve

Applicable Divisions: Mages

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose an Arcane spell you have prepared. You may cast it without expending a use, even if you have no uses left.

Siege Magic

Applicable Divisions: Mages

This division may attack structures on the battlefield. When they do, roll an additional 2[CD].

Arcane Artillery

Applicable Divisions: Mages

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose an adjacent zone to this division. All divisions in that zone take 2 piercing damage.

Strafing Run

Applicable Divisions: Flying

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose a space within Range 8 of you. All officers within Blast 2 of that space take 4[CD] Piercing 2 damage.

Airlift

Applicable Divisions: Flying

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose a space you can see within Range 10 of your current location. You are moved to that location, ignoring height and terrain effects, but provoking opportunity attacks as normal. If you make a swift task in the same turn that you issue this order, the momentum cost is reduced by 1, to a minimum of 0.

Life Support

Applicable Divisions: Medical Unit

1/scene, when an officer in the same zone is dealt damage that would reduce their HP to zero, they may Avoid Injury without spending their Determination. Additionally, when this occurs, they regain 8[CD] HP.

Attentive Aid

Applicable Divisions: Medical Unit

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. All allied officers adjacent to the ordering officer, including the ordering officer, regain 7 [CD] health.

Extra Care

Applicable Divisions: Medical Unit

1/round, when an allied officer in the same zone is healed, the healer may reroll any blanks.

Healing Support

Applicable Divisions: Medical Unit

3/scene, you may issue this as an order. Take the First Aid Major action, and roll an extra 4[CD] for the amount healed.

Play On, Play On

Applicable Divisions: Military Band

At the end of each round, all unbroken allied divisions in the same zone regain 2 morale instead of 1, and all allied officers in the same zone regain 1 willpower.

Inspiring Tune

Applicable Divisions: Military Band

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. All unbroken allied divisions in the same zone restore 5[CD] Morale.

Ballad of Death

Applicable Divisions: Military Band

2/scene, you may issue this as an order. All attacks you take until the end of their turn gain the Daunting 2 effect. Immediately take the attack Major Action.

Fierce Drums

Applicable Divisions: Military Band

When an officer in the same zone takes the Demoralize action, they deal +2[CD] damage.

Excellent Authority

Applicable Divisions: Tactical Corps

When an allied officer in the same zone takes the Direct Major Action or issues an Order, they gain 1 bonus momentum.

Calculated Strike

Applicable Divisions: Tactical Corps

2/scene, when an allied officer in the same or an adjacent zone makes an attack against a Pinpointed enemy, they may forgo the advantage to add +2d20 to their roll instead.

False Orders

Applicable Divisions: Tactical Corps

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. Choose an enemy division in the same zone and perform a Difficulty 1 Reason + Intrigue task. On a success, it moves to an adjacent accessible zone of your choice and cannot be issued orders for the rest of the round, other than Brace.

You may spend bonus momentum to move additional divisions this way. For every bonus momentum you spend, move an additional division. It cannot be issued orders for the rest of the round, other than Brace.

Strategic Insights

Applicable Divisions: Tactical Corps

2/scene, when an allied officer in the same zone takes the Pinpoint Major Action, they may create an additional advantage.

Scouted for Ambush

Applicable Divisions: Tactical Corps

3/scene, when an allied officer takes the Hide Major Action anywhere on the battlefield, the Difficulty is reduced by 1.

Catapult Barrage

Applicable Divisions: Mangonel, Trebuchet

1/scene, you may issue this as an order if you are in a zone this division can target. Choose a space within Range 8 of you. The division makes an attack with Blast 2 targeting all officers present, allied and enemy, contested by Agility + Skirmish.

Targeted Strike

Applicable Divisions: Mangonel, Trebuchet

This first time this division damages a structure, roll double its [CD].

Long Fire

Applicable Divisions: Trebuchet

1/scene, you may issue this as an order. The trebuchet may make an attack against any division or structure on the battlefield, regardless of zone distance.

Army Talents

Like player characters, the player’s armies have Army Talents which provide certain benefits to taking certain actions in narrative (non-combat) play, often enhancing the outcome of a character’s particular course of action if successful. While each talent is rooted in the features of the army itself, they primarily provide benefits to the player characters themselves, most often when taking actions that involve or take advantage of the army.

If an ability provides a bonus a limited number of times (such as once per session), that limit applies to the entire party, not each individual character.

Alert Watchmen
Your army has a robust watch protocol preventing the risk of ambush. While your army is camped, it cannot be surprise attacked and can always report who came and left the encampment.

Additionally, when your army is prepared for an ambush, you may automatically succeed on any Task to find a place to conceal your army.

Camp Healers
Your army has a number of well-trained healers in its midst. When traveling with your army, if you roll on the Injury Effect table, you may roll twice and choose either result. In addition, when attempting Tasks that use Medicine, you may always act as though you have a relevant Focus if you are being assisted by healers from your army.

Chain of Command
Your army has a robust and strict hierarchy, and can function for periods of time without its highest commanders. If your army is unattended for up to a week, it will maintain discipline and obey its most recent orders. Additionally, you gain +1d20 on Tasks to mitigate Complications caused by your army.

Diplomats Corps
Your army always has someone who speaks the language of and knows the general culture of anyone you encounter, so long as there is a major political power of that culture. You may always Succeed at Cost when convincing someone to parley before battle.

Enhanced Interrogation
Your army specializes in extracting information from captives. When you succeed on an intrigue task to interrogate a prisoner held by your army, you gain two Bonus Momentum that can only be spent on the Obtain Information momentum spend.

Fearsome Reputation
Your army is known to be ruthless and terrifying. 1/session, when you perform a Task to intimidate someone, you may roll an extra die by invoking the reputation of your army.

If an enemy town has an army smaller than yours, they will automatically surrender unless their liege is present.

Gossip Mill
3/session, when you spend momentum to Obtain Information, you may ask an additional question to learn information from people in your army.

Impeccable Logistics
Your army is a master of its supply chain. If your army’s supply line is cut off, your army can go two months without running out of resources. Additionally, the momentum cost to Create an Advantage to acquire an item is reduced by 1, to a minimum of 0.

You may always Succeed at Cost on any task to make your army undergo a forced march. When undergoing a forced march, your army can move at double speed.

In it for the Coin
Your army fights, above all else, for the pay. You suffer no Complications or penalty to your reputation if you turn against someone who cannot or refuses to pay your army.

Additionally, if your army is hesitant to follow an order, you always know what price it would take to convince them otherwise and how to get it.

Liege’s Legion
Your army fights in the name of a liege. Before you attempt a Task involving your army, you may invoke its liege’s name to ask a nearby lord or populace for assistance. If they have a positive opinion of the army’s liege, roll an extra die. If they have a negative opinion, you immediately generate a Complication instead.

Mess Tents
Your army’s cooks are some of the best in the land and can make delicious food with the simplest of supplies. When your army is well supplied, you gain +1d20 on Diplomacy Tasks to interact with members of your army.

Pampered and Provided
Your army is well equipped to host a person of status. When a noble or royal is traveling with you, they are always given treatment above expectations, unless you order otherwise.

While they are in your care, when you perform a Diplomacy Task to interact with them, you may reroll one die on the Task.

Plague Resilient
When you perform a Task to contain, treat, or study a disease affecting your army, gain an extra die. If you have a medical unit in your army, you may also gain a die when performing a Task to contain, treat, or study a disease in a city or town.

Raiders
Your army is especially good at looting and pillaging. When you allow your army to loot a settlement, you gain an Advantage on all Tasks relating to your army for the remainder of the session.

Additionally, when you do, each member of the party may specify an object or possession captured that they wish to have as theirs, which they will obtain undamaged.

Ransom Cages
Your army is equipped with secure means of transporting prisoners and hostages. Captured characters cannot escape your custody unless you allow them. In addition, 1/session you gain a free Advantage on any Task to intimidate someone if your army currently has prisoners.

Siege Masters
When your army is engaged in an Extended Task or Challenge for a siege, the momentum cost to reduce the time a Task takes is 1.

When you use a Siege type division in your army to reduce the cost of creating an advantage, you may reroll any number of dice once on the task. You must keep the new result.

Skilled Scouts
Your army has trained for scouting ahead and learning about the enemy. You may reroll a die on a task to have your army perform a scouting mission, and may choose to keep either result. The first momentum you spend to gather information from a task related to scouting,

Strict Discipline
Your army is held to the utmost standard and follows orders without question. 1/session, you may automatically succeed on a Task to issue commands to your army. You do not suffer Complications when rebuking or inflicting discipline on your army.

Swords for Hire
Your army is always on the lookout for new work. When attempting a Task to convince a prospective patron to hire you, you may reroll any number of dice in your pool. In addition, when negotiating your pay, you may choose to increase the Complication range by 2 (Complications on 18-20) in order to gain an extra die.

Strangers in a Strange Land
The primary force of your army is foreign to these lands, making it more insular and self-reliant. Your army is immune to attempts to sneak outside spies into your ranks. Whenever you perform an Authority Task to interact with members of your army, roll an extra die.

Undying Commitment
Your army is unilaterally devoted to your cause. 1/session, after you appeal to the Common Cause to spend your Determination on a Task related to your army, you regain it.

Your army may call upon the party to comply with the Common Cause. If the party chooses to Challenge it instead, the army will abandon you until you regain their trust, up to the GM’s discretion.

Warriors of the Faith
Your army fights in the name of a religious institution. Characters of the same faith will not fight your army unless they believe you are going to attack them or if given permission by a religious authority of your faith.

When you perform a Task with Faith related to your army, you may roll an additional die.

Part Six: Gamemastering

Chapter Twelve: Running the Game

This chapter provides guidance for GMs who are running a game in Ascension.

Principles of Gamemastering

Ascension’s Principles of Gamemastering are a guide to help you navigate the responsibility of being a GM and enhance the experience of all players at the table, including yourself.

Facilitate fun

The first and primary responsibility of a GM is to facilitate the game and the experience of their players. Setting expectations early for what kind of game this is going to be, establishing boundaries with your players, and checking in with them about their comfort levels with certain subject matter is an important and necessary part of making sure that everyone (including you) has fun. Topics like character death, marginalized identity, sex and romance, etc., can be sensitive subjects and comfort levels with them may vary from player to player. Make sure that you and your players are all on the same level about including or excluding any sensitive topics before your game starts, and continue to monitor the vibe of the table and check in with your players and with yourself when sensitive topics come up as your game progresses.

Making use of safety tools (like an X card or pre-campaign survey) that help players know if certain uncomfortable subjects are going to be relevant and/or let players excuse themselves from a scene if it becomes too much is another good way to help facilitate fun at your table.

Ask questions

Asking questions is a great and easy way to engage your players in what’s going on, and to build on player decisions to create interesting situations. Ask questions about everything, from what characters are feeling about what’s going on to the decor in their surroundings, and let their answers guide what happens next. For example, if you ask characters what they are wearing to a fancy ball, have your NPCs in the scene react to the PCs’ outfits, creating drama or intrigue if appropriate. Whenever you have the opportunity to let your players change the story, even in small ways, take it! And always, always ask the most important question as often as you can: What do you do?

Also, it’s important to address yourself to the characters they’re playing, not your players (ask Adelinde the knight what she’s wearing to the ball, not Seth, her player). Doing so will help players immerse themselves in their characters and the world, which will help them answer your questions in a more character driven way.

Aim the camera at PCs

The PCs are the protagonists of the story that you are telling together, and they should know that and feel that. Say yes to their ideas and let them try taking their own course of action as much as possible. If a PC wants to attempt something that is totally illogical and doesn’t make sense in character or in universe for them to do, it is of course acceptable and your job, even, to prevent that action from being taken, but rather than a flat denial, provide alternate options that a character can attempt instead, or present the consequences of that action before the Task is attempted so that PCs can make their own decision to back away from a course of action for themselves.

Part of aiming the camera at your PCs is allowing them to affect the story as it progresses. The world that surrounds your PCs should be interesting and engaging, and they should feel compelled to interact with the NPCs you place in their paths, but be wary of placing too much importance on your “original vision.” The PCs will do things that surprise you: they may engage with characters you didn’t think were important and refuse to engage with characters that you do, they may take actions you never thought of and ignore the paths you thought were obvious. Lean in to the moments when PCs forge their own path, and focus on honoring their choices in the story you are telling together, rather than making them serve the story you envisioned before the game started.

Make failure interesting

Player characters are competent and skilled individuals, but failure is inevitable, and sometimes they will fail rolls. When PCs fail, making the consequences of failure interesting will help keep players engaged and invested in what happens next, and will make failure feel narratively rewarding for players as their actions affect the world around them regardless of success. If a PC is trying to open a locked door but fails the Task, don’t just tell them they can’t open it, but take the opportunity to introduce something new: they can’t open the locked door and they scratch the door so that people will know someone was there.

Make the world complicated

Ascension is a game that expects you to be engaging in politics and intrigue as well as warfare on small and grand levels. Politics and warfare can happen in a simple, straightforward world where everyone’s motivations are exactly what they appear to be, but will be far more interesting when the world and the NPCs that inhabit it are just as complicated and personally motivated as the PCs will be. You don’t need to make charts or spreadsheets of every character that exists and their relationship to everyone else (though these things can be helpful and fun if that’s the kind of preparation you enjoy doing), but you should keep in mind that NPCs are characters of their own with their own agendas and lives that exist outside of the moments when they interact with the PCs. Entwining the political and the personal, making characters that are just as real as the PCs, will create natural drama that engages your PCs and may even surprise them as they’re reminded that things are happening even when they’re not around to see it.

This is also a game that expects and flourishes in a medieval setting, and the world of the medieval period, whether our real one or fantasy, is a complicated and very different place from our modern one. You don’t need to be a history major or have read every book in the library about the period in order to run this game, but it may prove helpful to familiarize yourself with the medieval time period and some of its attitudes and cultural norms. Knowing the ways in which people back then thought and acted differently beyond their lack of modern technology can help you to make interesting story beats and narrative devices that challenge your players and drive the story forward.

Collaborate with PCs

As a GM, you are working with your players to tell an interesting story, not against them. You are not trying to defeat their characters and bring them low, but to give them opportunities where their characters might succeed or fail and where either case will enrich the story as it goes forward. Your Threat pool is not a resource to use to hurt your players, but a resource to use to complicate the story and make challenges that are narratively interesting for the PCs to overcome. Ultimately, this is a game about telling a story together with your players, not a game in which one side of the table wins or loses, and everyone at the table will have more fun in a collaborative environment instead of a combative one.

Threat

As detailed in Chapter Three: Basic Rules, Threat is the GM’s resource for altering a scene, either by improving the odds for NPCs or by creating Complications and challenges for PCs to overcome. Because Threat is used primarily in ways to make things more difficult for the PCs, you can expect that PCs will often act and strategize such that they give you as little Threat as possible, and perceive the Threat pool as an antagonizing force. It is important, however, that you as the GM do not perceive or use the Threat pool as a means to punish your players or make their Tasks needlessly Difficult. While Threat may exist in opposition to the players, you as the GM are not in opposition to them. As such, when spending Threat to create Complications or introduce risk or adverse effects, it is crucial that your Threat spends make narrative sense and don’t make Tasks excessively Difficult. Just like players must make their Advantages make logical sense in a scene, you also must make your Complications make logical sense.

At the beginning of every session, the GM starts with an empty Threat Pool that grows as players give Threat or roll Complications. Players should always be aware of the amount of Threat a GM has, and when adding or subtracting Threat, the GM should be clear when they are doing so and for what reason. Threat is a means by which the GM can build tension and dramatically change the players’ circumstances, but the feeling of unknown danger should be built through narration and atmosphere, not hidden mechanics.

The GM does not have a Threat pool during Combat, however, just as the players don’t have a Momentum pool. Instead, NPCs have special abilities that grant them chances to gain bonus dice on Tasks or extra effects on their combat Tasks. For more, see Threat in Combat.

Values and the Common Cause

As a GM, one of the ways to create character conflict and introduce opportunities for rich narrative roleplay is to highlight a character’s Values. Knowing the Values of all of the PCs will prove helpful when planning sessions and creating Complications or narrating scenes, as they can provide a straightforward framework for creating drama and tension in your game. Having a reference list of PC Values in front of you is a useful GM tool so that you can identify moments that test a character’s value and call upon them to Comply with or Challenge a value, especially when players may not notice themselves.

When considering ways to introduce conflict or tension into your game, consider the Values of the PCs: is there a character who has a Value that might conflict with someone else’s? What kind of situation would reveal that conflict and bring it to the forefront of the scene? Is the Common Cause that the party is working towards in conflict with a character’s Values? How might the challenges they face as they work towards that goal cause them to confront this contradiction?

Moments that test a PC’s Value are not just merely mechanical opportunities to gain Determination, but moments when characters must confront their deepest held beliefs and decide whether they still hold or not. These are impactful decisions that should hold weight in whatever scene they are occurring, and as the GM, it may be helpful to ask the PC questions in this moment or help describe the scene such that you prompt the PC to reflect on what is going through their head and what they are doing at that moment. When a player asks you if a moment is a test of their value that can allow them to Comply with or Challenge it, encourage them to explore why they feel it to be appropriate to their character and how the character might be feeling about it.

Betrayal and Party Conflict

Circumstances may arise where a character in the party decides to act directly against the Common Cause, or take actions that outright betray their fellow party members. In a situation like this, when the party is divided and not every character is working on the same side anymore, characters who are not acting in accordance with the Common Cause lose access to the group Momentum pool. Instead, any Momentum they generate from abilities or attempting Tasks is saved to their own personal Momentum pool, which only that character may save to or spend from, and this lasts for as long as the character is acting in direct opposition to the party’s goals. A character that briefly takes a single action in opposition to the party (for example, assassinating someone the party was trying to ally with), would not draw from the group pool while attempting that action, but may regain use of the group pool when the action is done and they return to supporting the Common Cause.

If a character loses access to the group pool for an extended period of time, you should talk to your players and ensure that they are still having fun in the midst of an extended betrayal arc, particularly the player doing the betraying. A character at deep odds with the rest of the party will likely need to reconcile with the rest of the characters eventually in order to continue being a part of the story, and whether they choose to do so or not will have consequences in character and potentially out of character that you as the GM should keep an eye on and help players navigate.

Tasks

Whenever the outcome of what a character wants to do might be in question, or where the possibility of failure or generated Complications could be particularly interesting, the GM should call for a Task to be attempted. As the GM, it is your responsibility to determine what Attribute and Skill combination would be appropriate for the action being attempted. Players may try to convince you to allow a certain Attribute/Skill combination different from the one that you stated, and you may let them if you wish, but it is up to you whether you think their argument is reasonable.

It is also up to you to determine the Difficulty of a Task. When deciding the Difficulty of a Task, you should be taking into account what the character is trying to do and what circumstances they are attempting it under. For example, a PC trying to persuade a guard to let them into the castle may have an easier Difficulty if they are friends with that guard, while they might have a much harder Difficulty if they were already caught trying to sneak in by someone else. You may use Complications to increase the Difficulty of a Task beyond what its logical Difficulty might be by introducing some new challenge to the scene. For example, if a PC is trying to persuade a guard to let them into the castle, you could introduce a Complication where the guard has heard rumors of a thief on the loose, and so is more resistant to letting strangers inside than they might be otherwise. Because the GM already has the power to set the Difficulty of Tasks as they please, using Complications to adjust the Difficulty of a Task should always involve the introduction of a risk or challenge that would not have otherwise been there. And in situations where you don’t think the Difficulty would change significantly but the risk of adverse consequences should be higher, you may also spend Threat to change the Complication range rather than adjust the Difficulty. It may be helpful to keep each of the PC’s character sheets on hand or a list of all of their Traits to reference when a character’s Traits would provide an obvious Complication. Players may also forget to use their own Traits when they might be relevant for Creating an Advantage, so it will be helpful to be familiar with their Traits so you can prompt them when the option is possible.

One factor that you should also keep in mind when setting the Difficulty of a Task is the vibe at the table and the atmosphere of the situation. In a very high stakes scene, where the risk of failure could be very significant, it may be appropriate to have several high Difficulty Tasks in a row. But in a lower stakes scene, like haggling at the market, it may not be very fun if your players are faced with a Difficulty 3 or 4 Task to accomplish something that doesn’t feel very important to them. Similarly, the timing of high Difficulty Tasks is important, as asking for a Difficulty 3 or 4 Task at the beginning of session when there is no Momentum in the pool, or after a series of failed rolls has led to several Complications and low morale, may not be the best option for facilitating fun in the moment. It is far more important for your players to have fun and feel like success and failure is meaningful than it is for every Task to have the most accurate representative Difficulty.

When determining the outcome of a task, consider what the actual goal that is trying to be achieved is and what the consequences of success or failure might be expected to be. Don’t make a regular failure more punishing than might be expected as a default; instead use rolled complications or spend threat to Create Complications that might escalate a basic failure into a more tense situation. Failing to pick a locked door by default probably wouldn’t mean more than the door can’t be opened and the lock might be scratched, but if you want to raise the stakes from the failure you can spend two threat to introduce that shortly after the party hears the guards rushing down the nearby hallway or that the lockpick damages the lock such that nobody could open the door anymore, even with a key, and they will have to find a different path entirely.

On the flip side, it may be tempting to reward players if they roll very well. Instead, Ascension encourages you to leave the choice of earning additional boons on a greater success up to the players. After revealing the consequences of their success on the task, you can encourage players to use generated momentum to increase the degree of success of their task by Creating an Advantage, perhaps offering them what that advantage might entail. If a player generates three momentum from a task to convince a king to let them hunt a dangerous bandit hiding in his private hunting woods, the king might agree to their request and you could suggest to the players that if they spend two momentum to Create an Advantage the king is so convinced by their arguments he offers to send some soldiers with them on their hunt. This leaves the choice of capitalizing on their success up to the players, letting them either take it in the moment or to save it for a situation they feel they may need it for later. The players may find the extra soldiers helpful and take you up on it, or they may determine that holding onto the momentum to use in the inevitable fight with the bandit would be preferable to spending it in the moment.

Sometimes, players attempt to perform an action that might affect another task before performing the primary task. If a player is trying to search the slums for a runaway princess, that itself might be a Awareness + Intrigue task. However, they may ask if they can stop and ask locals if they have seen a girl matching her description passing by, taking advantage of their superior presence and diplomacy to aid their search. Because the princess is still hiding, this can’t supersede the primary task or the relevant attribute and skill, but that shouldn’t stop them from using this to improve their chances of the main task; especially since failure on this task could alert the hiding girl someone is searching for her, so it is not without risk. Instead you can have the player attempt this diplomacy task as a secondary task, which if successful can lower the Difficulty of the primary one they still need to attempt, effectively creating an advantage through their success. This type of secondary task should not use the same attribute and skill as the primary one—otherwise it can be considered implied as part of the task itself. But do not be afraid to reward player creativity by allowing them to find ways to apply their character’s strength to a situation that might not immediately call for it.

Extended Tasks

Extended Tasks (see Chapter Four: Advanced Rules) are a special kind of Challenge meant to simulate intense or stressful actions that occur over a period of time. These Challenges don’t need to be time limited Tasks, but there should be some element of time pressure that makes an Extended Task feel necessary. An Extended Task that doesn’t need to be completed in under a specific amount of time in order to be successful may still have greater consequences the longer it takes to complete, making players feel invested in accomplishing the Extend Task efficiently. Without time pressure, an Extended Task is likely to feel boring or like meaningless dice rolling, and in either case, Extended Tasks are more complicated and thus should be used sparingly to maximize their effect.

Example scenarios that would be well suited for an Extended Task:

  • Sieging a city.
  • Chasing a character through a crowded city.
  • Preparing an elaborate or complicated magical ritual.
  • Riding down and capturing/killing escaping soldiers after a victorious battle.

The Progress Track of any Extended Task should be on a scale of 10-25. Easier Extended Tasks should have a Progress Track of 10-15, while harder Extended Tasks should have a Progress Track of 15-25. One thing to keep in mind as you set the Progress Track is that if the track is too high, it runs the risk of becoming tedious. Make sure that as players attempt their Tasks and roll dice to determine their Progress, you are not just calling for rolls and applying the results, but narrating the consequences of each Task, so that every Task made feels important and relevant, with the Progress generated reflecting how effective each Task is to accomplishing the overarching goal. As a result, Extended Tasks may take a long time, maybe even a full session, and you should encourage players to narrate and roleplay the lead up and aftermath of each Task they attempt.

One helpful approach to longer Extended Tasks is to break up the Progression Tasks with shorter, individual scenes that may or may not relate to the Extended Task itself. For example, if two PCs are researching a complicated arcane ritual together, you can intersperse their rolls with scenes of the rest of the party out shopping in the market for materials or weaponry. If the party is sailing a ship from one coast to another, you could allow for a romantic scene between two PCs as they overlook the sea together or a friendly conversation between a PC and the ship’s cook between Progression Tasks to navigate and sail the ship. An extended task can even occur in the background of an entire session. The party can be sneaking through the tunnels beneath a city under siege to evacuate civilians while they occasionally roll Progression Tasks for their army to hold out against the attackers. If you opt for this method, you may want PCs to perform Tasks unrelated to the Extended Task as part of their scenes. Do not be afraid to do this, but always consider whether this task is more appropriate as a separate task or as a Progression Task.

Negotiation

Negotiation Challenges (see Chapter Four: Advanced Rules) are a special kind of Challenge meant to give structure to scenarios where PCs are engaged in high stakes negotiation with one or more NPCs. Not every instance of negotiation between PCs and NPCs is necessarily a reason to use the Negotiation rules—though how much you use these rules (if at all) is up to you and your players. The rules for Negotiation are primarily for high stakes scenarios where the outcome would meaningfully change the course of the narrative. For example, trying to convince a neutral NPC to give the PCs a discount at a food stall would not be a very worthwhile scenario to use the Negotiation rules, whereas trying to convince a neutral NPC to supply the PCs’ army before they go into battle would be a much better opportunity to employ them.

Unlike in combat, the Major Actions included in the rules for Negotiation don’t have specific Attributes and Skills listed for the Tasks needed to be performed, and they cover a wider breadth of options for a negotiation than simply rolling to persuade. Because not every PC in your party is likely to have high Presence and Diplomacy scores, the Negotiation Tasks are there to provide opportunities for every PC to be able to contribute to a negotiation scene using their particular abilities and focuses. While the descriptions of each Major Action may seem better suited to some Attributes and Skills over others (e.g. Read being well-suited for Awareness), PCs should be encouraged and rewarded for coming up with unique Attribute + Skill combinations in order to accomplish the Tasks, so long as they make logical sense. And of course, what makes logical sense or is fitting with the situation is ultimately up to you as the GM.

Despite the similarity to the flow of combat, Negotiation shouldn’t be thought of as an antagonistic “one side vs. another” scenario. NPCs that are completely unwilling to work with the PCs and/or are outright enemies of the party should not be targets of a Negotiation, but NPCs that are neutral or maybe even have a bad opinion of the party but could genuinely have their minds changed are good targets of a Negotiation scene. And while NPCs may start out opposed to the PCs and their goals, as a Negotiation scene progresses, players should be rewarded not only for good outcomes on their rolls, but also for their roleplaying choices. Even if the player isn’t taking the Persuade Task, PCs that say or do things that might naturally persuade the NPC they are negotiating with should feel like that matters. Alerting PCs that they’ve triggered the NPC’s Values (positively or negatively) is a good way to do this out of character, but also in character allowing an NPC to warm up to the party or give them information that might help them later in the conversation are all good ways to facilitate the vibe of a good Negotiation scene.

When players set out to try a Negotiation Challenge and you want to impose limits on what they can or cannot achieve, it’s good to establish that ahead of time. If there is an NPC that the players want to form a lasting alliance with but you don’t want that to be possible just yet, communicate to the players before the scenario begins that they can earn up to a large favor but not a lasting alliance. Similarly, if you want a Negotiation scene to be more or less difficult, you can increase or decrease the Favor requirements to achieve certain rewards as necessary.

Using Magick in Narrative Play

The rules of Ascension assume that the world you are playing in will, like its core setting of Edhela, have at least some amount of magick, and thus provide options for your players to take in order to play magick users. However, as the GM and arbiter of the game, it is ultimately your decision whether or not magick is available to your players and to what degree it may be used outside of combat. Ascension is intentionally designed to support both narrative and combat play that include or entirely exclude magick, depending on the game that you wish to run.

If your setting includes magick, you may decide whether you wish to include access to magick during narrative play. Magick, by its very nature, can be difficult to define in terms of its powers and limitations. As such, Ascension leaves the exact capabilities of magick outside of combat deliberately ambiguous to allow you to determine how much you wish to allow it to impact the flow of your gameplay and story.

Magick, like everything else in Ascension, relies on Tasks to determine the outcome of any attempted actions. When a player with magick wishes to cast a spell or perform some sort of feat with magick, like all other actions, they first describe to you what they wish to accomplish and then it is up to you to determine whether or not the action calls for a Task. All magick Tasks should use the player’s Magick Attribute, though you should still set the relevant Skill and Difficulty.

Consider what magickal effects are available in your world and how difficult they are to accomplish, as well as what types of magick each domain may have access to. Does magick play a role in medicine? What about communication? Can it be used to create material out of nothing or transport objects far distances? Is there magic that is possible, but forbidden?

By its very nature, affecting the world with magick should be difficult, even for those well trained, and the greater the impact the harder it should be. The Difficulty of a magick Task often should be comparable to the Difficulty of a similar non-magick Task. Opening a locked door likely won’t be lower Difficulty for a mage than a traditional lock pick, nor will carrying a heavy ox up a hill be lower Difficulty telepathically than by hand. Some magick Tasks may not have a direct comparison, but often may have a similar Task of lower Difficulty to compare to, such as alchemical transmutation relative to cooking or metallurgy, which can be used to help set the Difficulty of the magick Task a step or two higher.

Like with any Task, if you feel that what the player is wishing to accomplish is impossible, either by the rules of your setting or due to the character’s own present limitations, simply inform the player they are incapable of such a feat instead of allowing them to attempt an impossible Task. Encourage them to instead consider other solutions and to rely on their party to find another path around their current problem using the resources at their disposal. Similarly, some feats with little narrative impact may be of trivial difficulty and be of Difficulty 0. Do not be afraid in these cases to let characters with magickal abilities perform such little feats from time to time, showing off their unique training in small, fun ways without the need to always overcome a Task for the smallest spell.

Magick should not be the universal solution to all problems. Used too frivolously, magick can easily create an imbalance between players, where characters without magickal abilities are left sitting on the sidelines as the magickal characters are able to solve every problem before they get a chance to contribute, which can quickly become an unfun dynamic for the party. Keep the breadth of party skillsets in mind when you create problems for them to face, and don’t be afraid to leverage both your ability to set Difficulty and create Complications to encourage equal opportunities to contribute to the narrative for each player, providing opportunities where the optimal or even only solution to a dilemma they face is a non-magical one that the rest of the party is well suited to provide.

Powerful Magick

When it comes to particularly powerful or intensive magickal effects, it may be best to require a Challenge or Extended Task to accomplish them instead of simply requiring a high Difficulty Task. Not only does this mean that narratively consequential actions require more time and effort to be dedicated to their achievement, but it can allow the rest of the party to be involved in the casting even without having any magick of their own.

If your setting allows a powerful enough Light Magic wielder to revive a fallen comrade, they may require special materials to be gathered for the ritual. If such magick is deeply forbidden, it may require finding a secluded spot for the casting and someone to stand watch outside to keep from any prying eyes discovering what is going on. Making the spell a Challenge allows for the rest of the party to contribute to these steps, making the final accomplishment a collaborative achievement for everyone involved.

Similarly, not every step in the Extended Task must rely on magick. Constructing an Arcane Engine to lift a castle into the sky might be easily designed by a mage, but they may lack the strength to lift the components into place that one of their allies may provide. And a friend with a keen Awareness may be able to better spot a mistake in the construction caused by a Complication, preventing a disastrous outcome of the effort.

Some examples of tasks that are considered powerful or intensive magick in the Edhela setting are:

  • Carving the landscape to redirect a river
  • Creating a magickal device
  • Teleportation
  • Healing the king’s sickly child
  • Communing with the dead
  • Breaking into someone’s mind

Ultimately, when to call for a Challenge or an Extended Task for magick is up to you. Not every setting is the same, and what may be considered highly powerful magick in one setting may be ubiquitous in another, so think about the boundaries in the context of your world. A useful framing is to consider the impact a magickal effect will have on the narrative. The bigger the impact, the more likely achieving such an effect should require a Challenge or Extended Task.

Restricting Access to Magic

When you choose to run a game of Ascension without magick or with restrictions on which domains of magick are available, you should make sure to communicate with your players these limitations ahead of time so they know their options before building a character.

You may choose to only allow players to utilize spellcraft in combat, but not during narrative play. If you do, once more, inform your players of this at the beginning of the campaign, and do not allow them to choose any of the Magick Narrative Talents, as they will not be applicable to your game.

When to Use Combat

Combat is a core element of Ascension gameplay and tests the player’s ability to operate as a strategic team as they face foes on the battlefield. Tactical combat can be intense and exciting moments that display the leadership and martial expertise of the characters, fighting in high stakes battles to determine the fate of their home, their ambitions, or their lives. However, combat can also be intensive and time consuming, which can sometimes feel more disruptive to the pacing of the story than exciting. Knowing when a fight scene should be run as tactical combat and when a scene should be run narratively is an important skillset of the GM and a worthwhile consideration whenever a fight breaks out during play.

Not all fights need to be run as combat encounters—some scenarios that come to blows may be better resolved using narrative tools instead. A bar fight could be handled as an Extended Task, with the party needing to perform Skirmish Tasks to subdue their opponents before the city watch shows up to break up the fight and arrest them. An assassination might be best run as a Timed Challenge, with Key Tasks involving breaking into the target’s home, sneaking past their guards, and performing the killing blow. A duel could be a single opposed Skirmish check, or a Challenge made up of multiple, as the GM determines is appropriate. In these cases, combat stats do not apply—such as HP or resistance—and player death is far less a risk than narrative consequences are.

The purpose of the combat rules is to provide a streamlined and fair resolution to battles that allow the players to use their strategic planning and unique character abilities to turn the tides against a foe.
