It tests the characters in high stakes scenarios with dire consequences in defeat, and handsome rewards in victory. Combat, like all other rules in Ascension, is a tool towards the story. While a campaign can be built solely around combat, Ascension encourages using combat to advance the narrative of the characters, and show the highest stakes encounters that a party faces.

Below is a list of useful criteria to consider when determining whether a scenario is better suited to be resolved using the tactical combat rules or to use narrative mechanics.

  1. Party Participation - Does the fight include the entire party? Tactical combat expects the whole party of PCs to be engaged in the battle. If a fight involves only one or two members of the party, it is probably ill suited for using the combat rules and instead could be better resolved through a narrative extended task.

For example, Adelinde sneaks off from the group to go confront the man she believes killed her father and challenges him to a duel. Instead of having the rest of the party sit and watch Adelinde engage in a long combat scenario on her own, the GM has her spar with the man briefly in a series of skirmish tasks before the man flees to his fortress. They then advise Adelinde she would have to bring the party with her for a greater battle there if she wished to get to the man again.

  1. Premeditated or Impromptu - Was either side expecting to get into a fight? As a general rule at least one of the parties engaged in the combat should be prepared for a battle. Many skirmishes—especially those on the battlefield—involve both sides entering ready to engage, and are natural for tactical combat. When surprise is in play, in contrast, the situation can be a bit more ambiguous as to how to run the fight. If neither side was expecting a fight to break out, such as street fights, brawls, or assassinations, it is usually easier to resolve the conflict narratively. However in ambushes or surprise attacks, where one party has prepared for a battle, the surprise is part of the combat strategy and thus would be a suitable element to a combat encounter.

For example, while traveling through rural Oriande, a group of bandits attack the party on the road. While they were not expecting combat, the bandits certainly were, and the party deserves a chance to defend themselves against the coordinated attack on their caravan, so the GM has them enter into tactical combat as they grab their weapons and enter the fight.

In contrast, after overhearing a group insulting the Meian Isles in a tavern, Erik starts a bar fight with the offenders and is quickly backed up by his friends. Because neither side was expecting a fight that evening or even brought their weapons and armor, the GM instead chooses to run the encounter as a Challenge, with the party performing a series of Skirmish based Key Tasks to brawl with the other patrons.

  1. Duration - How long is the fight expected to take? Tactical combat is expected to take multiple rounds as the battle develops and strategies shift. If a fight is expected to be resolved in an instant, without much strategic play involved, the scenario is probably better suited for narrative tasks. A good rule of thumb is whether or not the fight is expected to last longer than a round if it were run tactically. If not, the scene should be run narratively. If so, it may be worth running with the combat rules.

For example, Lorenz is leading the party on a prison break mission and wants them to sneak up behind the four guards at the main gate and knock them out. Because knocking out the guards would be a quick action if the party succeeds, the GM could just call for a Group Task to determine if it works or not instead of having the party enter combat.

However, if the guards got wind that the party was coming and were ready for an attack, then it might be worth running as a combat scenario as with the guards in full combat position it will take longer than a single round to take them down.

  1. Strategic Complexity - Is strategy, positioning, and coordination important to the fight? Tactical combat is designed to be, as the name implies, tactical. Players characters are usually expected to coordinate their movements and actions towards achieving a central goal and will spend some amount of time planning how to attain it. Because the tactical combat rules are designed around using a gridded map of some kind, it is generally assumed that where each combatant is standing is relevant to the fight. If a fight does not require tracking the positions of combatants on a grid, it probably does not need to be run as a combat encounter. Similarly, if the party does not need to coordinate their actions strategically to ensure success, a combat encounter might not be appropriate.

For example, Rylan leads the party to break into the castle of the king’s ally, the villainous Countess ter Rovira, and assassinate her to cut her off her support for the king. After a Challenge to sneak their way to the countess’s room, they take their positions around the bed in case she wakes up. Because they have her surrounded, surprised, and outnumbered, there is no doubt whether they can overwhelm her even if she wakes up, the only worry is her alerting her guards before she dies. So instead the GM calls for a Group Task for them to sneak to beside her bed and for Rylan to attempt an intrigue task to kill her quietly.

In contrast, when the countess’s vengeful son pursues the party with his army, the ensuing battle will be more easily resolved if both sides can strategically command their armies and plan their maneuvers around a battlefield, so it would be run as a mass combat encounter.

  1. Stakes - What are the consequences of losing or winning this battle? Combat should feel big and exciting, providing narrative consequences to the success or failure of the party. Winning the battle should somehow advance the party’s objectives, while losing should spell some sort of danger or threaten a great risk. If there is no chance of the party winning a battle or likewise of them losing, then running a combat encounter has little value because the outcome can’t be affected. A minor fight, like a street duel, probably isn’t high enough stakes to run combat for, while a decisive clash of armies would be prime for tactical combat.

For example, the party convinces a Margrave to give them the gold they need if they agree to perform a mock battle against some of his knights in his arena as a spectacle during his heir’s birthday celebration festival. Because the battle is for sport and the party gets the gold either way, the outcome of the battle matters only for their reputation, so the GM can elect to run it as a Challenge instead of running a full combat encounter for it.

However, if the margrave reveals at the start of the battle their deal was a trick, and he in fact intends for the party to fight his knights to the death, the stakes are greatly increased and the party has much more riding on victory. Therefore, the battle should be run as a combat encounter so the party can strategize on making sure all of them can make it out of the battle alive.

It is always recommended to speak with your players at the start of a campaign how much combat they should expect to see/want to see over the course of a campaign. Some parties may wish to have opportunities to negotiate their way out of combat regularly, and resolve the narrative conflicts with peaceful and diplomatic approaches. Other parties may wish to focus on combat play exclusively, engaging in conquests and warfare while focusing less on narrative play. Setting these expectations ahead of time is always recommended for the GM and can lead to a better overall experience for all players involved.

Non-Player Characters

Though the PCs are the protagonists of their story, they are not the only characters that inhabit the world that they’re in. Non player characters (NPCs) are those other characters, who are played by you, the GM. While the task of being every single other character in the world may seem daunting, very rarely should the PCs need to interact with many NPCs at a time, and large groups of people do not need to be highly described with their individual members. NPCs will often play major roles in the story, however, as the PCs work to influence, befriend, seduce, or oppose them over the course of their adventure, and so it will prove valuable to keep track of important NPCs, their motivations and maybe even stats if necessary as you go along.

Most NPCs don’t have a full set of Attributes or Skills like PCs do, as outside of combat, NPCs should primarily act and react to the actions of the PCs as is narratively appropriate without needing to make Tasks. If an NPC is attempting to poison a PC, that NPC doesn’t make an Intrigue Task in order to do so. Instead, the PC should make a Task to discover the poison before drinking it, or to resist suffering the full extent of the poison’s effects if they do, and the GM should set the Difficulty of these Tasks as they feel is appropriate. If the NPC attempting to do the poisoning is a very capable assassin, then you may want to set the Difficulty very high, but if the PCs are very suspicious and this is the first time this NPC has done this, then you may want to set the Difficulty to discover the poison lower.

However, there may be instances when a PC is attempting to act directly on an NPC that making an Opposed Task feels narratively appropriate, or where the PCs are attempting to have an allied NPC assist with or attempt a Task on their behalf, such as being challenged to a duel, or brewing a dangerous potion. In these cases, it may be necessary to have an NPC roll dice to determine the outcome of their actions, particularly for an Opposed Task, and so will need Attributes and Skills in order to have a target number. NPCs that you intend to use in combat or that fit into one of the combat classes may use the stat arrays listed in that class’ stat block (see Chapter Thirteen: Combat as a GM).

When an NPC without a combat class needs to roll dice for a Task (or if you’d just prefer not to use those stats), you can determine their target number for that Task without needing to assign all their Attributes and Skills by using the chart below. NPCs are always assumed to have an applicable Focus for the Task they’re performing.

Threat and Momentum

During narrative scenes, NPCs won’t typically be attempting Tasks, and so have no need to spend or generate Threat. If an NPC’s presence or actions might create a challenge for the PCs or make their course of action more difficult, it may be appropriate to spend Threat to Create a Complication or to increase the Complication range of that PC’s Task. If a PC is attempting to convince the king that they are telling the truth, having the evil vizier whisper in the king’s ear would be an appropriate Complication that increases the Difficulty of a Task, instead of making the vizier roll their own Task to sway the king.

NPCs that are allied to the party and trying to help them follow the same rules and should rarely be attempting Tasks on their own. However, if the instance arises where it might be appropriate for an allied NPC to attempt a Task, they may spend and save Momentum to the party’s Momentum pool at the players’ discretion.

NPC Values

Similarly to their Attributes and Skills, not all NPCs will have defined Values. Because NPCs do not have Determination, their Values are more to help guide you as the GM when playing them, and do not need to be explicitly written out unless you are running a Negotiation encounter, in which an NPC’s Values are necessary as they serve a role in a Negotiation’s mechanics (see Chapter Four: Advanced Rules). However, writing down an NPC’s Values can be helpful, as having them in mind can help you create interesting character conflict for your NPCs that the PCs can engage with. If a PC wants to convince an NPC to support them in a rebellion against their monarch but doing so would go against that NPC’s Values, then that could indicate that the Difficulty of the PC’s Diplomacy Tasks against that character should be very high, or could make attempting to sway that NPC towards that course of action impossible entirely.

But while an NPC’s Values should reflect their deeply held convictions and motivations, they do not have to be entirely static. Though NPCs are by definition not the protagonists of this story, the story will be all around richer and more fun for you and your players to experience the more interesting and dynamic your NPCs are. They can change their minds, experience character growth, succumb to their best or worst instincts, and Values can be a good medium to reflect those character choices.

Chapter Thirteen: Combat as a GM

When running combat scenarios, the GM has their own units to control: the NPCs who are going to battle against the PCs. While most of the elements of combat for the GM are the same as they are for players, this section details all the specific rules for creating and running combat encounters, as well as how to use NPCs in combat.

Sorties and Encounters

When characters in Ascension go to battle, they always do so with a goal or specific objective in mind that they are trying to accomplish by taking on the enemy. These combat scenarios are called Sorties, and each Sortie should have a clear goal and stakes: there is something that must be accomplished, and there will be consequences if the players fail.

A Sortie is typically made up of 1-3 encounters, often (but not always) with rests in between. Before it begins, the goal of the Sortie should be clearly defined by the GM and/or the players, with clear stakes established; the players do not need to know what the explicit outcome will be if they fail, but they should be aware of the implications of failure. Once this has been established, the Sortie begins.

Building Encounters

While the archetypical fantasy battle is often a straight up battle between two opposing sides that ends when all characters on one side have been defeated, Ascension makes use of Objectives in order to make encounters more interesting and dynamic than a simple rout. Every encounter should have a main objective that is made known to the players before the battle begins, which if accomplished means the encounter ends with the players victorious.

The following are example Objectives for combat encounters:

  • Rout the Enemy: The players must defeat all enemy units on the battlefield in order to achieve victory.
  • Control: The GM establishes 2-4 ‘Control Areas’ on the battlefield. The players have a number of rounds (typically 6) to achieve control of a majority of these areas. Control is achieved by having a higher number of friendly units in each area than enemy units.
  • Control Areas [sidebar]: Control Areas are typically 2-4 spaces on each side.
  • Recon: The GM establishes 4-6 Control Areas on the battlefield, but only one is the “true” Control Area. The players have a number of rounds to discover the true Control Area and take control of and defend it. Characters inside a Control Area can use a Minor Action to search it, discovering if it is the true Control Area or not.
  • Escort: The players must escort an ally or object across the battlefield without them being defeated and/or destroyed. The GM establishes an Area on the map, and the players achieve victory once all of their characters and their ally unit are inside the Area.
  • The ally or object being escorted should not act on their own, but rather move only when a PC that they are adjacent to uses the Move Minor Action.
  • Holdout: The players’ Deployment Area is also their Control Area, which they must defend for a number of rounds. At the end of the set number of rounds, the players must still control their Deployment area by having more friendly units in the area than enemy units.
  • Capture: The GM establishes a Control Area, which is the enemy stronghold, on the opposite side of the battlefield from the player’s deployment area, which is the players’ stronghold. The players achieve victory when they reach the enemy stronghold and capture it by defeating all enemies in the stronghold, and they are defeated if enemies capture their stronghold.
  • Escape/Arrival: The GM establishes an Arrival or Exit Area on the battlefield, opposite the players’ deployment area. The players have a number of rounds to reach this Area before they are defeated, and the players only achieve victory when each of their units is in that Area.
  • Demolition: The players must destroy specific enemy structures in a certain number of rounds order to achieve victory.
  • Demolition Targets: These can be structures as listed in Mass Combat, or other objects like arcane sigils or trebuchets. Demolition Targets should be static objects that don’t move and don’t take turns, but have HP. You might also give them special features, like Resistance or buffs/debuffs to apply to adjacent characters.

Bonus Objectives

In addition to the encounter’s objective, the GM may make use of bonus objectives as optional goals that players can try to accomplish in order to achieve a greater outcome or reward. Bonus objectives do not need to be accomplished in order for the party to achieve victory in an encounter, but when the party completes a bonus objective, each PC gains one point of Determination.

Example Bonus Objectives:

  • Defeat a Specific Foe: The GM marks a specific enemy unit on the battlefield that the players must defeat before the battle ends.
  • Rout all Enemy Units: The players must defeat all enemy units.
  • Payloads: Payloads are size 1 objects on the field that may represent intel, supplies and gear, or other resources. Players must escort a certain number of payloads from where the GM places them on the map to certain Extraction Areas, Blast 1 areas on the map in order to succeed. Once a Payload is delivered to an Extraction Area, it has been safely delivered and disappears from the map.
  • Payloads only move when PCs take the Move Minor Action while adjacent to them, and the payload remains adjacent to the PC during the course of their Move.
  • Rather than starting at certain positions on the field, payloads may also be dropped when enemies are defeated.
  • Scouting Party: At the end of round 2 of combat, a scouting party appears at the edge of the battlefield and at the end of every succeeding round, it moves a number of spaces necessary to reach the opposite edge of the map by the end of round 5. Players achieve victory when they defeat the scouting party before it escapes.
  • Scouting Party: This is a Size 2 unit representing a small party of scouts. The scouting party begins Hidden, and at the end of its movement, the scouting party automatically Hides.
  • Arcane Beacons: The GM places a number of Arcane Beacons on the map equal to the number of PCs +2, and at least 5 spaces away from the other beacons. The players achieve victory by destroying all beacons by the end of the encounter.
  • Arcane Beacons project a Burst 2 aura of enfeeblement. PCs in the area gain +1 Difficulty on all Tasks.
  • Protect all Allied NPCs: The players must finish the battle without a single allied NPC being defeated.

The GM may also employ regular objectives as bonus objectives in order to create a dynamic encounter. For example, if an encounter has the Escape objective, you might use Demolition as the bonus objective, incentivizing players not to just sprint for the finish line, but to spend time attacking the demolition targets.

Balancing Encounters

The recommended number of enemy units in an encounter depends on the relative intended difficulty/importance of that particular battle. Each battle should have a number of enemies relative to the number of players, with every 5 chaff counting as 1 enemy, and every Veteran or Elite counting as 2.

  • Small Skirmish: # of enemies = 2 x Players
  • Important battle: # of enemies = 3-4 x Players
  • Climactic battle: # of enemies = 5-6 x Players

In general, the GM should not take more NPC turns than twice the number of PC turns, so in encounters where the PCs might face a number of enemies greater than 2 x PCs, you should keep surplus enemies as reinforcements. Even with reinforcements, the GM should try to keep the total number of NPC turns equal to 2 x PCs, so as to avoid deploying an overwhelming enemy force.

If the GM is bringing in reinforcements during the combat, the number of reinforcements should be included in the total of enemy units for determining encounter balance. If you are preparing an important battle for a group of 4 players, you might ready 15 enemy units in total for the encounter, but only deploy 8 at the start of the encounter and hold the other 7 back to use as reinforcements later on.

Reinforcements always deploy at the end of the round, and should typically enter the battlefield from demarcated Ingress Areas, so that players always know where reinforcements are going to appear.

NPCs in Combat

Most NPCs in combat will be enemy units, characters acting in direct opposition to the player characters and seeking to defeat them. Enemy units are always controlled by the GM. Sometimes, however, there may be NPCs in combat who are allied with the PCs and fighting alongside them. These NPCs are called allied units and may be controlled by the GM or by the players.

The GM always deploys enemy units first, placing them anywhere on the battlemap. The players may then place their characters in the Deployment Area on the battlemap, which is designated by the GM.

Like PCs, each NPC gets one turn in each round of combat, during which they normally take one Major Action and Minor/Free Actions. However, there are some restrictions on what NPCs can or cannot do in Combat which make them differ from PCs.

Turn Order

Enemy units never take the first turn in initiative, unless a special Feature grants them the ability. If there are more NPCs than PCs in a round of combat, initiative passes back and forth between PC turns and NPC turns until there are no more PCs, and then the rest of the NPCs may take their turns in any order.

Actions

NPCs each get a Major Action and two Minor Actions on their turn, but do not have access to the full range of Actions PCs do and may take only the actions listed in their statblocks and listed below. Most notably, NPCs by default cannot take the Console, Demoralize, Pinpoint, or First Aid Major Actions.

Minor Actions

  • Aim: Unit may re-roll a single d20 made on their next attack, keeping the second result.
  • Block: Unit or an adjacent ally they are blocking gains +2[CD] Temporary HP.
  • Brandish: Unit may roll an +1[CD] on the damage roll of their next weapon attack.
  • Climb: Unit climbs up or down a Height 1 obstacle. This counts as Voluntary Movement.
  • Draw Item: Unit may draw an item carried on their person or pick up an item within the same or an adjacent space as them. If an item does not require a Major Action to use, it can be used immediately, allowing them to draw and use the item with a single Minor Action.
  • Stand: Unit stands from prone, losing all effects of the status. A unit may not drop prone and Stand in the same Turn.
  • Interact: Unit interacts with an object in the environment. Particularly complex actions may require a Major Action instead.
  • Move: Unit moves up to their speed. This unit may not take this action if they have already used the Sprint Major Action this turn. This counts as Voluntary Movement.
  • Remount: Unit immediately climbs back onto a creature they were riding. This may only be done by units knocked Prone off their mount. This counts as Voluntary Movement.

Major Actions

  • Assist: Unit nominates an ally they can communicate with and declares how they are giving aid. During the ally’s Turn, roll the results.
  • Attack: Unit attacks.
  • Cast a Spell: Unit casts a magickal spell.
  • Disengage: Until the end of their turn, unit’s movement does not provoke opportunity attacks.
  • Guard: Unit finds some defensible position. Faith + Skirmish Task with base Difficulty of 0, or 1 if protecting an ally. Success increases the Difficulty of any attacks made against the unit by +1 until the start of that unit’s next Turn.
  • Hide: Unit hides. Difficulty 2 Agility + Intrigue Task (+1 if the unit is already engaged with an enemy). Success means that the unit is hidden from sight and cannot be targeted by attacks unless the enemy uses a Major Action to search for them. Can only be attempted while in Cover or far away.
  • Refocus: Unit regains their full WP.
  • Search: Unit searches for a hidden enemy. Difficulty 2 Awareness + Intrigue Task with a range equal to unit’s Awareness. On a success, the enemy is discovered and no longer gains the benefits of being hidden from the unit.
  • Sprint: Unit moves a number of spaces up to three times their Speed. The unit may not take this action if they have already used the Move Minor Action on this turn. This counts as Voluntary Movement.

Reactions

  • Opportunity Attack: When an enemy takes any Voluntary Movement while inside the unit’s Reach without taking the Disengage Major Action, the unit can make a single melee weapon attack on the enemy target.

Threat in Combat

Unlike in narrative play, the GM does not have a Threat pool in combat, and NPCs do not generate any Threat from rolling extra successes on a Task. NPCs may only gain bonus dice and extra actions from special abilities listed in their statblock.

When an NPC rolls extra successes when attempting an attack in combat, they may turn the number of surplus successes into bonus damage. For example, if an NPC rolls 3 successes against a defender’s 1 success, they can turn the 2 bonus successes into +2 damage.

If a PC or NPC generates a Complication on a roll, that Complication goes into effect immediately, applying +1 Difficulty to that character’s next Task.

Damage and Injuries

Damage and injuries are streamlined for NPCs, so that the GM has less to manage during a combat encounter. Some NPCs might be powerful enough to function similarly to PCs, but most NPCs are much simpler.

The following rules apply to NPCs:

  • Unless otherwise specified, NPCs only have a single health bar (their HP value), which is equivalent to their Brawn. NPCs do not suffer from Wounds when their HP is reduced.
  • Tier 2 units gain an additional point of HP. Tier 3 units gain an additional 2 points of HP.
  • If an NPC has more than 1 Health Bar (such as by being a Veteran or Elite), they can suffer Wounds following the same rules as players, suffering a Wound for each Health Bar they are missing from their Max HP.
  • NPCs are always defeated when they go down to 0 HP. When a player character deals enough damage to an NPC to defeat them, they may choose whether to do so lethally or non-lethally, killing the NPC or allowing them to live and be captured.
  • If they choose to defeat the NPC non-lethally, they generate 1 Threat. This is the only time Threat can be added to the pool during combat. It still may only be used during narrative play.

Recharge Abilities

Some NPCs will have abilities with a special tag: “Recharge [!]”. Once an ability with the Recharge tag has been used, it can’t be used again until the ability is recharged. At the start of that NPC’s turn, roll 1[CD]. If an effect [!] is rolled, the ability recharges and the NPC may use it on their turn again. If not, they may not.

Other NPC Statistics

The other statistics, such as Attack Targets and number of [CD] an attack deals follow the same rules as Player Characters. If an Attribute or Skill of an NPC is altered, it should alter the derived statistics appropriately. For example, increasing an NPC’s Skirmish by 1 increases the Target of their Attack by 1 and increases the number of [CD] their attack deals by 1.

NPCs always act as though they have a Focus when attempting Tasks in combat.

Size

NPCs may be bigger than a single space on the battlefield if appropriate to their type or to the story (e.g. a Monstrosity that is a wild boar might be size 2, while a Crusher that is a Giant might be size 3). Size 2 enemies are two spaces high and on each side, while size 3 enemies are three spaces high and on each side. Attempts to grapple Size 2 or 3 characters increase in Difficulty by +1 and +2 respectively.

Building NPCs

Ascension doesn’t provide a catalog of prebuilt NPCs for GMs to use in encounters, but rather provides a list of basic classes, templates, and features which can be combined to quickly create custom enemies of varying difficulty and skill.

Classes

When building an NPC, their class is going to be the first thing a GM will want to choose, as it provides their basic array of Attributes, Skills, Focuses, and attacks, as well as their basic Traits. If building an NPC who is an arcane mage, you might choose the Elementalist for their basic class, or the Bladesman class if building a soldier who wields a sword.

There are three tiers of NPCs, Tier 1, 2, and 3. When building an NPC, select its tier—some of the values of the NPC are determined by its tier, with the notation A/B/C, with A being its Tier 1 value, B being Tier 2, and C being Tier 3. For example, if an NPC has an Agility of 10/11/12, its Tier 1 form has 10 Agility, and its Tier 3 form has 12 Agility.

Each class also comes with Optional Features, which can be added to any NPC to increase the complexity and power of a unit. A good rule of thumb is that an NPC can have a number of optional Features up to its Tier. Many NPCs can have a Major Feature—these are particularly powerful and having one of them makes the NPC a larger threat, without changing its tier.

NPC tiers equate roughly to player levels:

  • Tier 1: Levels 0-4
  • Tier 2: 5-8
  • Tier 3: 9-12

When an NPC has multiple health bars (such as the Veteran and Elite described below), you can also give them an Optional Feature that is only enabled once they have been reduced by 1 or 2 health bars, making them a more dangerous threat closer to defeat.

Templates

If you want to customize an enemy further, you can give them one of the following templates in addition to their class: Veteran or Elite. These templates can make an NPC harder to fight, and can grant them the use of interesting other Features which can increase their power and complexity (see NPC Templates).

NPC Types

The different types of NPCs are designed to have unifying strengths and weaknesses that should allow players to strategize around. Each NPC class will have one of the following types:

Sword  NPCs have high Agility and usually have 6 Brawn unless modified by a template, making them weak to attacks that are defended with Brawn (e.g. Spears). Sword NPCs tend to have high movement speed, attack multiple times while dealing less damage on single attacks, and compensate for their low HP by being harder to land hits on.

Spear NPCs have high Coordination and usually have 6 Agility unless modified by a template, making them weak to attacks that are defended with Agility (e.g. Axes). Spear NPCs have long reach allowing them to threaten large areas on the battlefield, can pierce through armor, and are often mounted allowing them to have high mobility as long as they don’t enter difficult terrain.

Axe NPCs have high Brawn and usually have 6 Coordination unless modified by a template, making them weak to attacks that are defended with Coordination (e.g. Swords). Axe NPCs tend to deal very high raw damage, and their high brawn gives them large HP pools, but they generally have simpler abilities compared to Swords and Spears.

Bow NPCs have high Awareness. They tend to suffer in melee, making them weak to any sort of melee engagement once their enemy closes the distance. Bow NPCs tend to deal respectable damage at long range, and often are able to use other means to make navigating the battlefield difficult as long as they are standing.

Arcane NPCs have high Reason. They tend to have low resistance, HP, and poor counterstrike ability, making them the easiest NPC type to take down with targeted attacks, however they compensate for this for wielding long range spells that shred through armor. Arcane NPCs often are able to cast spells that target whole areas on the battlefield, and being hit by their spells usually cause a short term negative condition.

Light NPCs have high Faith. They tend to have respectable resistance and some means of melee combat, but their strength is their ability to support their NPCs by healing and buffing them with their spells. They sometimes can wield powerful offensive spells like Arcane NPCs, but usually are less versatile if they do.

Dark NPCs have high Presence. Like Arcane NPCs they tend to be easily killed with targeted attacks, but also are extraordinarily dangerous at targeted attacks with their shorter range spells that shred through armor and often inflict nasty status ailments. Dark NPCs also sometimes are able to inflict multiple characters with debilitating conditions at once.

Gauntlet NPCs have respectable Agility, Brawn, and Coordination. They often are able to switch up their attacks, being able to target any of Agility, Brawn, or Coordination with their melee strikes. They don’t tend to deal massive damage, but excel at grappling and inflicting short term negative conditions on their enemies.

Control NPCs have high Presence and low Skirmish. They don’t deal much physical damage, and instead focus on weakening/hampering their enemies, or supporting/creating opportunities for their allies. Control NPCs have mostly ranged abilities, and are weaker in direct melee.

Deploying NPCs

Sword, Spear, and Axe units should usually be the most prominent enemies on the battlefield, and they should usually be in roughly equal balance with each other. When placing enemies on the battlefield, it is best to clump these enemies together by type, e.g. placing a group of 2-3 Sword NPCs in one spot and a group of 2-3 Axe NPCs in another. This way, the players are able to effectively strategize on where to send their own Characters. If all NPCs types are mixed together, then this intended layer of strategy becomes redundant since all of the battlefield is equally dangerous for all players.

Use caution with Bow NPCs. They can be particularly devastating if there are too many of them placed in hard-to-reach places, such as behind ramparts of towers.

Likewise, too many Arcane and Dark NPCs on the battlefield may create an unfair scenario where the enemy is able to cripple the players before being able to close the distance.

Refrain from accommodating a poorly balanced party of Characters by not using enemies that they have no strengths against (i.e. designing battles without Spear users to make up for the fact the Characters have no Axe user). Finding ways to strategize party composition to be prepared for any sort of enemy engagement is the point of the game!

NPC Templates

Veteran

Veterans are experienced warriors, leading their fellow soldiers by command or through example.

Veteran Features:

  • Veteran: The Veteran has 2 Health Bars.

Optional Veteran Features:

  • Uninhibited: The Veteran may take a second Major action on their Turn.
  • Critical Blows: When the Veteran rolls Successes that exceed the Difficulty of their attack, they add +2[CD] for each excessive success.
  • Warrior’s Spirit (Recharges [!]): The Veteran activates this ability as a Minor Action. Until the start of their next turn, all Tasks they attempt gain +1d20.
  • Follow-up Blow: The Veteran adds +2[CD] to an attack against a target that has already been attacked this round.
  • Inspiring Leader: The Veteran can use a Reaction to allow an ally to reroll an attack.

Elite

An Elite is a powerful enemy, capable of taking on several opponents at once. If an Elite is in play, the Players’ objective is usually to defeat the Elite.

Elite Features:

  • Elite: The Elite has three Health Bars.
  • Vantage: The Elite takes two turns in a single round. They regain all uses of their reactions at the start of each of their turns.

Optional Elite Features:

  • Tough: The Elite gains +5 HP to each Health Bar.
  • Get into Position: At the beginning of their turn, the Elite can use a free action to order one ally within line of sight to move up to their Speed.
  • Inspiring Leader: The Elite can use a Reaction to allow an ally to reroll an attack.
  • Triumphant Shout (Recharges [!]): The Elite uses a Minor action to give every other NPC on the field +2[CD] on the first Attack attempted on their Turn.
  • Critical Blows: When the Elite rolls Successes that exceed the Difficulty of their attack, they add +2[CD] for each excessive success.
  • No Mercy: All of the Elite’s attacks gain +2[CD].

Chaff

Chaff are enemy units that are individually very weak, but become much stronger when operating in groups. All Chaff have the “Chaff” tag. Adding chaff to a battle allows for there to be many enemy units on the battlefield to simulate a large enemy force without making the odds of victory impossible, and the Chaff health rules make it possible for PCs to defeat more than one chaff at a time, making it possible to have an overwhelming enemy force without making combat take an egregious amount of time.

Group Health

Each group of Chaff shares a pool of HP equal to the Chaff’s individual amount of HP times the number of Chaff. For example, each sword Chaff has 4 HP, so a group of 5 sword Chaff would have a pool of 20 HP. Whenever an individual Chaff NPC would take damage, the entire group pool is reduced by the damage taken. Chaff do not suffer Wounds, and they cannot regain HP.

Whenever the Chaff HP pool is reduced by an amount equal to an individual Chaff’s HP, one Chaff is defeated. If enough damage is dealt equivalent to multiple Chaff, the equivalent amount of Chaff are removed. For example, if 12 damage is dealt to a group of 5 sword Chaff, two of the Chaff are immediately defeated.

Chaff are extremely vulnerable to area of effect attacks, because these attacks deal damage to each individual Chaff in the group, reducing the group’s HP pool multiple times.

Group Actions

With the exception of the Move Minor Action, Chaff can only take the Major and Minor Actions listed in their specific stat block. Up to 5 Chaff can act simultaneously on a single Initiative count, taking their Minor and Major actions together. Chaff may also make Opportunity Attacks.

Chaff can make Group Attacks, detailed in each chaff’s specific stat block. The effectiveness of the Group Attack usually increases based on the number of participating Chaff. A Chaff must be able to reach the target to participate. Opportunity Attacks made by Chaff can also be Group Attacks.

Adjutants

As commanders of an army, the PCs will have a vast number of fellow soldiers at their disposal to utilize in combat in the form of their divisions. However, circumstances may arise where the narrative demands a particular allied NPC join a battle alongside the party, or where a player might wish to play a different character in a particular battle, whose abilities and talents might be better suited to the situation. In these instances, players may choose to employ an Adjutant.

Adjutants are supporting characters that represent the lower-ranking soldiers under the PCs’ command, and when deployed may give the players an opportunity to utilize different skill sets in battle that their own PCs may not have in their party. Outside of combat, adjutants are allied NPCs under the GM’s control, but in combat, players control adjutants, either by using an adjutant in place of their normal PC in that battle, or by attaching an adjutant to their PC.

Players may have a maximum number of adjutants in a single combat equal to the number of PCs.

Adjutants in Combat

If a player is using an Adjutant in place of their PC, Adjutants have the same access to Minor and Major Actions as a player character and function identically in combat.

However, if a player wants to use both their normal PC and an adjutant in battle, they may choose to deploy their adjutant as an Attached Unit. Attached units begin the battle attached to each other and cannot be detached during the battle (unlike an attached division), and are made up of the Leading Character and Supporting Unit. Attached units occupy the same space, but only the Leading Character may take actions of any kind, and the player is always restricted to the same number of Major Actions per turn, regardless of who the Leading Character is.

Players may use a Minor Action to switch which unit is the Leading Character. If they switch Leading Characters after using a Major Action, using another Major Action would still require a Swift Task or Determination spend, even if they are using a different character to do so. Actions taken by a Leading Character do not count as being performed by the attached unit even if they occur on the same turn, so abilities that require a specific action to be taken—like aiming before an attack, or a swift task action that is made cheaper if using a Major Action to attack first—must all be performed by the same Leading Character in order to gain the benefits.

When beginning battle with an attached Adjutant, the PC always begins as the Leading Character.

When targeted by an attack, the Leading Character always attempts the Task to defend. If the Leading Character would suffer any damage as a result of an attack or hazard, their Supporting Unit also suffers the same initial damage result, but modified by their own resistance. If a Supporting Unit is defeated, they immediately retreat from the battlefield and may no longer be used in the scene, rolling once on the Injury Table at the end of combat as normal. If a Leading Character is defeated while the Supporting Unit still has HP remaining, they immediately retreat from the battlefield and may no longer be used in the scene (also rolling once on the Injury Table at the end of combat as normal), while the Supporting Unit remains and continues the scene as a normal unit.

Creating an Adjutant

Adjutants are always created using Standard Array Creation instead of the Lifepath, but they may have only 3 Focuses and 1 Value instead of 6 and 4 respectively. Adjutants also do not gain any narrative talents.

Adjutants level up with the PCs, and should always be at the same level as the player characters. However, Adjutants do not use the same level ascension chart as the PCs, and instead use the following:

Chapter Fourteen: Mass Combat as a GM

With the importance of war in Ascension, players are likely to end up marching alongside and commanding armies. Armies can play an important role in both narrative and tactical combat. This chapter provides guidance for GMs on how to use mass combat effectively in their Ascension campaigns.

The Players’s Army

In a game of Ascension involving mass combat, the players often will have one army that is their primary force over the course of the story. While its strength may wax or wane over time, it will remain as a core part of your encounter design for any mass combat scenario, and you should make sure to keep in mind its size and composition when doing so.

As the GM, you set the scale of the PCs’ army to what you think is appropriate for the narrative. If they are serving as a duke’s personal advisors, a scale 6 army would be appropriate. If they are an up-and-coming mercenary army, then a scale 3 army would be more natural. This can change and shift over time as the party’s power and influence shifts, in response to narrative developments.

You may decide what degree of influence to grant the players over the composition of their army. Some circumstances may call for giving them a fixed army made up of divisions you choose—such as serving as newly recruited commanders for a queen’s army. Others may call for giving them full agency over the divisions in their army—perhaps running a mercenary company or ruling as the council of a republic. It is up to you what best fits the game you want to run, but it is useful to keep in mind the impact the army’s construction can have on both the narrative and the combat balance. An army of only cavalry will behave very differently from an army with primarily ranged or support divisions.

  • Having too many divisions on the battlefield can slow the game down. For a given battle, try to limit the number of divisions in each army to one fewer than the number of players and take advantage of the scale bonus.
  • The more control over an army’s composition the players have, the more they will be able to tailor their force to their party composition. This will usually make them more powerful in battle.
  • Most officers, PCs and NPC alike, benefit from an infantry division’s buff. As such, it is generally recommended that ⅓-½ of an army’s fielded divisions should be some form of infantry.

Players should always have complete control over what stratagems they equip their divisions with, as this is how they can shape their strategy and strength.

Special divisions, such as mages or pegasi riders, can and often should be more limited. They may require specific allies or resources to train, potentially remaining unavailable to the players until they achieve certain narrative objectives (see Progression below).

Army Progression

Unlike a PC’s talents and abilities, the power to determine the strength or weakness of the player characters' army rests solely within the GM’s hands.

The scale and composition of an army is not a linear narrative progression and may grow or collapse over time. For example, your party may begin with a massive scale 8 army serving as the king’s entourage, only to midway through the campaign find themselves barely with a small scale 1 band of followers after the scheming archbishop has him overthrown. In order to regain a larger army and retake the throne, the players will need to work to rebuild their strength through accomplishing narrative challenges and progressing through the story.

Similarly, narrative beats can cause the number and kind of divisions an army has to fluctuate. Convincing a skeptical Thaloran duchess to join their side could allow the players to add a mage division to their forces, while earning the patronage of a wealthy Oriandi banker might allow them to upgrade the equipment of their infantry from light to heavy. Alternatively, alienating the Thaloran duchess may cause her lent mage division to abandon the army, forcing the players to either go on without that division or hire another division to replace it.

Determining the narrative progression of an army and its place in your story should be a conversation you, the GM, engage in with your players. While you will give the ultimate ruling on what your players will be allowed to have in their army, allow your players to guide the story. Particularly when it comes to the players suffering consequences and losing parts of their army/resources, it should only come about as the result of the story, ideally from choices that the PCs themselves made. For drastic consequences that would change the very shape of the story (e.g., beginning as captains in the king’s army and then losing access to their army after being framed and exiled for the murder of the king’s son), it may be useful to discuss those ahead of time, maybe even as part of your pitch for the campaign itself if it’s important to the plot beats you have planned.

Using the Army Narratively

When players are in command of an army, that army should affect not only the way they do combat but also the way they move through the story. Armies are full of people and have a lot of needs in order to be kept maintained, combat ready, and happy. In addition, armies are big forces with threatening presences, and having an army should impact the way player characters are perceived by other characters inhabiting the world. These are all aspects of having an army that can provide ample opportunity for interesting complications and challenges to arise outside of mass combat.

Outside of combat, Tasks that have to do with the army will arise as players make choices and attempt to accomplish things with their army or about their army that carry a risk of failure. These Tasks are no different from the regular rules for Tasks and Challenges, save that they may be impacted by the army’s Talents and Traits in addition to those from the PCs. In addition, having an army may introduce new challenges to what might otherwise be straightforward Tasks, due to the complexity of managing a great number of people. For example, a PC attempting to haggle for passage over a bridge that needs to make a Difficulty 3 Presence + Diplomacy Task might ask if they can use their army to intimidate the soldiers guarding the bridge. If they have a relevant Talent or Trait, the GM might simply allow them to succeed or to lower the Difficulty of the Task, or they might instead ask for a separate Task first to see if the army is disciplined or well-supplied enough to actually be intimidating.

An army’s Traits and Talents are not just there to provide mechanical benefits to Tasks and Challenges, but can also be a jumping off point for prompting action. Different divisions in an army can be utilized for different tasks outside of battle, like sending your Light Cavalry ahead to scout the enemy lines, or using your Mages to translate obscure texts, or using your military band to put on a performance in a city you are entering. Each division is also made up of individual people with their own information that can easily be pulled into scenes as needed. For example, if PCs need someone to run a message to a nearby city, or if they want to learn more about how a particular poison might work, they could ask for a soldier in their cavalry or their medical unit respectively to see to those things.

Having an army also introduces more opportunities for utilizing Ascension’s advanced rules. Major army activities such as long marches, sieges, or training are incredibly well suited for Extended Tasks and Challenges, mechanics meant to simulate long and arduous tasks that can’t always be accomplished by one person alone. And while armies are of course meant to do combat, their presence as merely a threatening force can be very useful in creating scenarios for Negotiation, as neutral parties unwilling to engage with the party’s goals become more willing to negotiate terms in the face of an overt threat. These situations are great opportunities to give PCs the opportunity to demonstrate leadership or be forced to make hard calls.

Armies do not merely create advantages for PCs to use during combat encounters, but are hordes of living, breathing people. While the army rules often abstract away from these individual people for the sake of the game’s playability, it’s important that PCs not take their army for granted or treat it as a set of buffs and nothing more. When the PCs are on a streak of successful combat encounters, introduce some Complications in the form of supplies running low, or soldiers becoming more eager to sack and pillage as they become overconfident in their successes. Similarly, if the PCs are feeling lost or have had a streak of failures, introduce soldiers from their army who can give them advice or prompt the party to remember their army’s Talents and Traits that can assist them on Tasks.

Most importantly, remember the Principles of Gamemastering. Your players’ army is not just a tool for them in combat, but a tool for all of you, and especially the GM, to create an interesting story.

Army Combat

With the exception of the presence of the army and the battlefield’s division into zones, running a mass combat encounter is generally the same as running small scale combat. Engagements are still divided into Sorties and Encounters, with specific objectives set defining the aim and flow of the battle. When running mass combat, it is most important to understand the impact that the presence of armies can have on the balance of a battle and the potential interactions it can add to an encounter.

Mass combat encounters can be used as part of the same Sortie as a standard combat encounter. The players may use their army to assault the stronghold of the treasonous count as one encounter, then in the next encounter engage in small-scale combat as they go personally to capture the count within their palace. How to use the presence of armies is up to you.

When to use Mass Combat

Mass combat is an opt-in element of Ascension’s gameplay that doesn’t need to be utilized in your story unless that’s something you and your players decide would be fun for you. Because mass combat adds more complexity to already complex tactical scenarios, GMs should be strategic about when and where they decide to use mass combat in their campaign.

Just because a party of player characters is commanding an army doesn’t mean they will always be with their army, and whenever a party gets into a combat encounter without their army nearby, the combat encounter should proceed without mass combat elements (and it goes without saying that whenever PCs enter combat without their army, any enemies they are up against shouldn’t have an army either). Similarly, even if the PCs have their army nearby but are attacking/being attacked by a smaller group of enemies that are acting without an army (e.g., a party of assassins have infiltrated the camp to try and steal an important artifact from the commander’s tent), the combat encounter should not involve mass combat elements.

The length that a battle is expected to take may also impact whether a battle should involve mass combat or not. Combat in general should be used to play out moments of decisive action: if the PCs are using their army to besiege a city and slowly starve it out, the bulk of that action should be played out through Extended Tasks and narrative challenges, while storming the city and breaking down its walls would be a suitable scenario for a mass combat encounter. If the city being stormed is relatively weak and doesn’t have an army present to defend it, then mass combat may not be necessary at all to represent the battle.

Building a Mass Combat Encounter

Because mass combat only adds an additional layer of complexity onto standard combat, building a mass combat encounter still requires all the pieces that a standard combat encounter will have: enemy units, objectives, and a battlefield.

Despite the mechanical and narrative complexity that mass combat may add to an encounter, the focus of any combat encounter, mass combat included, should always be on the actions of the player characters, utilizing mass combat mechanics to heighten tension and provide new ways for player characters to achieve their goals. As such, mass combat encounters should typically make use of the same objectives as small-scale combat. If a battle’s main objective revolves solely around one army defeating another, it may place the burden of victory on the fraction of the party with higher Authority skills.

Army-focused objectives make excellent bonus objectives, however, and can incentivize players to use their army in interesting ways.

Examples of army-focused bonus objectives:

  • Rout: The players have until the end of the encounter to achieve more victory points than their enemy. At the end of each round, players and enemies score victory points based on the number of Broken divisions on each side.
  • Break It Down: The GM marks at least one structure on the battlefield that the players must destroy within a certain number of rounds.
  • Capture Zone: The GM establishes a zone on the battlefield. The players must achieve control over that zone with their armies by a particular round or by the end of combat. Control is achieved by having a higher number of friendly divisions in the zone than enemy divisions.

The Battlefield

In a mass combat encounter, the battlefield should be divided into zones which represent strategic regions on the battlefield. As the GM, it is your job to divide the battlefield into zones, which can be determined however you’d like. If using a pre-drawn map, it may be helpful to use the map’s scenery and objects to determine how to place the borders of your zones. For example, if you are using a battlefield with a river and a road crossing it, both the river and the road would be natural places to draw zone borders. The placement of zones will not affect the movement of the PC or NPC units on the map, but physical structures or terrain effects on tiles will. If there is a wall on the battlefield, obstructing movement from one zone to another, PC or NPC units also cannot move over the wall without a flying speed or taking the Climb action.

When determining how many zones your battlefield should have, as a general rule, a battlefield should always have a number of zones at least equal to the divisions in the largest of the engaging armies. For example, if your players have an army with 5 divisions and the NPCs’ have an army with 3 divisions, your battlefield should have at least 5 zones. This may be different if you are using a map or scenario where it would make sense for the battlefield to be small and choked (like crossing blades in a tight mountain pass, for example). Also keep in mind how many rounds it would take for a division to cross from one end to the other. Most divisions are limited to one movement each round, so if there are 10 zones between where a division starts combat and where it may need to go in order to make an attack or accomplish an objective, it will likely not be able to do that within 6 rounds of combat.

A battlefield should have no fewer than three zones and no greater than ten. It is recommended roughly to have a battlefield zone be no smaller than 5x5 and no greater than 12x12. However, they can be shaped however you wish, so long as they are contiguous.

Balancing a Mass Combat Encounter

In most mass combat encounters, the opposing army should always have the same number of divisions as the party’s. The scale of your NPC army may be higher than the PC’s army if they are facing a much larger force, in which case each point of scale above the number of divisions adds +1 morale and +1[CD] to each division and their attacks.

The number of NPC units in a mass combat encounter should follow the same guidelines as a standard combat encounter. Because of the complexity created by mass combat and the scale of the violence a mass combat encounter is emulating, a mass combat encounter should always be an important or climactic battle, and have a number of NPC units as is suited.

Because interacting with an army often relies upon a high Authority skill, something that many NPC statblocks lack, mass combat also has a special NPC Template: the Commander. The Commander template, much like Veteran or General, gives NPCs additional HP and higher Authority so that they may give their army orders more successfully. The Commander template also gives an NPC unit the ability to give an army order and take a second action, making them powerful enemies. When figuring a Commander into your encounter’s balance, they should count for 2 enemies instead of 1.

NPC Armies

When designing an NPC army, you may compose it in whatever way you wish. However, an NPC army should be constructed with 1) the PC’s army in mind, and 2) to complement the NPC units leading it. If your players have an army made up of majority flying units, you may want to have at least one division of Bowmen, but you may not want to fill your army with projectile divisions, which will put your players at an extreme disadvantage. Strive to reward your players for what they’ve invested in, which may mean equipping your enemy army with divisions they will be strong against and divisions they will be weak to, but not stacking your army one way or another. In addition, your army should match and support the NPC units you are going to deploy in the encounter. If you add cavalry to your army, make sure to have mounted officers who can benefit from its buff. You also don’t want to add a siege weapon division without ensuring you have officers with high study.

It’s best practice to only give 1–3 divisions in an NPC army a stratagem. This decreases the amount of information you have to keep track of when running the encounter as well as allows the players to reap the primary excitement of using these tactical tools to bring themselves to victory.

NPC Template: Commander

Commanders are units specialized with giving orders to an army.

Commander Features:

  • Commander: The commander has 2 Health Bars and gains 4/5/5 Authority if they did not already.
  • Tactician: When the Commander issues an order, they may also take an additional Major Action.

Optional Features:

  • General: The Commander has 3 Health Bars instead of 2.
  • Braced: The Commander has +1d20 on Tasks to Brace.

Monumental Foes

A Monumental Foe is a special type of force unique to NPCs. While in most mass combat, the abilities of the army are divided neatly between officers and divisions, a monumental foe is an enemy powerful enough to take on full divisions, but still retains the fine control that allows it to act as an officer on the battlefield. These can be dragons, powerful archmages, demonic monsters, or anything of the sort.

Monumental Foes function as both general and division. On their turns, Monumental Foes may choose whether to take a standard action or perform a division attack instead. Monumental Foes always Brace against division attacks made against them, though they suffer the same restrictions when using the Brace reaction on attacks against other divisions. All Monumental Foes also begin with the Vantage feature, which allows them to take two turns in a round.

When adding a Monumental Foe to a mass combat encounter, it counts as a division for the purposes of determining the number of divisions in your NPCs army, and counts for four units for the purposes of determining NPC deployment.

Attributes and Skills

Monumental Foes are larger than life, and possess a unique ability to have attributes above the regular limit of 12. Some may have one, or even the occasional two, attributes at 13 or even 14. Rare and extremely deadly Monumental Foes may possess a single attribute of 15. However, rarely should a monumental foe ever have more than two attributes above 12.

Monumental Foes are still limited to a maximum of 5 in every skill.

Health

Monumental Enemies are unique in that they have both a standard 3 bars of HP as well as a morale equal to its own faith. The monumental enemy is only defeated when its HP is reduced to 0. Monumental foes begin with the Monumental feature.

Monumental: All damage against the monumental enemy’s HP is divided by half (rounded down). If its morale is reduced to 0, they lose this feature and take damage as normally. Any further morale damage is taken as willpower damage instead.
